In benchmarks the metric proved robust to visual degradations and stable within and across datasets, including out-of-domain data, where stable evaluation matters most.
arxiv-2605-07886:
Ziyan Li and Naoki Hiratani expose a hidden distortion in online learning, where a model updates as data streams in rather than training on a fixed set. Studying kernel regression, they derive a closed form for the function that online learning actually produces and compare it with the offline answer.

Online kernel regression, they show, is exactly equivalent to offline regression fed shifted, inaccurate target outputs: an implicit target shift baked into the teaching signal. Correcting for that shift, in closed form or iteratively, makes online learning provably recover the same predictor as offline training. On continual image classification benchmarks, online gradient descent with corrected targets even beat learning with the true targets.
arxiv-2605-08086:
Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Haochen Liu, and James Hahn survey how 3D rotations are written down in computing. Graphics, robotics, and machine learning all need fast, exact ways to store and update a pose. The choices include Euler angles, axis-angle forms, quaternions, matrices, exponential maps, and newer continuous and random forms.

The authors weigh each choice on smoothness, gimbal lock, speed, storage, blending, and how forms combine. They mix algebra with uses such as cartoons, pose tracking, guidance, and shape matching. The evidence favors quaternions, which are small and quick. Six-part continuous forms suit neural networks best. The survey is a hands-on guide to picking a form.
arxiv-2605-08186:
Wei-Ping Huang, Chee-En Yu, Guan-Ting Lin, and Hung-yi Lee unify a scattered practice: adapting generative speech and language models at test time by minimizing entropy. For classification the trick is well understood, but for autoregressive models, methods relied on separate heuristics such as teacher forcing with pseudo labels or policy-gradient reinforcement learning.

The authors derive the exact entropy objective for autoregressive models and show it splits into a token-level policy gradient term plus a token-level entropy term. Earlier methods appear as partial versions of that single formula. Using the Whisper speech recognizer as a testbed, the unified method improved results across more than twenty domains, including noise, accents, and multiple languages.
arxiv-2605-08286:
Hyunmog Kim builds a test for equivariant neural force fields. It finds how much fine angular detail a trained backbone keeps. Such models predict molecular forces while respecting rotation symmetry. A trained backbone may silently drop high angular detail. Fine chemical work needs that detail, so a silent loss is a real risk.

The test injects a controlled angular wiggle into the field. It freezes the backbone. A small prediction network then reports which parts can still be read back. On aspirin, recovery held at one spherical harmonic degree. It collapsed at the next. That cliff matches the predicted boundary. The pattern repeated across four independently trained backbones and a second metric. A finite-degree theorem calibrates the tool.
arxiv-2605-08386:
Ziyang Yu, Yongliang Miao, Liang Zhao, Bowen Zhu, and coauthors organize agent skills so they can be reused at the right size. Skill libraries let language model agents carry procedures between tasks. Flat, one-size prompt blocks create a bind, though. Coarse skills drag in irrelevant context. Rewriting a whole skill for each task is slow and costly.

SkillLens arranges skills in a four-layer graph. The layers hold policies, strategies, procedures, and primitives. Retrieval works at mixed granularity. A random walk over the graph expands the first matches. A verifier then accepts, splits, rewrites, or skips each unit. Compatible pieces are reused as-is. Only the mismatched parts get adapted.
arxiv-2605-08586:
Mamadou Keita and Christopher Homan argue that computer science conferences should require proof that reported experiments really ran. Current practice leans on self reported checklists, optional code sharing, and logs the authors control, none of which tie printed numbers to an actual run. They name the gap experiment nonrepudiation and state the security properties a valid protocol must meet.

Their working system, K-Veritas, written in Go, signs experiment reports without touching training data and already keeps a public registry of sealed records. The authors call for an open shared standard built with the community. Research publishing gains a concrete way to make results tamper evident and harder to fake or later deny.
arxiv-2605-08786:
Christopher Lohse and five coauthors find the root cause of system anomalies with PRIM, a meta learned Bayesian method that skips model fitting at test time. Root cause hunting is hard because errors propagate, causal structure is uncertain, and inference is slow. PRIM trains on a synthetic prior of causal models, learning to spot which mechanism changed between normal and anomalous periods while averaging over structural uncertainty.

Its transformer process attends jointly to normal samples, anomalous samples, and node structure, delivering answers in milliseconds for systems up to one hundred variables. On synthetic and two realistic benchmarks it rivals methods handed the true causal graph, and light fine tuning helps further. Operations teams gain near instant diagnosis.
arxiv-2605-08986:
E. Jafarov, S. Nagiyev, and J. Van der Jeugt solve one clean case of an electron gas in a wire. The wire is not the same in all ways. Its mouth is shaped like a wave spring. The electron mass shifts with how far it sits from the core. That shift breaks the wire's even form. They work the case two ways, the stock way and a non stock way. Wave forms come out in Laguerre terms. The split tone scale comes out with them.

The side part of the mass law also solves clean in the non stock way. Its wave forms use Gegenbauer terms, for both par states. Bound ties and odd cases close the work. Clean cases like this one ground gut feel. They also test the codes used on real wires.
arxiv-2605-09186:
Liding Xu, Yugeng Zhou, and Sebastian Pokutta ask whether language-model agents can speed up research on mixed-integer programming, a core method for hard planning problems. Testing an idea inside a solver normally takes much coding, fixing, tuning, and large test runs. Their 2026 paper places agents inside a harness built around SCIP, an open solver, so they can write, check, and test solver add-ons.

The test case asks agents to spot global patterns hidden in a model's constraints and build handlers that spread known values through them. On a standard benchmark set, the agents recover known patterns and produce working handlers. Inside a safe sandbox they also tune and debug their work. Five extra benchmark cases were solved by new spreading methods the agents found.
arxiv-2605-09386: Zero-shot text-to-speech clones voices never heard in training, and scheduling the generation steps matters. Dong Yang, Yiyi Cai, Haoyu Zhang, and others schedule kinetically optimally with moment correction for metric-induced discrete flow matching. The 2026 paper makes voice cloning faster and more faithful.

arxiv-2606-04086:
Chang-Yan Wang and Xue-Feng Zhang study in 2026 how two quantum strings, extended objects in a many-body system, interact when they are simply forbidden to cross each other. That hard-core rule alone creates an effective attraction or repulsion, but its form is hard to measure because the distance between strings is not a local quantity.

The authors show that full counting statistics, the complete distribution of a measured count rather than its average, captures this nonlocality naturally. They derive an exact formula by isolating the virtual process where the strings touch and hop back. The resulting potential is governed by the entanglement entropy of half a string, a link confirmed by high-precision numerics. They suggest the trick extends to other topological defects.
arxiv-2606-04186:
Nicholas Lee and colleagues report in 2026 a fast quantum chemistry method that runs in a few GPU hours. Their approach mixes a classical selected-configuration solver with quantum hardware, and neither side dominates.

The classical part picks the most important electron patterns. The quantum part then refines the energies for those patterns. For systems ruled by dynamic electron correlation, a regime where quantum methods usually struggle, the mix did well. It recovered over ninety-five percent of the correlation energy given by a trusted classical method. Accuracy matched the best classical tools on the test molecules. The authors argue the hybrid route is the near-term path for useful quantum chemistry.
arxiv-2606-04286:
Linsen Li, Aron Culotta, and Nicholas Mattei present a text-based causal method in 2026. It untangles which aspects of a service truly move its overall rating. Aspects tend to move together, so raw sentiment counts cannot isolate any one factor's effect.

Their method builds on a causal language model. It adds temperature scaling to calibrate who counts as exposed to an aspect. That tuning avoids over-adjusting for confounders, the hidden factors that muddy such studies. Tools to inspect the confounders found come with it. Tests used over six hundred thousand reviews of United States schools, plus semi-synthetic data. The method gave more reliable estimates than prior tools. Views of school leadership and test performance stood out as key drivers.
arxiv-2606-04486:
Zhao proposes a new way to watermark text from diffusion language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They do not write left to right like standard models. Watermarks embed a hidden statistical signal. The signal lets generated text be identified later. Most known schemes work locally. They nudge each next word based on the words before it. That design fits poorly when many positions are sampled jointly, as diffusion models do.

Zhao's watermark instead controls a global sketch. This is a compact vector that summarizes statistics of the whole sequence. Diffusion sampling can steer the sketch as text forms. Detection then depends on the global statistic, not on local contexts. The signal is order-agnostic. It is not a simple bias toward certain tokens. The paper analyzes the method's distortion, meaning how much it changes text quality. It also analyzes soundness and robustness against removal attempts.
arxiv-2606-04686:
Vercellino and colleagues test whether a small quantum computer can forecast how much cash ATMs will need, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum reservoir computing. Their framework uses parametrized four-qubit circuits as reservoirs, with partial measurement and reset. Only a classical ridge-regression readout is trained.

The quantum models do not beat the classical Prophet benchmark on mean absolute error or normalized mean squared error. They are more competitive on dynamic time warping, a metric rewarding matched temporal shape over exact values, indicating a partial ability to capture temporal structure.
arxiv-2606-04786:
Rossi and co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum chemistry, the use of quantum computers to model molecules. Their subject is ADAPT-VQE, an adaptive method that builds a compact trial description of a molecule step by step. At each step, the method scores candidate operators, meaning small changes that might improve the description, and then adds the best one.

The authors rewrite that scoring step using an exact change to the Hamiltonian, the equation that gives a system its energy. Their rewrite gives the same scores as standard fermionic Rotoselect, yet needs about half as many circuit runs on average. That saving brings its cost close to the cheaper gradient-based method. Benchmarks cover lithium hydride, beryllium hydride, and water, each at normal and stretched shapes. For lithium hydride, the weakest case, one pairing built an accurate answer while skipping the usual optimization stage altogether.
arxiv-2606-04886:
Chanda, Das, and Das explain a cosmological observation with friction, in a 2026 arXiv astrophysics paper. Results from the DESI survey prefer dark energy whose equation of state appears to cross the phantom divide in the recent past, behavior requiring phantom dynamics. Their scenario instead invokes dark energy: the quintessence field that drives cosmic acceleration loses a little energy to dissipation as it rolls. That simple ingredient produces both the evolving behavior and the apparent crossing.

The key result is economy: even weak dissipation of the quintessence field suffices to explain the current DESI observations. No phantom field is needed. Apparent phantom crossing becomes an artifact of ignoring dissipation when reconstructing dark energy's history from data. The paper adds a candidate to the rush of models answering DESI, and it makes a methodological point: the dark energy we infer depends on the assumptions baked into the reconstruction.
arxiv-2606-05086:
Chun-E Fu and Wen-Xuan Ma study how fermionic Kaluza-Klein modes mix in thick braneworld models under background perturbations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Braneworld models place our four-dimensional universe on a membrane inside a higher-dimensional space. Fermions spread into the extra dimension as a tower of Kaluza-Klein modes with different masses. For a still background these modes form a clean orthogonal set.

Perturbations vary along the extra dimension. Expanding the Dirac operator in the old basis produces nonzero overlaps between levels, adding off-diagonal couplings to the mass matrix. The authors resolve the states with a singular value decomposition of that matrix, preserving the five-dimensional chiral structure. They find parity-odd perturbations mix only same-parity modes and keep the symmetry. Parity-even ones mix across parity, break the symmetry, and polarize the mode densities toward the brane, lighting up dark modes.
arxiv-2606-05186:
Felipe Chavarro Polania tests staged factorial screening for budget-constrained micro-pretraining in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automated research loops must triage many candidate training recipes on shared accelerators before budgets are spent. Best-so-far searches can find better recipes, but they never reveal which factors, depth, width, batch size, or learning rate, actually drive performance differences.

On an autoresearch-derived single-GPU training loop, Polania ran 613 experiments. These included screens at two, five, and ten minutes, seeded reruns, anchor checks, and baselines, plus a 60-minute bridge package and continuations up to 24 hours. The penalties from batch, depth, and width were largest at short budgets and relaxed as budgets grew. Designed screens retained clear factor attribution after correction where random search offered none. The workflow is bounded and practical: screen briefly to find high-penalty directions, confirm anchors with repeated runs, then refine locally in the reduced space.
arxiv-2606-05886:
Filothodoros rewrites Bragg diffraction as the shadow of a polylogarithm in a 2026 arXiv paper. Diffraction peaks reveal a crystal's lattice, and the classic Bragg law fixes their positions. Real materials blur those peaks through finite coherence and disorder. The usual fix is extra broadening pasted onto the theory. Filothodoros instead sums weighted interference from many planes into one generating function. The polylogarithm's parameters carry coherence length directly.

Perfect coherence returns the standard Bragg law, so the old theory sits inside the new one. Shorter coherence reshapes peaks' positions, widths, and profiles from a single source. Peaks themselves sit at the function's boundary edge as its argument nears a branch point. That view ties diffraction line shapes to complex analysis. partly coherent or disordered materials gain a model with fewer ad hoc patches. The paper appeared in Physics Letters A.
arxiv-2606-06286:
Gianluca Barmina, Peter Schneider-Kamp, and Lukas Galke Poech separate two kinds of memorization in this 2026 arXiv paper on language models. A model can often be forced to recite training data when an attacker feeds it the right prefix. That is capability. Propensity asks a different question: does the model leak such data under ordinary prompting, when nobody is trying to extract it?

Their framework, PropMe, turns standard memorization scores into propensity scores by contrasting attack settings with everyday ones. A tracing tool, SimpleTrace, matches model outputs against full training corpora to find verbatim and near verbatim leaks. Testing two fully open models on corpora in two languages, they found a consistent gap. Prefix attacks drew out far stronger memorization than normal prompts, where leakage stayed rare. Continued training on partly new data also reduced how much of the older corpus the model could reveal.
arxiv-2606-06486:
Mingyang Liu and co-authors rethink what regret means when your opponent learns back in this 2026 arXiv paper on game theory. In repeated games, standard external regret compares your earnings with the best fixed strategy in hindsight. But adaptive opponents react to your history. That comparison misses the what if that matters: what would have happened had you played differently all along, with everyone responding? Their Repeated Policy Regret builds exactly that comparison.

The paper first finds necessary conditions for keeping this regret sublinear: limits on how much the comparator strategy may vary, and on both sides' memory lengths. Then it gives algorithms for a problem that is non convex in the strategy space. The payoff is end state quality. When everyone minimizes Repeated Policy Regret, outcomes can beat classical regret minimization, because the metric respects repeated play's history dependent reality.
arxiv-2606-06586:
Jonathan von Rad and co-authors teach models to remember facts in every language, not just English, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models trained mostly on English know many facts yet fail to state them in other languages, a flaw called cross lingual factual inconsistency. The team built PolyFact, a parallel question answering dataset of one hundred thousand Wikidata facts in twelve languages. On two seven billion parameter models they compared three fixes: light continued pretraining, supervised fine tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO.

Reinforcement learning won consistently. It improved both consistency across languages and recall in languages never trained on, while continued pretraining on parallel text added little. Looking inside the models, the training had reorganized their routing. Language specialization in the MLP layers and attention heads shrank. Shared cross lingual representations grew. The inconsistency, the authors conclude, is less missing knowledge than unreliable access to knowledge already present.
arxiv-2606-07586:
Li and co-authors teach an AI coding agent to deploy language models onto edge hardware by watching a human-guided run, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial neural processing units are energy-efficient chips for on-device inference, but porting a model onto one is labor-intensive. In stage one, humans guided an agent through deploying a 1-billion-parameter Llama model on AMD's XDNA 2 chip. It achieved speedups of 2-fold on prefill and 4-fold on decoding over an optimized baseline, while documenting lessons as structured notes.

Stage two distilled that documentation into an 8-phase agent skill system enforcing numerical correctness at each phase. The agent then deployed 8 models, from 0.5 billion to 4 billion parameters. Each took within 0.5 to 4 hours of wall time with no human guidance. All passed correctness gates; 3 matched or beat the reference deployment's performance. The authors claim several models had never run on this hardware through open tooling.
arxiv-2606-07686:
Rupasinghe and co-authors extend physics-informed neural networks, models that learn while respecting known equations, so they can also learn from written and structural knowledge, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their test case is microbial communities, modelled with generalised Lotka-Volterra equations that describe how species grow and affect each other. Equations alone miss outside influences that field papers describe in plain text.

The framework feeds in findings mined from peer-reviewed metagenomics literature, plus network structure between species, alongside abundance measurements. On real and simulated data from human and plant communities, the method beat the prior state of the art by up to fifty-three percent, even before knowledge was added. Adding the literature and network knowledge lifted accuracy further, by up to twenty-three percent on one measure and forty-seven percent on another. The inferred interaction networks also matched ecological roles reported in print.
arxiv-2606-07786:
Diao, Ding, Geng, and Liu analyse a spectral problem that arises when an elastic body turns invisible to an incoming electromagnetic wave, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The frequencies at which invisibility can occur are called transmission eigenvalues. For coupled elastic-electromagnetic systems the problem is mathematically delicate, since the governing equations are neither elliptic nor self-adjoint in the usual sense.

For general bounded domains with rough boundaries, the team proves the positive eigenvalues form a discrete set whose only possible accumulation point is infinity. For round, radially symmetric domains they prove a whole sequence of eigenvalues exists and derive how it grows. Along that sequence the electromagnetic parts of the vibration concentrate sharply at the boundary, while the elastic displacement spreads through the whole body. Gradient bounds quantify the boundary blow-up. The authors note the effect could seed super-resolution imaging methods for such coupled materials.
arxiv-2606-07886:
Roman, Siddiqui, and Busani study how yttrium iron garnet films crystallise on silicon, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The material, YIG, is prized for magnonic devices, circuits carrying signals as magnetic waves. Its structure supports long-range magnon propagation. The team deposited a film three hundred ninety nanometres thick by RF sputtering onto silicon with a silica buffer. It was then annealed in oxygen between seven hundred fifty and eight hundred fifty degrees.

Two sample sets separated the substrate's role: one had patterned hole pairs etched into the buffer as crystallisation seeds, the other was plain. Analysis showed the film is off-stoichiometry, rich in iron and oxygen, and that annealing changes neither that balance nor the substrate. Diffraction showed full crystallisation at eight hundred degrees for one hour in patterned samples. Plain samples were crystallising at seven hundred fifty degrees after three hours, evidence the seeds speed the transformation.
arxiv-2606-07986:
Navonil Deb, Younghoon Kim, and Sumanta Basu build valid statistical inference for the frequency-by-frequency wiring diagram of many time series, in this 2026 arXiv paper. For stationary series, a spectral precision matrix at one frequency encodes which components are directly linked at that rhythm. Testing those links is hard: Fourier transforms bring truncation and smoothing biases, and the complex-valued matrix breaks standard methods.

Their framework uses the full likelihood of neighbouring Fourier transforms rather than isolated ones. They construct a debiased complex graphical lasso estimator: a sparse precision estimate with its shrinkage bias corrected, at any chosen frequency. Its sampling distribution is pinned down, and covariance estimates pool information across neighbouring frequencies. The key is controlling all three biases at once. In simulations the method kept reliable coverage away from zero frequency and detected links with better power than the benchmark.
arxiv-2606-08086:
Jiannan Chen and Haiping Fu of Nanchang University construct measures that only ever move one way along the level sets of harmonic functions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is asymptotically flat three-dimensional manifolds with simple topology and nonnegative scalar curvature. Monotone measures are prized there because they underwrite key inequalities and notions of mass.

Their measures are calibrated against the model case. On spatial Schwarzschild manifolds, the geometry of a non-rotating black hole, they stay constant outside round spheres. The derivation follows Miao's strategy rather than the ODE analysis of earlier work. As applications, the authors recover and generalise known geometric and mass-capacity bounds. They also obtain integral formulas for the mass-capacity ratio. Whatever the measure does between two level sets bounds the geometry there.
arxiv-2606-08286:
Chu, Smith, and Pardo present an interface for exploring audio effects by browsing a map, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Audio effects shape sound throughout music production, but most software presents them as separate modules with parameter knobs, a layout that favors targeted adjustment over playful exploration. That separation makes it hard to build intuition about the wider space of possible sound changes. FXplorer instead organizes effects within a two-dimensional space informed by how the sounds are perceived.

In FXplorer, sound transformations become a continuous landscape that users can browse rather than a list of isolated presets. The system combines established spatial interaction techniques and familiar workstation controls with embedding-based methods for similarity and meaning-based search. Users can edit presets and slide between them interactively, moving from one effect character toward another. The authors aim the tool at composition, production, and live performance.
arxiv-2606-08686:
Suman Chabri and Anand predict the crystal structures of disordered alloys with an information-based neural approach, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chemically disordered alloys, including high-entropy alloys, pose a significant challenge for phase prediction. The number of possible atomic arrangements explodes combinatorially. Exploration of compositions requires an efficient way to search the potential energy landscape, plus a metric for how much of it has been covered.

They demonstrate alchemical Monte Carlo sampling, which swaps atomic identities to explore arrangements. It is driven by a graph convolutional neural network that predicts energies from atomic neighborhoods. Information entropy supplies the coverage metric for the explored landscape. They also evaluate a cheap structural descriptor, the bond disproportion vector, against a state-of-the-art overlap method.
arxiv-2606-09086:
Zhao and colleagues generate realistic citywide travel flows from the calendar alone, without historical trip data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Origin-destination flows count trips between regions and underpin transport planning, but fine-grained records are often missing. DynaOD builds flows from context. Its key idea is to model time two ways. Discrete directional trends capture shifts in city activity, like the morning rush. Continuous evolution captures how shifts unfold.

Jointly encoding both produces time-varying region profiles. These condition pretrained static flow generators in plug-and-play fashion, so existing models gain dynamics without retraining. The design also supports scale and transfer between cities. On large real-world datasets, DynaOD beat standard baselines on predictive accuracy and fidelity, meaning its synthetic flows match real flow stats, not just averages. The code is available. The work targets planners needing plausible data where sensors and surveys fall short.
arxiv-2606-09186:
Huang and colleagues build an AI that listens, watches, speaks, and thinks at once without freezing mid-conversation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Humans interact full-duplex: talking while listening, redirecting mid-sentence. Omni models handle speech, vision, and text in one serial pipeline, so deep reasoning or a tool call pauses dialogue, while shrinking the model to stay real-time guts its capability.

DuplexOmni splits into two layers running asynchronously in parallel. The interaction layer takes streaming audio and video and produces streaming text and speech with low latency. The thinking layer is pluggable, any large model or tool agent, consulted in the background, results folded into later responses. A Writer-Director pipeline makes the training data: overlapping speech, silences, interruptions, user supplements, delayed thinking feedback. Benchmarks are strong, behavior natural, with candid limits: video is thin for lack of data, and English lags because training speech is mostly Chinese.
arxiv-2606-09286:
Li and colleagues teach a humanoid to carry boxes, push carts, and ride a skateboard using only onboard depth, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agile interaction demands whole-body coordination: the object's dynamics change its balance and contacts continuously. Existing controllers lean on dense reference trajectories and perfect state information, collapsing outside the lab. VAIC uses only onboard depth, proprioceptive history, and decoupled commands.

Training uses two-stage distillation. A privileged teacher masters skills using precise object kinematics and exact states, only available in simulation. A student distills them, replacing full-body tracking with velocity targets plus an interaction indicator. A recurrent adaptation module infers unobservable object dynamics from depth and proprioception: what the object must be doing, from how the world responds. One policy then ran box carrying, cart pushing, and skateboarding, beating baselines. Train with omniscience, deploy with senses: a bridge from simulation to real robots.
arxiv-2606-09886:
Yuhao Zhang trims the expert pool of sparse mixture-of-experts models by grading teamwork, not solo acts in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models route each token to a few experts from a large bench. The whole bench must sit in memory, which makes big models dear to serve. Pruning cuts the bench, but old scores grade each expert alone.

Zhang's SHAPE treats a layer's routing traces as a joint game. A Shapley-style tally, drawn from real top-pick teams, credits each expert for what its team-ups add. A quality-coverage rule then keeps the smallest set that holds a set share of the good mass in each layer. A bisection step matches a set keep rate. On three fresh backbones, SHAPE held accuracy well at twenty and forty percent cuts, with no retraining. Peak graphics memory fell in step.
arxiv-2606-10086:
Battu develops a theory of how AI assistance changes a system's ability to keep exploring, in a 2026 arXiv paper on complex systems and cognition. His central variable is adaptive responsiveness: how well a system can still find new paths when conditions change. Systems evolve over rugged landscapes with many locally reinforced setups. Predictive AI can either replace exploration or amplify it, and the paper models both cases.

When predictive AI dominates, it substitutes for exploration, cutting responsiveness and causing early convergence, hysteresis, and collapse of exploration: systems grow efficient locally but rigid overall. In other regimes, the same help expands movement across the landscape. The swap effect hinges on starting routines, so weak explorers are most at risk while strong ones may gain. Long-run effects hinge on the setting and the design of use, not on AI power alone.
arxiv-2606-10186:
Das and Sarkar solve a battery of extremal problems for a class of analytic functions defined by an exponential condition, in a 2026 arXiv paper on complex analysis. The class consists of normalized starlike functions, whose images are star-shaped domains, singled out by requiring a certain derivative ratio to be subordinate to an exponential function.

They determine sharp upper bounds for the first three initial inverse logarithmic coefficients and sharp upper and lower bounds for the difference of consecutive ones. They also derive sharp bounds for a second-order inverse logarithmic Hankel determinant and sharp bounds for a third-order Hermitian-Toeplitz determinant. Finally, they fully solve the extremal problem for a generalized Fekete-Szegő functional with two parameters. In each problem the estimates are proven sharp, with extremal functions characterized in full, completing the coefficient picture for this exponential starlike class.
arxiv-2606-10686:
Rigas and colleagues rebuild a neural solver for pulsar magnetospheres in this 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. A pulsar's magnetosphere, the plasma-filled magnetic bubble around a rotating neutron star, is governed by equations that resist direct solution. A recent physics-informed neural network solver worked, but needed hours of training and heavy manual tuning. The framework swaps in Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, adds an adaptive training pipeline, and uses a physics-based convergence criterion instead of hand-set cycles.

Equation residuals fall to about a millionth in double precision, two orders of magnitude below the baseline, and convergence takes under twenty minutes in single precision. The solver handles stellar radii shrunk by up to eighty percent, where scale disparities defeat traditional solvers, and corrects the formula linking open flux to a key equatorial point. The framework is released as the open-source library PulsarX.
arxiv-2606-10886:
Nikulov argues that textbook superconductivity clashes with thermodynamics in this 2026 arXiv paper. The standard story says the superconducting state wins when its free energy drops below the normal state's. Nikulov claims that bookkeeping quietly credits a solenoid's power source with creating magnetization energy rather than field energy. Through the closed Gorter cycle, he adds, the Meissner effect implies negative surplus work.

On his reading, the equality of free energies at the transition in a critical field cannot be derived without breaking the second law. The field's faith in that law hid the contradiction for decades. He points to levitating magnets gaining height, and hence potential energy, at the transition as the visible symptom.
arxiv-2606-11286:
Wang and four co-authors present FreeBridge in a 2026 arXiv paper, a model of how single cells change under treatment. Imaging assays measure cell reactions to drug and genetic perturbations, but cells are fixed when imaged, so trajectories are unobservable. Modelers see only separate control and treated populations, the marginals, and must infer the transport between them. Matching endpoints alone does not pin down the intermediate evolution.

FreeBridge formulates this as a Schrödinger Bridge problem under endpoint-only supervision. Atomic states are segmented single-cell representations, defining a fixed cellular manifold. The model learns stochastic transport constrained within that geometry, using latent support regularization to keep intermediate states near observed morphologies. Across the BBBC021, RxRx1, and JUMP benchmarks, FreeBridge kept competitive or improved endpoint fidelity and mechanism-of-action retention under a unified protocol. On BBBC021 it further reduced support violations, evidence that geometric grounding matters.
arxiv-2606-11686:
Sawyer Zhang, Alexander Wang and Sophie Lei propose a sharper way to test software agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Judging a deployed language model agent by one overall success rate shows that it regressed, but not where. The authors split one production ordering agent into fixed layers, covering routing, intent signals, memory, safety and more, and test each layer separately.

Each layer gets its own assertion slice that runs in a deterministic pure mode with no language model involved. The full suite of 238 baseline cases runs in about two and a half seconds on every code change, against locked per-layer baselines. The team then deliberately breaks one layer at a time. The overall pass rate barely moves, dropping only a few points, while the matching layer's slice collapses by twenty-five to ninety-one points. Damage stays off other slices, and the pattern repeats on a second, different deployment.
arxiv-2606-11786:
Joanito Agili Lopo, Yunita Sari and Guntur Budi Herwanto improve translation for a low-resource language in this 2026 arXiv paper. Kupang Malay, spoken in eastern Indonesia, lacks the large parallel text collections that machine translation normally feeds on. Standard fine-tuned language models degrade badly on such languages.

Their model, Lius, is trained with instructions built from explicit lexical and semantic features drawn from a bilingual dictionary, so the model learns word-level knowledge directly. Training uses Continual Instruction Tuning, an iterative scheme that revisits instruction-based learning in rounds rather than one pass. On several evaluation metrics, Lius beats standard instruction-tuned models by four to six points. It surpasses dedicated neural translation systems and multilingual language models by ten to thirteen points. The model keeps its broader multilingual skills and handles sentiment analysis and question answering competently, though native speakers still rate its output below high-quality standards.
arxiv-2606-11986:
Niklas Elmqvist, Panagiotis D Ritsos and Peter W S Butcher rethink interaction itself for multi-device analytics in this 2026 arXiv paper, presented at NordiCHI 2026. Classic interaction models assume one person, one interface, one stable loop between action and display. Cross-device and ubiquitous analytics break every part of that picture. Their model borrows distributed cognition: thinking and information live across minds, speech, bodies, artifacts and devices.

Interaction becomes the propagation of information state across these substrates, not traffic through a single screen. Generalising data visualisation theory, they define input and output channels that carry state through substrates whose availability depends on context. A voice command, a glance and a hand-off between screens become comparable moves in one framework. The authors demonstrate it by reanalysing several ubiquitous, immersive and situated analytics systems, giving designers a shared vocabulary for systems where the interface is the whole environment.
arxiv-2606-12386:
Éltető and co-authors automate the scientist's hardest choice: which experiment to run next, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such modeling explains behavior with an explicit mechanism, not just predictions. Progress stalls when tests cannot tell rival mechanisms apart. Their framework, ATLAS, keeps an ensemble of sparse neural networks as living hypotheses about the mechanism. It then designs tests chosen to split those hypotheses as sharply as possible, and iterates.

They test it on recovering reinforcement learning agents, software learners like Q-learning, from bandit-task behavior. ATLAS invents varied experiment sequences with temporal structure tailored to each agent's traits. Models are scored three ways against the truth. Across all metrics, ATLAS needs five to ten times fewer samples than random testing. It also holds up against experiments designed by human experts from the literature. Automated design, tuned to competing theories, could speed such modeling far beyond cognitive science.
arxiv-2606-12686:
Kehoe and colleagues use deep James Webb Space Telescope spectra to study gas flowing into and out of distant galaxies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The galaxies sit at redshift near 3, so their light left when the universe was young. Outflows expel material and regulate star formation, while inflows supply fresh fuel. The team traces cool gas through absorption lines of iron, magnesium, and sodium in NIRSpec spectra.

Combining 3 surveys gives samples of 176, 197, and 315 galaxies per tracer. Outflow speed shows no significant correlation with galaxy properties, yet galaxies with detected outflows tend to have higher stellar mass and star formation rates. The clearest result concerns viewing angle: face-on galaxies show stronger absorption and faster outflows, while highly tilted galaxies more often show inflowing gas. This first such evidence at this distance matches winds launching perpendicular to galaxy discs, with fresh gas arriving along the plane.
arxiv-2606-12786:
Zhou and He analyse the well-posedness and stability of suspension bridge models coupled with Cattaneo heat conduction, comparing systems with and without viscoelastic memory, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The model couples a vibrating cable and a Timoshenko beam deck through elastic springs representing the suspenders, with thermoelastic damping from the Cattaneo law, which gives heat a finite propagation speed. Operator semigroup theory is the main tool for deciding whether solutions exist, are unique, and decay over time.

For the memoryless system, the authors prove well-posedness and polynomial energy decay. The rate is t to the power minus one half when a parameter ratio matches, and slows to t to the minus one quarter when it does not. They also prove exponential stability is unachievable under specific coefficient configurations. Adding viscoelastic memory changes the picture qualitatively: the memory system is also well-posed, but now achieves exponential decay.
arxiv-2606-12986:
Alenezi reviews the rise of AI-native software engineering and its effects on practice, education, and the workforce, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The paper draws together 48 peer-reviewed publications from 2016 to 2026, found and analysed through a 4-agent research workflow and checked against sources.

The synthesis is organised along 9 themes and 3 arcs covering practice, education, and workforce. A scientometric analysis finds an inflection in which annual papers on language models for software engineering grew 5-fold after late 2022. The paper adds a framework for AI-native practice around intent, collaboration, and verification; a 9-dimension competency model; a 4-phase curriculum roadmap; and an agenda of 11 research gaps. Alenezi stresses that the evidence on productivity effects is contradictory and context-dependent, so training engineers for judgment, verification, and orchestration, rather than code production alone, is the central challenge.
arxiv-2606-13286:
Mitsiou and Krikidis analyse error rates for quantum communication in this 2026 arXiv paper. They study phase-shift keying, a scheme that encodes symbols in the phase of a light signal, using phase-squeezed states. Squeezing cuts phase noise at the cost of more noise elsewhere, suiting a receiver that measures only phase. The authors adopt the Mark-II adaptive receiver, a realisable phase measurement. Their analysis builds on its phase probability operator measure in the Fock basis, the count of photon number states.

They develop routes to the symbol error probability. One derives the phase distribution from the squeezed noise and folds in the receiver's uncertainty through an angular convolution, a mixing of angle distributions. Because that step has no closed form, a second model produces a closed-form answer. Results show phase squeezing lowers error probability compared with coherent light, and the gains grow for larger alphabets.
arxiv-2606-13486:
Smits presents CRAFTIIF in this 2026 arXiv paper, an unsupervised framework for spotting anomalies in multivariate time series. Such data, many sensor channels evolving together, contain at least four kinds of anomaly: isolated spikes, sustained level shifts, changes in rhythm or frequency, and breakdowns in the correlations between channels. Most detectors handle only one or two kinds, and few explain which signals or anomaly type triggered an alarm. CRAFTIIF is designed to cover all four types at once, without dataset-specific tuning, and to stay interpretable.

The method draws hundreds of random analytic wavelet features from four wavelet families, each family targeting a specific anomaly character. Wavelets dissect signals by timescale, so spikes, shifts, and rhythm changes leave distinct fingerprints. An isolation forest then flags points that are easiest to separate from the bulk. Because features are organised by type and channel, a detection can be attributed to its cause.
arxiv-2606-13786:
Ribes Metidieri and colleagues revisit the moment when a small black hole, spiraling around a much larger one, stops circling and plunges inward. Such extreme mass-ratio inspirals are key future targets for space-based gravitational wave detectors. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies tilted, nearly circular orbits in Kerr spacetime, the swirling geometry around a spinning black hole, using catastrophe theory, which sorts the ways smooth systems suddenly change behavior.

The transition still obeys the same Painlevé one equation known from level orbits. The physical starting conditions pick out one special solution, called the tritronquée solution. The authors compare new analytic forms of that solution against direct numerical integration. Accuracy is similar, while the analytic form stays more stable in later steps. Level orbits match a fold catastrophe and tilted orbits a cusp catastrophe. Crossing fold lines slowly explains why the same equation governs both cases.
arxiv-2606-13886:
Chandra, Damodaran, and Wang add a physics safety net around robot control models without retraining them. Vision-language-action models map camera views and instructions straight to robot actions, yet they learn by copying demonstrations and can command impossible moves. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents PhysVLA, a plug-in wrapper that checks each predicted action at run time and corrects it only when needed, adding under one millisecond per step.

Two layers do the work. A phase-aware state machine splits tasks into approach, grasp, transport, and place. A selective Euler-Lagrange gate, based on rigid-body motion equations, switches on only when a dynamics check flags inconsistency. Across four backbones on LIBERO-Spatial tasks with a Franka Panda arm, success rose by up to seventeen points and stability by nineteen. Efficiency improved by up to fifteen percent. On a real Agilex Piper arm, success gains reached fifty percent.
arxiv-2606-14086:
Chen and colleagues make speech emotion recognition explain itself, then fix the noisy labels teaching requires. Explainable systems cite speech emotion descriptors: prosodic features like pitch and volume, plus speaker traits like age. Reliable descriptor labels are scarce, so training data is annotated automatically and imperfectly. Their 2026 arXiv paper adds two post-training tools: a confidence score selecting trustworthy data, and reinforcement learning rectifying descriptors on the fly.

Experiments ran on IEMOCAP and MELD, two standard benchmarks. Systems using either component beat baselines with no selection or rectification. The best system, integrating both, gained two point nine percent absolute on IEMOCAP, three point seven percent relative. On MELD the gain was three point three percent absolute, five point four percent relative. Label quality, handled by selection and live correction together, matters as much as model design for SER.
arxiv-2606-14286:
Van Deyck, Van Acker, Chaffey, and Van Hertem let an optimizer decide how many DC breakers a future power hub needs, and where. Multiterminal high-voltage DC grids will need switching stations joining converters and lines, but a DC fault can cascade into large outages, and breakers are expensive. Current practice picks from pre-defined protection strategies. Their 2026 arXiv paper formulates a mixed-integer linear optimization minimizing protection cost plus fault-impact risk.

It designs the connectivity of external connections and the breaker arrangement inside the station, across many operating conditions. A case study with six external connections used a year of pre-fault power flow scenarios. The method outputs the optimal breaker count, given component failure rates and breaker cost relative to fault impact, and each additional breaker's marginal risk reduction, showing where spending stops paying. Sensitivity analyses show how cable failure rates and breaker costs shift the optimum.
arxiv-2606-14386:
Xia and Wang build a 2026 arXiv theory of why machine aided discovery stalls. Their setup mixes local search with large language models. The models propose bold new hypotheses. The authors argue that fresh ideas stop helping when they add no new information. This can happen even when the idea space still looks large.

They state a search compression claim with three parts. First, the explored ideas must compress. Second, the new idea must escape the span of what was explored. Third, it must still point toward the target signal. Tests support the claim. The team used synthetic setups, Chinese stock factor files, and symbolic regression tasks. Random jumps widened coverage but did not raise yield. Directed jumps helped only in thinly covered spots that held real signal.
arxiv-2606-14586:
Xiang, Zhang, and Mao make self-supervised image representations readable in a 2026 arXiv paper. Self-supervised learning extracts useful features from unlabeled images, but those features stay opaque vectors that people cannot inspect. Their framework, S2COPE, instead describes each image as a set of concepts written in natural language.

A vision-language model proposes candidate concepts for an image. A self-supervised objective then scores how well each concept fits that image while distinguishing it from others, and the feedback becomes preference data that trains the model to propose better concepts. Across eight diverse visual datasets, the concept representations transferred without adaptation and beat earlier interpretable approaches on downstream recognition. In medical imaging, the discovered concepts exposed spurious visual cues and supported a more robust classifier, showing self-supervision can yield human-readable representations.
arxiv-2606-14786:
Fan and co-authors detect copied videos at platform scale in a 2026 arXiv paper. Video platforms must spot reproduced content to protect creators and keep recommendations diverse, beyond filtering harmful material. Their production system, MatchLM2Lite, judges pairs of videos using video, audio, and text signals to produce fine-grained reproduction scores.

A high-capacity multimodal language model, MatchLM, acts as teacher and sets the performance ceiling. Its skill is then distilled into MatchLite, a compact student built for low-latency, high-throughput inference inside real-time recommendation systems. The teacher improved the F1 score by a wide margin over the previous production model, and the student retained most of that gain while cutting computing cost roughly thirty-five-fold. Deployed at scale with end-to-end latency under thirty seconds, the system reduced the reproduced video view rate measurably without hurting engagement.

Biondini and coauthors derive a modulation theory for lump waves in the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation in a 2026 study. Lumps are stable, fully two-dimensional localized waves of the KPI equation, unlike its unstable line solitons. A slowly varying mean field can bend and reshape a lump as it travels. No Whitham-style theory existed for such genuinely two-dimensional structures.

The authors derive a system of four hyperbolic equations describing how lump parameters evolve with the mean field. The system passes the Haantjes tensor test for integrability and admits a Hamiltonian form for steady mean fields. A reduction then treats a lump meeting a rarefaction wave in the mean field. Sharp conditions decide whether the lump passes through or gets trapped inside the wave. A lump moving horizontally is transmitted only when its starting amplitude clears a stated threshold. Numerical simulations of the full equation match the predictions closely.

Yu develops a bookkeeping framework for the Navier-Stokes regularity problem in a 2026 analysis paper. The equations govern fluid motion, and whether their solutions can form singularities remains open. A singular point must dodge the smallness regime at every scale, through windows. The paper answers with an audit that tracks critical quantities across windows.

The audit shows persistent badness cannot survive free of charge. It must generate untaxed critical supply or accumulate leakage from cutoffs and pressure tails. A second theorem transfers a clean model's regularity gap back to Navier-Stokes solutions. The transfer needs three structural inputs, including stability of a quotient construction. Every residual that could obstruct it is itemized as a ledger entry. The upshot is a conditional reduction, not a regularity proof. Any surviving singularity must be an organized, reproducible defect cascade, or defeat the controls. That narrows where a proof or a counterexample must aim.

Huong, Duy and Dong propose a dark-sector model in a 2026 particle theory paper that tackles two puzzles at once. Neutrinos have tiny but nonzero masses, which the Standard Model cannot explain. Dark matter, the unseen mass shaping galaxies, also needs a stable particle candidate. Their framework links both puzzles through one new dark gauge symmetry.

The model uses an inverse seesaw, where light neutrino masses are suppressed by a small parameter. Instead of inserting that smallness by hand, the parameter arises from corrections by dark fields. When it vanishes, lepton number symmetry returns, so its small size is natural in the technical sense. The same dark symmetry keeps the dark matter candidate stable. Günther and colleagues argue for explanation cards in a 2026 paper on explainable machine learning. Tools that explain algorithmic decisions often mislead quietly: what an explanation seems to say is not what it actually shows. Some popular methods are even uninformative about how a complex decision function behaves, yet users cannot tell from the output alone.

An explanation card would travel with each explanation, adding facts about robustness and validity plus plain reading instructions. That shifts the burden from users, who now must guess the limits, to providers, who must state them up front. Worked examples show how to build cards for counterfactual explanations, which describe what would need to change, and for SHAP, which credits input features. A tiny stability region around a counterfactual, for instance, warns a loan applicant that the suggested change is nearly unreachable. Cards also link to duties under the European AI Act.

bernard-gui-practica-inquisitionis-1886:
Bernard Gui, inquisitor of Toulouse from 1307 to 1323, wrote the Practica Inquisitionis, the Practice of the Inquisition into Heretical Depravity, around 1323. Célestin Douais edited the Latin text in 1886. Gui's manual is the working handbook of the medieval Inquisition, written by its most famous practitioner at the height of his career.

Five parts give the forms for citations, arrests, and sentences, and the questions to put to each kind of heretic. Gui describes the beliefs and rites of Cathars, Waldensians, Beguines, and Jews with a clerk's cold care. burns-poems-chiefly-scottish-1786:
Robert Burns was a young Scottish farmer who wrote poems in the Scots dialect he spoke at home. Friends paid to print his first book at Kilmarnock in 1786. The volume made him famous across Scotland almost at once.

The poems mix humor, tenderness, and anger at hypocrisy. Well-known pieces include To a Mouse, The Cotter's Saturday Night, and Holy Willie's Prayer, a sharp satire on false piety. Burns writes about mice, lice, prayers, and ploughmen with equal care. This first edition, often called the Kilmarnock edition, is the landmark book that launched Scotland's national poet.
cagliostro-memorial-1786:
Alessandro, Count di Cagliostro, stood at the center of the Affair of the Diamond Necklace, the scandal that shook the French court in 1785. This Memorial, printed at London in 1786, is his legal brief in that affair. It is the primary document of the eighteenth century's most notorious occultist at his moment of trial.

Cagliostro pleads his innocence in the theft of the great necklace meant for Marie Antoinette. His story mixes high society, forged letters, and his own Egyptian Masonry. Adventurer, healer, and accused fraud, he writes to save his name and life. The memorial lets readers judge the count in his own words. Henri de Curzon edited La Règle du Temple at Paris in 1886 for the Société de l'Histoire de France. Its hundreds of clauses order prayer, meals, dress, discipline, and battle conduct for the brothers. Curzon's edition became the standard one, cited by every modern history of the order since.
