Cells with the risk form stored more fat droplets yet survived the fat stress better than normal cells. Gene activity patterns differed by form, and mixed-form cells sat in between. The authors offer the system as a precise platform for studying gene-linked liver disease.
pmc-13357086:
Ya Zhou and co-authors studied in 2026 how a long non-coding RNA called LINC00665 helps breast cancer cells dodge death. Such RNAs steer cancer growth but make no protein. Using binding predictions and lab assays, the team traced how an RNA-tagging enzyme raises this RNA and how it acts on other molecules.

The tagging enzyme METTL16 boosted LINC00665 through chemical marks. Silencing LINC00665 slowed breast cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion, and raised cell death. The RNA soaks up a small regulator, freeing a partner protein that drives malignant behavior; restoring that protein undid the silencing effect. The chain offers new targets against breast cancer spread.
pmc-13358586:
Do-Hyun Kim and co-authors compare workout plans for women after menopause in a 2026 study from South Korea. Seventy-four women who were overweight or obese trained for 12 weeks. Groups exercised at moderate pace, at hard pace, or a mix of both, while a fourth group did not train. All training groups burned the same weekly energy by design.

Fitness, measured by peak oxygen use, rose in every exercise group compared with the control group. Weight and body mass index also fell in all three training groups. The study suggests that for these women, steady training matters more than the exact pace, as long as the total work is matched.
pmc-13358786:
Bruno Valle Pinheiro and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on freeing patients from breathing machines. A machine that breathes for a patient saves life, but the diaphragm, the main breathing muscle, weakens fast when the machine does all the work. That weakness then makes it harder to stop the machine, a trap the authors call a self-feeding cycle.

They argue for settings that keep the diaphragm working at a safe level: not idle, but not strained either. Too much help wastes the muscle; too little can injure it. Their piece guides intensive care teams toward a middle path that protects the muscle while the lungs heal.
pmc-13360786:
Suheda Atas Ipek led a 2026 real-world study of sorafenib for thyroid cancer that no longer answers to radioactive iodine. This cancer type is called differentiated thyroid cancer, and sorafenib is a key drug once the iodine route fails. The team gathered 176 patients treated across 16 centers between 2000 and 2024. They tracked spread sites, dose cuts, blood inflammation markers, and a thyroid protein level before treatment.

Patients were followed for a median of 24 months, and the median time before the cancer grew again was 21 months. The team used survival curves and layered tests to find which traits predicted a better or worse course. Real-world data like this show how a drug performs outside trials, in older and sicker patients. The results can help doctors set honest expectations and spot who needs closer watch.
pmc-13361086:
Diana Tatarciuc and co-authors review heat-proof antioxidant enzymes as future drugs in a 2026 paper. Enzyme drugs often fail because they fall apart at body conditions. Enzymes from heat-loving microbes, or built by protein engineering, keep working under stress. They are already common in industry, but their medical use is scattered and mostly early-stage.

The review sorts proven enzyme drugs from hopeful lab candidates. Animal studies give early proof that sturdy antioxidant enzymes can help in heart disease, brain disease, and inflammation. The authors judge what stands between these results and real patient care, such as dosing, safety, and delivery. Their map aims to help drug developers pick the candidates most worth pushing forward.
pmc-13362186:
Haochen Ni and co-authors review plant nanocrystals as stabilizers for advanced emulsions in a 2026 paper. Cellulose nanocrystals are tiny rods spun from plant fiber. They can hold oil and water together in Pickering emulsions, where solid particles, not soaps, keep drops apart. In pure form they cling poorly to oil, so the emulsions break under stress.

The review covers two fixes. Chemical changes tune the crystals' surface charge, water liking, and grip at the oil boundary. Partner materials can also team up with the crystals, building stronger films around drops or webs in the liquid. Such stable, plant-based emulsions suit carrying health compounds in foods. The authors map design choices for makers of greener delivery systems.
pmc-13362486:
Su-Jin Kim and colleagues report a 2026 trial of electric muscle stimulation for adults with night leg cramps. Twenty adults took part: half used a device that sends mild pulses to both calves, and half did static stretching instead. Both groups trained three times a week for four weeks, and the team measured how much stimulation it took to trigger a cramp, plus pain scores.

Both groups improved, but the device group improved much more. Their cramps took far stronger stimulation to trigger, and their pain scores dropped further than the stretching group's. The trial is small, yet it suggests the device could offer a drug-free way to ease night cramps, a common sleep disruptor for older adults.
pmc-13362586:
Sandra Yi Cheng Chee and colleagues report a 2026 study of airway shape and throat tissue size in 404 Singapore children aged 7 to 11. They visited a national dental center for braces care. Narrow airways and swollen tonsils or adenoids raise the risk of disordered breathing in sleep. The team read head X-rays taken from the side and set fresh local norms for airway and face measures.

Airway measures shifted with age, sex, and jaw pattern. Enlarged tonsils and adenoids together showed in about half the children, and enlarged tonsils alone in about a third. The local norms give dentists and sleep doctors a fair yardstick for judging Asian children's scans, and the high rates argue for routine airway checks.
pmc-13362986:
Jean-Claude Lavoie and Ibrahim Mohamed wrote a 2026 review on adding glutathione to the IV feeding of preterm babies. Babies born early face heavy oxidative stress from oxygen therapy and IV nutrition, and their stores of glutathione, a key protective molecule, run low. That stress is tied to lung, eye, and gut damage. The review weighs the proof for topping up glutathione through the feeding line itself.

The authors argue for the oxidized form of the molecule, which suits IV use, and they review lab proof that it lowers oxidative stress plus the safety record so far. Shielding the feeding bags from light helps some, they note, but not enough. They conclude the time has come to adopt the supplement.
pmc-13364486:
Yerzhan Imanbayev and co-workers test 2026 waste plastic as a cheap add in for road tar in Kazakhstan. Roads there crack in cold and rut in heat, while trade polymers cost too much. The team blends two common waste plastics into hot tar and checks strength and heat life.

A dose near one to one and a half parts in a hundred gave the best gains in rut defense and stiffness. One plastic mixed more smooth, the other gave more heat strength. Blends with a trade stretch polymer beat state norms by wide gaps. The route recycles waste into longer lived roads.
pmc-13366386:
Petra Czarniak and co-authors systematically review which medications switch the pregnane X receptor on or off. This receptor controls genes that break down and excrete drugs and toxins, and it also influences fat and sugar metabolism. Their 2026 review searches five databases and follows standard systematic review guidance.

From more than twelve thousand screened records, 101 studies met the criteria, supplemented by further research and review articles. Forty-two studies covered prescription drugs and forty covered non-prescription products that regulate the receptor. Forty-seven studies reported effects of this regulation on diseases including cancers, metabolic conditions, and inflammatory disorders, in both beneficial and harmful directions. The authors conclude that many common drugs alter the receptor with clinically relevant consequences, such as changed drug efficacy, but that the potency of most regulators is still poorly quantified.
pmc-13366486:
Yifan Cui and co-workers grow in 2026 a live build stuff from the slime of a soil germ, a stuff that can grow itself. Most live stuffs trap live cells in dead frames, which caps growth. This slime flows for print, firms on cure, and feeds cell growth.

Cross links and clay or gum adds tune its stiff rank by more than ten fold. Print forms hold sun germ cells that live and grow for a month, and the frame spreads to fill its shape. The stuff could yield self grow coats and green build parts.
pmc-13369186:
Ahmad Ramazani and co-workers test in 2026 concrete slabs built to block rays still well after a hard air blast near a nuke site. Blasts crack slabs, and cracks leak rays. The team first reads ray pass through whole slabs, blasts them, then reads the pass a new.

A tuned mix of stone dust, fibers, and heavy sand lifts strength and cuts ray pass in whole slabs. A spiral core wrap adds more: slabs with both tricks take blast with near no harm and keep most of their ray block. Mix lone slabs leak far more post blast.
pmc-13370786:
Axioti and colleagues build drug-delivery polymers that use far less polyethylene glycol, or PEG, than usual, in 2026 materials research. The best variant, built from diglycerol, hexanediol, PEG, and divinyl adipate, raised curcumin's solubility through encapsulation. Tests in intestinal and breast cancer cell lines, plus whole-animal models in worms and fruit flies, supported biocompatibility and stability. Axioti presents the design as a tunable, greener platform for drug delivery.
pmc-13371286:
Sona Shrestha and Vishnu Khanal studied early breast feeding in the hills of Karnali, Nepal, in a 2026 survey. They asked 423 mothers of young children aged six to 23 months how feeding began after birth. Two points were checked: a first feed in the first hour, and breast milk only for the first two days.

Babies born small, born at home, or born to mothers with health trouble were less apt to get milk only. Help from a trained birth worker raised the odds. The results point to home births and small babies as groups that need more support in the first days of life.
pmc-13373786:
Tamara C Borsboom and co-authors probed sex gaps in a swollen chest artery in a 2026 study. Tissue and blood came from 32 patients who had the swollen part cut out, at a mean age near 66. Two sound aortas served as a base for checks.

Waals were scored for spring fiber loss, gel build-up, muscle cell order, and scar change. Stains and blood hormone reads were added to the mix. The swollen width was much the same in men and women. Yet women's walls showed more worn change. Sex-linked paths may drive the ill in part, and care may one day need to split by sex.
pmc-13375586:
Krithik Vishwanath and co-authors set plain smart tools next to clinic tools in a 2026 test. Two clinic aides built for doctors were tried next to three top plain models. Tests held 500 exam asks, 500 health guide asks, and 100 true asks from ward work.

Twelve US doctors scored 1,800 pairs of replies, blind to which tool wrote which. The plain models won in all three tests. The clinic aides trailed, though they are sold for ward trust. The team says paid clinic wraps need their own open proof, not trust by name, before wards lean on them for calls.
pmc-13378886:
Mustafa A Hammad, Wasef Alhroub, and Ahmad Isaid report a 2026 case of a rare inherited muscle condition in a six-year-old boy. His parents are related by blood. From birth he had drooping eyelids and limited eye movement, and he developed slowly worsening weakness in the muscles near his shoulders and hips.

Brain scans and metabolic tests were normal, which made the cause hard to pin down. Gene sequencing found a new change in a gene called MYH2, which builds a protein used by skeletal muscle. pmc-13379386:
Azad and colleagues describe patients with oral potentially malignant disorders, mouth lesions carrying a raised risk of turning cancerous, at a dental school in Alborz, Iran, in 2026 oral health research. The combined retrospective and prospective cohort included 50 patients diagnosed between 2019 and 2025, with standard checklists, examinations, and tissue analysis recording lesion type, site, risk factors, and change over follow-up. Women made up 64 percent of the population, and most patients were aged 40 to 60.

The commonest lesions were plaque-type oral lichen planus and, next, non-homogeneous leukoplakia, favoring the cheek lining and tongue. A burning sensation troubled 52 percent of patients at presentation. Microscopy showed lichenoid mucositis in 86 percent of patients, while mild dysplasia, the precancerous cell change, appeared in only 7 percent overall but in 57 percent of leukoplakia cases specifically. At follow-up, 80 percent of patients still had persistent lesions despite corticosteroid treatment, underscoring the need for long-term surveillance.
pmc-13381986:
Azindokht Babapour and colleagues report a 2026 study on freezing rooster semen without losing its quality after thawing, an important tool for conserving poultry breeds. Freezing often damages sperm. The team tested two sugars, trehalose and sucrose, as protectants that stay outside the cells, allowing a lower dose of a standard chemical protectant.

Semen from Green-legged Partridge roosters was frozen in straws under several sugar recipes. After thawing, movement, membrane health, DNA damage, and stress-related measures were assessed with automated and lab methods. Trehalose at the higher dose gave the best overall profile, with better movement and less DNA damage. Responses varied by measure, which the authors discuss.
pmc-13382286:
Sushil Mankar and co-authors present a 2026 case of a benign but locally aggressive bone tumour that kept returning in a man's knee over more than a decade. The tumour sat in the outer part of the thigh bone just above the knee, an uncommon spot for it. Standard limb-saving treatment scrapes the tumour out thoroughly, treats the cavity, and fills it with bone cement.

The patient first had that operation in 2012 after six months of knee pain and trouble walking. The tumour returned two years later, and again after further surgery. The report follows his repeated joint-preserving operations and long-term outcome, an area the authors note is rarely documented beyond ten years.
pmc-13385986:
Wang and co-authors test whether language models can classify why patient safety incidents happen. Their 2026 study fine-tuned four open-source models, BERT, LLaMA2, GPT2, and Phi-2, on real investigation reports from public health systems. Domain experts had labelled 300 reports containing 1,338 contributing factors, sorted into twelve categories across six system levels, from person and task factors to organisational ones.

The fine-tuned BERT model performed best, reaching 63.6 percent on the micro-averaged F1 measure, which combines precision and recall. Among the generative models, Phi-2 led with an F1 score a little under 55 percent. BERT was consistent across levels but often confused organisational factors with person factors. The authors argue progress depends on larger, high-quality labelled datasets, especially for rare categories.
pmc-13386486:
Moradi Bazghaleh and colleagues hunt for the source of leptospirosis, a bacterial fever spread through water and animal urine, in Iran's Gilan Province, in 2026 infectious disease research. From January 2020 to December 2023 the team collected 182 specimens from patients with fever and 120 environmental samples of water, soil, and wildlife tissue along the Caspian coast. Samples faced antibody tests, real-time PCR, sequencing, culture, and whole-genome sequencing to identify which Leptospira species circulate and how people meet them in this rice-farming region.

Of 41 cases confirmed by the antibody test, bacterial DNA was detected by PCR in 37, a yield of 90.2 percent. Sequencing found a lineage 98.1 to 98.9 percent identical to Leptospira kirschneri in 12 and 7 environmental samples. Rodent kidney cultures yielded isolates nearly identical to a serovar. Matching gene sequences across human, water, and rodent samples suggest a transmission chain. Rice farming carried an adjusted odds ratio of 2.7 for infection in the risk analysis.
pmc-13386986:
Sommer and colleagues track how an antibiotic shot plus resistant germs reshapes calves' gut flora, in 2026 livestock research. Calves received ceftiofur, an animal antibiotic, with drug-resistant E. coli strains mimicking pickup during treatment. Fecal samples over 35 days went through metagenomics and single-cell sequencing. Treated calves were compared with controls that received only the cocktail, to watch variety, resistance genes, and single cells shift under antibiotic pressure on a working farm.

Treated and control calves diverged in microbial richness and group structure across the period. Bacteroidaceae and Fibrobacter families were commoner without the antibiotic, while Akkermansia enriched in treated calves. In exposed animals, harm factors faded while beta-lactam resistance genes, including cfxA5 and cfxA6 in a Muribaculaceae lineage, increased. Single-cell data found Clostridium cells carrying macrolide genes in both groups. Sommer warns the treatment selects reservoirs even as it clears its targets.
pmc-13387086:
Austin E. Gillen and colleagues study how hibernating ground squirrels protect kidneys through repeated rewarming in a 2026 article. Thirteen-lined ground squirrels cycle between icy torpor and brief warm arousals some twenty times a winter. Each arousal reperfuses the kidney at body temperature, a stress that would injure most organs over time.

A 12-hour tidal-like rhythm appears to sync with those cycles to hold kidney function steady, the title findings suggest. The introduction frames hibernation as an untapped model for preventing kidney injury after blood loss. Lessons could also aid organ storage for transplant, where cold time limits graft survival.
pmc-13387686:
Cassi Crouse, Margaret Gettis, and Regena Spratling pilot a music device for calming newborns during eye exams in a 2026 report. Premature babies in intensive care face painful checks for retinopathy, a vision-threatening condition. A pacifier-activated lullaby device, guided by a music therapist with bedside nurses, was used with 25 infants.

Pain scores and vital signs worsened by the exam's end, then eased during five minutes of device use. Readings drifted back near pre-exam baselines after the session in their data. The team presents therapist-nurse teamwork on such devices as practical procedural support for fragile newborns.
pmc-13389286:
Savannah Brannan and Ben D Richardson examine, in 2026, how stress early in life reshapes behaviour and brain chemistry in mice, with effects that differ by sex. Many mental health conditions link both to childhood hardship and to sex, but the steps between early stress and later symptoms remain unclear.

Young mice went through a two-phase varied stress programme, then faced tests of exploration, reward preference, memory, and attention. Females showed stronger changes in exploration and reward response, while both sexes showed some memory and attention shifts. Brain recordings found reduced sensitivity in the locus coeruleus, a small cluster that supplies norepinephrine across the brain, in females only. The work ties early hardship to a specific stress circuit.
pmc-13390386:
Ana Mercedes Heredia-Velasquez and Ferran Garcia-Pichel test, in 2026, whether living soil crust grown at a solar farm can restore degraded land far away. Biological soil crusts protect dryland soils, but producing enough well-adapted starter material has limited restoration at scale.

Their crustivoltaics approach uses existing solar plants as large nurseries for crust microbes. The new test asks whether a Sonoran Desert facility on sandy soil can supply suitable starter for soils that differ in type or lie far from the nursery. Restoration ecologists gain a check on the portability of the method, a key question for remote degraded sites that have no solar farm of their own.
pmc-13390486:
Sixiang Xu leads a 2026 characterisation of a virus enzyme that can strip the protective coat from a dangerous Klebsiella strain. Klebsiella pneumoniae infects people and animals, and drug-resistant forms have pushed interest in phage-based alternatives to antibiotics.

The enzyme, DepZ57, comes from a phage specific to the K57 capsule type and cuts the sugar coat that shields hypervirulent strains. Laboratory analysis found the purified protein stable and water-friendly, with a typical twisted ribbon shape for its class. Stripping the capsule can expose the bacterium to immune attack and to drugs. Infection researchers gain a candidate enzyme therapy aimed precisely at one high-risk capsule type.
pmc-13391686:
Susana Vacas, Michele Introna, and Francisco Lobo write, in 2026, a response defending their editorial on mixing anaesthetic drugs in the era of precision monitoring. They thank the original authors for a thoughtful reply and agree that editorial fit, physiological interpretability, and clinical safety are not identical ideas.

They argue the three cannot be split in full when tools claim to track the body with care. Their word dangerous, they say, does not mean each mixed-drug case is unsafe. Nor does it mean skilled centres with set rules have caused excess harm. Doctors gain a sharp view of the clash. Do handy drug mixes blunt the fine tracking that new tools boast of? The tone stays civil, but the point is firm.
pmc-13391786:
Joasia Luzak and colleagues present, in 2026, the first empirical study of gender in enforcing the consumer right to choose repair. That right, central to sustainable consumption in European law, only works if all consumer groups can access and enforce it equally.

Survey data from more than three thousand consumers in the United Kingdom and the Netherlands show gender-based differences in acting on repair rights and in willingness to enforce them. Women faced distinct barriers and reacted more strongly to certain obstacles. Consumer law scholars gain evidence that formally neutral rules can operate unequally, a finding relevant to designing repair policy that works for everyone.
pmc-13392286:
Ying Fan and colleagues present, in 2026, a diffusion-based imaging method that restores high-quality optoacoustic images from very sparse data. Multispectral optoacoustic tomography gives rich biochemical contrast in tissue, but noise and sparse sampling often degrade its images.

Their network was trained on more than a quarter of a million in vivo images. It performs denoising and restoration together. An edge-aware module protects fine structure. A short-chain diffusion design supports fidelity. Imaging scientists gain a practical route to better images with cheaper, sparser hardware, which could widen use of optoacoustic imaging in laboratories and clinics.
pmc-13393486:
Seeni Mohamed Jaleel Nilofer Fathima and Chidhambaram Muthu Velayutham examined faculty appraisal systems in Indian pharmacy colleges. They asked whether the systems reward the work that modern drug training really needs: fresh course plans and inventive labs. Their survey covered twelve colleges in Tamil Nadu and four hundred twelve faculty members. Current scoring, they argue, counts publications, grants, and teaching load while missing course redesign and lab upgrades.

Faculty reported exactly that blind spot, and the authors tie heavy reliance on headcounts and gut-feel calls to weaker buy-in and stalled teaching renewal. Stats linked scoring rigour itself to stronger teaching innovation. Well-built systems, it seems, motivate rather than merely measure. The study closes with evidence-based directions for rebuilding the system so course building and lab excellence count beside standard output tallies.
pmc-13394286:
Gulistan Kochan, Eyyup Yasar, Ahmet Tumbul, and Ahmet Kilic built a family of zinc oxide nanocatalysts coated with a boron-doped polymer skin. They convert waste carbon dioxide into cyclic carbonates. Those chemicals are valuable for batteries and solvents, and the reaction keeps perfect atom economy. Five variants were made by precipitation and calcination and characterised with a dozen techniques, then tested on the reaction joining carbon dioxide to epoxides.

The standout variant, carrying a phosphonium salt partner, converted the test epoxide almost completely with near-total selectivity in two hours at moderate heat and ordinary pressure, without solvent. It handled a broad range of epoxides bearing different functional groups and survived five reuse cycles with its performance and structure intact. The authors credit cooperation between the acidic zinc and boron centres in gripping the epoxide while chloride opens its ring.
pmc-13394486:
Hiroaki Goto leads a 2026 study that tests drugs on tumours grown in gel, hunting cures for a rare child cancer. These tumours lack a protein named SMARCB1, also called INI1, which scrambles gene control. The team grew tumour pieces in three-dimensional gel drops and dosed them with many targeted drugs. Mouse-grown tumours gave the test pieces.

Several drug classes scored well in the gel test. One class, MDM2 blockers, worked only on tumours with enough of a guard protein named TP53. Sensitive cells switched on many genes after dosing, while resistant cells barely changed. The authors say the gel test can pick drugs patient by patient.
pmc-13394986:
Guy Hajj-Boutros leads a 2026 bed rest study on bone health in older adults. Twenty-two healthy adults aged 55 to 65 lay in head-down beds for fourteen days, mimicking space flight. Half did daily exercise, and half got passive therapy. Blood markers of bone building and bone loss were tracked for four months after.

Bone loss markers spiked right after bed rest in both groups. Building markers rose later, at one and four months. Standard density scans showed no clear change. Fine scans hinted at slight losses, but within the tool's error range. Daily exercise did not shield bones in this short trial. The authors note the body seems to rebuild on its own timetable.
pmc-13395186:
The International Journal of Molecular Sciences retracts, in a 2026 notice, a 2021 study by Mi-Lyang Kim and co-authors on statins in rat eyes. The study claimed the drugs guard nerves under long-term high eye pressure. A correction had already been issued when fresh doubts about figures arose. Editors re-checked the case and the materials the authors had sent.

The source materials could not fully prove the figures or the correction sound. The authors did not send the extra data asked for, despite repeated requests. The board lost faith in the findings and retracted under publisher policy. The editor-in-chief approved the step. The authors were told but gave no comment.
pmc-13396086:
Pâmela Caye and co-authors report the first use of gasless laparoscopy to treat a puppy with a giant kidney worm infection outside the kidney, in a 2026 case study. The parasite, Dioctophyme renale, barely responds to drugs, so surgery is the usual cure, and infection in a four-month-old is rare.

Standard keyhole surgery inflates the belly with gas, which can strain the heart and lungs of a small, sick animal. The gasless method lifts the belly wall with a frame instead, keeping pressure normal. The puppy came from a shelter hit by the May 2024 floods in southern Brazil. The report walks through the operation and recovery.
pmc-13396486:
Vasquez and co-authors analyze, in 2026, a twenty-year metagenomic time series of giant viruses in Lake Mendota, Wisconsin, the longest such record for a freshwater lake. From 471 co-assembled metagenomes spanning 2000 to 2019, they reconstructed 1,512 giant virus genomes. Viruses of the order Imitervirales dominated throughout, making up 89.6 percent of the genomes across seasons and years.

Gene duplication accounted for 23 percent of viral genes and horizontal gene transfer for 29 percent, marking both as engines of change in these viruses. Virus-host interaction networks intensified after 2009, when an invasive predatory zooplankton entered the lake, and positively selected viral genes rose after the invasion, especially infection-related ones. Genome-wide substitution rates in giant viruses resembled those of co-occurring bacteria but ran significantly slower than in smaller double-stranded DNA phages. The authors cast giant viruses as stable yet adaptable players in freshwater ecology.
pmc-13396686:
Jetmira Fejza and co-authors present an 88-year-old woman with a severe ear canal infection that ate into the skull base, whose treatment was then derailed by allergy. Their 2026 case report concerns malignant external otitis, an aggressive infection that usually strikes elderly people with diabetes or weak immunity, though this patient had no diabetes.

She arrived with severe ear pain and pus that standard treatment had not shifted, and scans confirmed bone infection of the temporal bone. During her hospital stay she developed a severe generalized allergic skin reaction to the systemic antibiotics she needed. The case shows two problems compounding: a dangerous infection and a shrinking list of drugs to fight it.
pmc-13397686:
Ruichao Cao and a large team test cerium oxide nanoparticles as a guard for worn spinal discs. Their 2026 study targets oxidative stress, the build-up of reactive oxygen that helps drive disc degeneration. The particles mimic a natural enzyme that clears those harmful molecules, and their tiny size suits the disc's poor blood supply.

Three disc cell types were grown with the particles to find safe doses, then stressed to see whether the particles protected them. Tests tracked cell survival, reactive oxygen levels and live-dead staining, while microscopy and blood checks followed where particles travel in the body. Tissue study in animals rounds out the case for a disc treatment built on antioxidant defence.
pmc-13397786:
Ali Abdow Hafsa and colleagues report how often semen tests come back abnormal among men seeking fertility help in eastern and central Uganda. Their 2026 study covers 155 men at three centres, including Jinja and Kayunga referral hospitals, between September 2025 and January 2026. Male factors drive a large share of infertility, yet Ugandan data on semen quality were thin.

Tests followed World Health Organization criteria, and about a third of men (33.5 percent, 52 of 155) showed at least one abnormal value. Misshapen sperm were the most common fault at 42.3 percent of abnormal cases, followed by weak movement at 38.5 percent in that group. Rates barely differed between sites, and the team modelled which personal factors tracked with abnormal results.
pmc-13398786:
Paul Medina-González and colleagues peel animal limbs layer by layer to learn how much each tissue limits joint movement. Their 2026 study measures passive bending range at six joints (shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee and ankle) in four four-legged mammals: rabbit, chilla fox, pig and pudu deer, one specimen each. Fossil reconstructions usually guess movement from bone shape alone, ignoring the soft wrappings that bound real joints.

Range was re-measured as anatomical layers were removed in sequence, splitting the total limit among skin, muscle and deeper tissues. Postures differ across the four species, from crouched rabbit to upright deer, letting posture effects show. The dataset gives fossil interpreters measured soft-tissue corrections instead of hunches.
pmc-13399186:
Yuxuan Lyu and colleagues review recent work on hydrogen sulfide donors built into nanostructures for cancer treatment, in a 2026 survey. Hydrogen sulfide is a gas the body makes in small amounts. At higher doses it can harm cancer cells. Gas therapy appeals because gases penetrate tissue quickly and rarely provoke drug resistance. The catch is control, since the gas spreads freely and can cause side effects.

The review sorts donors that assemble into nanoscale structures by their material, from purely organic designs to hybrid ones. Such structures release the gas more slowly and let researchers tune the release rate. They can also steer the gas toward tumors, passively or with active targeting. The authors cover treatments using hydrogen sulfide alone and combinations with other therapies. They close by weighing what still blocks clinical use, including release precision and safety, and by sketching designs they expect to see next.
pmc-13399286:
Julia Machado da Costa Pennone and colleagues wrote this 2026 letter taking stock of electrical stimulation meant to protect the diaphragm in critically ill patients. The diaphragm weakens fast once a breathing machine takes over, sometimes within days. Stimulation can target the muscle directly through skin electrodes, or reach it through the phrenic nerve in the neck. Implanted pacing is a more invasive option.

Early studies find stimulation feasible and generally safe. There are hints of shorter ventilation and better weaning success in patients needing prolonged support. The authors stress how thin that base is. Most studies are small and differ widely in design, which limits how far the findings travel. Unanswered questions include which patients benefit most, whether muscle or nerve stimulation works better, and what settings to use. The letter calls for proper trials before the technique enters care guidelines.
pmc-13400186:
Jisu Park and colleagues grew organoids from eighteen patients' glioblastomas, in a 2026 study. The mini-tumors predict who will respond to the standard drug temozolomide better than the field's standard biomarker. The organoid lines preserved their parent tumors' appearance and genomes, and their drug sensitivity was compared with the patients' actual progression-free survival.

The organoid results correlated strongly with how long patients stayed progression-free. They beat MGMT methylation status, the one accepted predictive marker, at forecasting temozolomide response. Studying the resistant models exposed the escape routes: mismatch repair deficiency, high MGMT expression, and switched-on programs for axon growth and cell adhesion. The authors position such drug testing as a working platform for a tumor that has defeated nearly every trial drug.
pmc-13400486:
Jesús Talavera-López, Elena Hernández-Rubio and Marta Soler report, in 2026, two Akita puppies with swimmer puppy syndrome, a rare newborn condition where the chest flattens and legs splay out. Affected pups cannot stand or walk normally. Both littermates also had a sunken chest defect and a heart shifted to the right.

Both pups lay flat on their chests with breathing trouble in their first weeks. X-rays confirmed the flattened chest and displaced heart. Care used intensive physiotherapy, careful positioning and a custom chest splint. Within 30 days movement and chest shape improved markedly. Two-year follow-up in one pup showed good function despite the heart staying slightly right of its usual place.
pmc-13400586:
Heather Shaw Bonilha and colleagues review, in 2026, how care systems handle swallowing problems after stroke. Swallowing trouble is common after stroke and affects complications, rehabilitation and quality of life. Yet management often fragments across hospital and community settings, with key choices made early and rarely revisited.

Recent work casts the condition as dynamic, needing follow-up over time rather than one acute decision. The review covers screening, bedside and imaging checks, feeding tube practices and barriers to reassessment after discharge. Variation in tube use and poor access to imaging in later care are recurring problems, and food restriction carries a heavy personal burden. The authors push for recovery-oriented pathways with continuity built in.
pmc-13401686:
Ali Mansoursamaei and co-authors argue for reconceptualizing dyslipidemia, the family of blood lipid disorders, in a 2026 narrative review. The textbook definition, built on single values such as LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides, may miss the biological complexity of lipid imbalance.

Their review, searching PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science through April 2026, focuses on patterns rather than single numbers: lipid ratios, subfractions such as oxidized and small dense LDL. Combined cardiometabolic markers like the TyG index. Lipid disruption, they contend, grows out of metabolic disorders and drug treatments jointly, and integrated patterns describe a patient's risk better than isolated deviations. The piece is aimed at clinicians and researchers ready to grade lipid health as a multidimensional profile instead of a pass-fail checklist.
pmc-13401786:
Johanna-Sophie Schlüter-Bartram and co-authors used the 1000 Bull Genomes Project as a test case for checking the metadata attached to huge sequencing datasets, in a 2026 study. Fast sequencing now floods livestock research with genomes, but labels such as breed and subspecies can be wrong, and errors poison downstream analyses.

Their framework cross-checked the NCBI BioSamples database against the DNA itself, using principal component analysis, admixture analysis, and distance measures. Missing breed assignments were the biggest drain on quality, affecting 360 samples, about 6 percent. Another 183 samples, about 3 percent, carried the wrong subspecies, and 1,635 animals were involved in breed assignment corrections of some kind. In total 603 animals got corrected breed or subspecies labels. The authors argue even flagship datasets need rigorous metadata audits.
pmc-13402286:
Yulong Wu and co-authors review how to design electrolyte additives that make water-based magnesium-air batteries work far better. These batteries promise cheap, safe storage, but the magnesium anode wastes away through corrosion, and dissolved oxygen from the air reaction makes that waste worse. The review gathers past additive results into structured data meant to guide smarter searches, including searches run by machine learning.

A central claim is that oxygen-driven corrosion deserves far more weight, above all for clean magnesium anodes sitting in additive-bearing fluids. Single additives have mostly been picked by trial and error; the authors instead lay out a clear design idea for pairing two additives so their jobs complement each other. Readers get both a map of what has been tried and a reasoned recipe for building hybrid additives on purpose rather than by luck.
pmc-13402886:
Moein Nikravan and colleagues profile clinical isolates of Enterococcus faecalis across three axes at once: its CRISPR-Cas immune system, its virulence traits, and its drug resistance. The species is a gut bacterium turned hospital pathogen. Once dismissed as a harmless commensal, it now ranks among the top causes of hospital infections. Those infections run from bloodstream and heart valve disease to urinary and wound cases, and the germ shrugs off many drug classes by nature.

Acquired resistance deepens the problem, including high-level gentamicin resistance and vancomycin resistance carried on mobile gene clusters such as vanA. By mapping defense systems beside attack traits and resistance genes in the same isolates, the study hunts for patterns that predict which strains turn dangerous. The authors frame the combined profile as intelligence for infection control in wards where this organism thrives.
pmc-13403186:
Kieran C O’Doherty and a broad author team define microbiome stewardship. They also set out guiding principles for putting it into practice. Microbes underpin ecosystem, plant, animal, and human health. Human activity is disturbing them with adverse effects. Yet almost no oversight exists to protect microbial communities or their functions. Partly that is because nobody has settled what to protect, or how.

The article builds a working definition meant to travel across public health, clinical care, environmental protection, food production, and agriculture. Implementation, they stress, will always be local. Habitat, goals, and intervention chances differ, so responsibility must be pinned to specific institutions case by case. The authors place stewardship beside One Health and related movements. They argue the missing piece in planetary health governance is a duty of care toward the microbial world.
pmc-13403986:
Sergio Guinez-Molinos and colleagues piloted the newest world disease code list in 2026 at a hospital in Curicó, Chile. Eight doctors and two coding staff learned the CIE-11 system and a national checking platform. They coded 457 hospital discharge records from medicine and psychiatry wards between March and June 2025.

For the main diagnosis, doctors matched the coder in 96 percent of records. Match with a national expert reached 93 percent on the same field. Side diagnoses matched above 90 percent across fields. Main slips involved missed code add-ons and misplaced external cause codes. The pilot gives Chile early proof for a wider rollout.
pmc-13404086:
Vera Janssen and a large team showed in 2026 that tiny curves where blood vessel cells touch can steer how the whole sheet of cells moves. Vessel-lining cells march together when new vessels grow, held by seams that also pass signals. At lopsided seams, the cell surface bends at a very small scale.

Those bends draw in curve-sensing proteins, among them BIN1 and SNX9. The proteins help remodel seams, set cell direction, and keep movement aimed. Shape at the seam thus acts as an organizer of group travel. The finding gives vessel growth a new control point to study.
pmc-13404186:
Na Yang and a ten-author team built a lab method in 2026 to measure an anti-rejection drug inside patients' white blood cells, not just in plasma. Such plasma checks miss how much reaches the cells where it acts. Their method reads the drug and its main breakdown product at the same time.

Samples came from 139 draws on 40 kidney transplant patients taking one of two drug forms. Levels inside cells varied a lot from person to person. Plasma and cell levels matched only weakly to moderately, with no clear sex gap. Cell-level checks could sharpen dose tuning for each patient.
pmc-13404486:
Annie Jeffery and colleagues traced UK mental distress in 2026 across fifteen years of national shocks, using survey data from 87,857 people. Distress scores climbed from 2009 to 2023 by just over one point on their scale. The team tested five shock moments for jumps or slow drifts in distress.

The Brexit vote and the first COVID lockdown each brought a sharp rise right after. Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the 2022 mini-budget fed slower monthly climbs instead. The second COVID lockdown showed no like signal in their models. Effects varied a lot by age, sex, background, wealth, and work status.
pmc-13404786:
Yuya Suzuki and co-authors tell of two women whose exercise lung pressure stayed high after a balloon procedure for chronic clots, in a 2026 report. Both had chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension that surgery could not fix, so balloon pulmonary angioplasty opened their lung arteries. Supervised heart rehabilitation then ran long term alongside vessel-dilating drugs.

One woman trained near her anaerobic threshold, while the other moved gradually to high-intensity interval sessions. Repeat catheter tests during exercise showed the pressure-to-flow slope falling over 12 and 18 months in the two cases. Peak oxygen use rose in both, from 16.2 to 20.2 in one case in the reported units. No bad events occurred during follow-up, and the authors frame rehab as workable and possibly helpful.
pmc-13407586:
Yukie Nakagawa, Hideto Okamoto, and Nobuaki Okumura report, in 2026, that royal jelly calms a harmful secretion pattern in ageing skin cells. Senescent skin cells are worn out by repeated division. They pump out inflammatory signals called SASP, which ages nearby tissue. Substances that quiet that output without killing cells are called senomorphics. Such agents are prized in skin ageing research.

The tests used lab-grown human skin cells aged by repeated division. Cells from older donors, including a 75-year-old, were also used. Royal jelly suppressed several SASP factors, including interleukin-6. It did so without poisoning the cells. Gene-readout analysis pointed to dampened inflammatory pathways and lower oxidative stress. The authors cast royal jelly as a multi-target natural senomorphic with cosmetic and therapeutic promise.
pmc-13407886:
Yuka Sakazaki and co-authors find, in 2026, a summer peak in sudden kidney injury among Japanese outpatients. Community-acquired acute kidney injury is common but its calendar rhythm was unclear, so the team analysed a national insurance claims database covering August 2016 to July 2018 and more than 4.28 million outpatients.

They counted 20,634 new community cases. Incidence climbed from June and peaked in July, when the adjusted rate ran 19 percent above the reference pattern, and July beat February in every subgroup examined. The seasonal swing interacted with age, hitting hardest in the youngest group, under twenty. Heat and other seasonal environmental factors are the natural suspects, and the authors suggest prevention efforts in outpatient care should respect the calendar.
pmc-13408686:
Mohammad Pourebrahimi, Saeid Eshghi, Mohsen Shirdel, and Nazim Gruda test in 2026 whether selenium and feeding schedules can rescue strawberries growing under salty conditions. Salt stress cuts strawberry yields worldwide, and selenium is known to bolster plant defences. Potted plants of one cultivar faced plain or salted nutrient solution, with or without selenium, under four different daily feeding regimes in a fully crossed design.

Morning feeding combined with selenium cut the yield loss from salt to about a quarter and gave the heaviest roots and shoots. Those plants also showed stronger antioxidant activity, more protective pigment, and better potassium and calcium uptake. Fruit selenium rose into the low milligrams per kilogram of dry weight, a biofortification bonus. The authors recommend the morning-plus-selenium pairing for controlled-environment growing, while urging tests on other cultivars and doses.
pmc-13409086:
Malcolm Battin and colleagues mine a decade of New Zealand national records in 2026 to pin down how often babies with brain dysfunction around birth die from it. Neonatal encephalopathy can follow oxygen deprivation and leaves survivors at risk of lasting disability, so honest mortality figures matter for counselling families and for comparing countries. National collection covers term babies from 2010 and late-preterm babies from 2016.

Most affected infants showed fetal distress or a sentinel event before birth, arrived with low Apgar scores, and needed resuscitation. Mortality for term babies sat at well under one per thousand births and did not shift significantly across the decade. Babies born a few weeks early died at roughly triple the rate. No significant difference appeared between prioritised ethnic groups, a finding the committee reports carefully given the small numbers involved.
pmc-13411286:
Mohitosh Biswas and colleagues chart in 2026 how common a risk gene variant is across Asia. The variant, HLA-B*15:02, can trigger life-threatening skin reactions to certain seizure drugs. Knowing where it clusters guides screening before those drugs are prescribed.

Frequencies drawn from a global allele database fell steeply from southeast to west Asia. Southeast Asia averaged the highest share, while West Asia barely registered the variant. The Philippines topped the country list at about 22 percent, followed by Vietnam and Indonesia. Guideline sources named four seizure drugs with strong evidence linking them to the variant's danger. Patchy data in some countries leave the map incomplete, the authors note.
pmc-13411886:
Cristina Priboi and co-authors survey in 2026 animal researchers in Switzerland about preregistration, the practice of logging study plans before experiments begin. Borrowed from clinical research, the habit fights selective reporting and boosts trust. Two platforms for animal studies exist, yet uptake stays rare.

The survey, itself preregistered, measured experience, attitudes, social norms, confidence, and perceived obstacles. Researchers weighed promised gains in rigor against fears of scooping, extra workload, and rigid plans in exploratory work. Suggestions for improvement pointed to simpler platforms, funder and journal backing, and training. Airing these views first, the authors argue, keeps a well-meant reform from backfiring on the bench.
pmc-13412886:
Mónika Katkó and co-authors measure in 2026 how a short spell of deliberate hypothyroidism reshapes blood fats in thyroid cancer survivors. Patients stop their thyroid hormone for four weeks before follow-up scans, creating a temporary hormone shortage doctors call iatrogenic hypothyroidism. The prospective study sampled 52 patients during normal replacement and again after withdrawal, splitting lipoproteins into subfractions and testing proteins that guard vessel walls.

Total cholesterol and both major cholesterol fractions rose sharply during the hormone shortage, as did two carrier proteins. LDL particles shrank toward a denser, more artery-harming form in the same samples. HDL, meanwhile, shifted toward larger particles with hints of stronger protective enzyme activity. The authors read the picture as mixed rather than simply harmful.
pmc-13413486:
Yuhui Chu and co-authors present in 2026 a deep-learning pipeline that stretches the sharp depth range of optical coherence tomography, a workhorse scan for tissue microstructure. A normal OCT lens keeps only a thin slice in focus, so fine detail blurs above and below it. Their cascaded network first aligns several images taken at different focal depths, then fuses them under a focus map, tuning itself on each new scan without needing a training library.

Tests on animal tissue and living specimens beat unfused images and older fusion methods on clarity measures. Signal-to-noise improved by up to 8.29 decibels over conventional approaches in their ex vivo benchmarks. The usable depth of focus roughly doubled, letting fine structures stay legible across a much thicker slab of tissue.
pmc-13413786:
Narathip Kongsamret and colleagues brew in 2026 a starter from a stingless bee's own gut to ferment the pollen those bees eat. Germs matched to the host promise safer, better feed for colonies under food stress. The team sifted 37 lactic acid bacteria from Heterotrigona itama. Three strains of one species passed gut-toughness, grip, and safety screens. Those three were paired with two yeasts that share the hive and love sugar-rich food.

Pollen brewed with the team beat plain-brewed pollen on protein uptake, acid output, and germ survival. It also scored higher on tests that fight cell damage. Fed workers ate more and weighed more than controls. They stored more belly fat, grew bigger food glands, and lived longer. Their gut germs shifted toward genera long tied to bee health.
pmc-13413886:
Hiromi Yee and co-authors pilot in 2026 a cognitive test battery designed for older adults whose poor eyesight makes standard tests unfair. Vision-dependent tools can overdiagnose impairment in this group, so the VISION-Cog protocol uses tasks that bypass sight. Forty-five community-dwelling Singaporeans with near-vision problems took the battery and a standard screen, then saw a neurologist whose diagnosis served as the reference.

Thirty-seven participants, 82.2 percent, finished the protocol in about an hour, and feedback called the length acceptable. Against the neurologist's judgment, the battery reached a discrimination score of 0.930 in this pilot, catching every impaired case while holding specificity at 78.0 percent in their analysis. The authors ask for a larger study before clinical use.
pmc-13415286:
André Luiz Martins and colleagues pool worldwide evidence on tooth decay in Indigenous children and teenagers, in a 2026 systematic review covering studies from 1968 to 2024. Ninety-five studies from nineteen countries entered the review, and fifty-nine supplied data for pooled averages. Decay was scored by counting decayed, missing, and filled teeth.

For baby teeth the pooled mean was about 3.8 affected teeth, and for permanent teeth about 2.4 affected teeth. North American studies showed the highest averages, well above Oceania and Asia. Permanent tooth decay rose with age and fell as national development scores rose. Six decades of data show no clear improvement over time.
pmc-13417186:
Hao Liu and colleagues present a chemical method for closing peptides into rings while adding a handle for later changes, in a 2026 study. Ring shaped peptides resist breakdown and enter cells better than straight ones, yet keep strong target binding. Their reagent reacts with cysteine, a sulfur bearing building block in the chain.

The rings carry a tetrazine handle that can click to other molecules in living systems. One new peptide bound tightly to a cancer linked protein in lab and animal tests. A companion assay lights up a dye only when a peptide enters a living cell, giving a clean measure of entry for drug hunters.
pmc-13417486:
Zhong Xhen Khor and Priya Gusain report advanced HIV with a severe fungal infection mimicking a hyperinflammatory syndrome, in a 2026 case. The man had long fever and low counts of all blood cell types, with no source found despite broad testing. Marrow examination showed immune cells swallowing blood cells, a hallmark of the syndrome called HLH.

Blood culture grew Talaromyces marneffei, a fungus that attacks weak immune systems. A scoring tool supported an HLH like picture, though full criteria testing was unavailable. Antifungal treatment alone brought rapid recovery, without immune suppressing HLH drugs. HIV and hepatitis C treatment followed successfully.
pmc-13419086:
Tonya Frommelt and colleagues study children of parents with depression, a group at higher risk of mental illness, to find early markers of that risk. Two candidates are a mental habit of reading mixed events in a dark way and the body's stress response. No earlier work had tested the two together in these children.

The study compared 80 children of depressed parents with 77 children whose parents had no mental illness, all aged 10 to 14 years. A sentence task measured the reading habit, while spit samples of the stress hormone cortisol tracked body response at six points around a stress test. Self-rated feelings added the child's own view of each stage. Joint results could point to children who would gain most from early support.
pmc-13419486:
Yunpeng Li and colleagues name a gene-silencing enzyme as a master driver of bladder cancer growth, immune evasion, and stem-like behavior. Bladder cancer keeps advancing in many patients despite better surgery and immune drugs, for reasons still partly hidden. The team combined single-cell readings with maps of where cells sit inside the tumor.

Network analysis joined with machine learning picked out SUV39H1 as a hub gene tied to worse outlook. The enzyme helps build a niche that shuts immune cells out while keeping a stem-like pool alive. That dual role, guarding the tumor and renewing it, makes the enzyme a tempting drug target. Blocking it might open the tumor to immune attack and cut its regrowth at the same time.
pmc-13420486:
Foram P Joshi reports a case series on Ayurvedic care for lower urinary tract symptoms in older adults, the mix of flow and urgency problems tied to bladder, urethra, and prostate change. Care ran for 30 days in the protocol described, joining herbal powders and tablets with a medicated oil procedure. Flow testing and a standard symptom score measured change before and after.

Average flow rose by 41 percent after treatment and top flow by 43.51 percent in the reported figures, with total voided volume up by over half beside them. Symptom scores eased by about 27 percent, and urine left behind after voiding fell by nearly 40 percent in the same account. Case series cannot prove cause, yet gains across every measure at once justify a controlled trial of the protocol.
pmc-13420686:
Matteo Pavone and colleagues review computer-guided surgery for checking lymph nodes in gynecological cancer, where node status drives both prognosis and treatment choice. Full node removal over-treats most patients, since most nodes prove clear, and the surgery brings lasting harm. Sentinel node checks already predict clear status well in vulvar and cervical cancers.

Live optical biopsy tools and AI image reading promise to judge nodes during the operation itself, without removal. High-frequency ultrasound and light-based tissue scans are among the methods maturing toward that goal. A reliable negative reading could one day make node excision needless for many women. The review weighs the proof behind each tool for teams planning robotic and digital operating suites.
pmc-13421386:
Thomas Pühringer and eight colleagues reveal, in a 2026 structural study, how the cell assembles the machine that starts DNA replication. When a cell enters S phase, three activator proteins join a ring-shaped motor loaded on DNA to form two CMGE helicases, which then unwind the double helix in opposite directions.

The team rebuilt the pre-initiation complex from purified yeast proteins and solved its structure with cryo-electron microscopy, catching the firing factors mid-assembly. The structure shows how stepwise binding reshapes the motor for DNA opening and how ATP triggers factor release. One factor, Sld2, both recruits a partner and helps split the paired helicases, expelling the lagging strand. The authors link the mechanism to human replication disorders.
pmc-13421686:
Gil-Hwan Kim leads a seventeen-author team identifying, in a 2026 study, a molecular switch that drives liver scarring. Liver fibrosis begins when hepatic stellate cells activate and lay down scar tissue. A protein called YAP is known to push that activation. Yet what switches YAP on in this setting was unknown.

The team found the kinase PAK4 sharply raised in activated stellate cells from patients and mice, matching disease severity. Silencing it calmed the cells' fibrotic behaviour, and deleting it in mouse stellate cells, or dosing a PAK4-blocking drug, eased fibrosis. PAK4 tags YAP at a previously unrecognised site, position 428, stabilising it. That tagged form was abundant in fibrotic human livers, marking a drug target.
pmc-13422586:
Saera Jung, Kihong Son and Andrew Coristine compare, in a 2026 analysis, how three regulators police the cybersecurity of AI-enabled medical software. Connected, updatable devices widen the attack surface, while traditional device risk rules were written for patient-safety harms and may miss threats to data integrity and service continuity.

The team read ten regulatory and guidance documents. They came from Korea's food and drug ministry, the United States FDA, and European Union bodies. For each one the team mapped its definitions, its life-cycle coverage and the proof it demands before and after market entry. Cross-sector instruments and published literature filled gaps. Their framework sorts where safety vigilance and vulnerability-focused security practice diverge, and they name the informatics-relevant gaps for device makers.
pmc-13423086:
Paulina Morales Ruiz leads a twenty-author team presenting the PregInPoxVac protocol, a phase 3 trial of the MVA-BN mpox vaccine in pregnant and postpartum women in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Mpox is endemic there, pregnancy raises the risk of severe illness, and no trial had yet tested vaccine safety or immune response in this group.

In Boende, 359 women aged 16 to 35 are being enrolled, all in the second or third trimester. They are randomised to two vaccine doses 28 days apart, timed either before 32 weeks of pregnancy or just after birth. A further group gets the vaccine after confirmed exposure. Results will be compared with an earlier adult study in Congo and Uganda, filling a data gap the World Health Organization has flagged.
pmc-13423786:
Anjali G. Borsum and seven colleagues review eight years of deliveries at the Medical University of South Carolina to test whether a mother's vitamin D level tracks with how early her baby arrives. Charts covered 15,506 women whose first vitamin D measurement during pregnancy fell between January 2016 and March 2024, and the team compared levels between preterm and term births.

Women delivering before 37 weeks averaged 31.3 nanograms per millilitre, against 34.8 among term deliveries, a gap of about 3.5 points. The gap widened for births before 32 weeks, whose mothers averaged 26.2, roughly 8.6 points below term. The authors call for trials of whether lifting vitamin D in pregnancy can cut preterm birth.
pmc-13424386:
Yamashita and colleagues report a 73-year-old man with two pancreatic tumors found side by side. Telling them apart was tricky. Pancreatic schwannoma, a benign nerve-sheath tumor, is very rare and hard to identify on standard scans. The team used contrast-enhanced endoscopic ultrasound to compare the two lesions. That is an internal ultrasound method with a contrast agent.

The larger body lesion measured 13 millimeters. It enhanced gradually, beginning 17 seconds after contrast injection. A second 6 millimeter lesion sat in the pancreatic tail. It enhanced rapidly at 12 seconds, a distinctly unlike vascular pattern. Needle sampling diagnosed the first as schwannoma. The second was a grade 1 neuroendocrine tumor, two unrelated growths in one gland. Both were managed with observation. The authors credit the contrast study for prompting biopsy of both lesions.
pmc-13424786:
Chujun Ye and five colleagues build a non-invasive way to tell apart the two causes of azoospermia, the complete absence of sperm: blocked ducts versus failed production inside the testicle. Today's answer usually needs a testicular biopsy, so the team combined super-resolution ultrasound, which maps tiny vessels using microbubbles, with gene and metabolite profiling in mouse models of each cause.

The imaging separated the causes cleanly. Production-failure models showed fragmented, under-perfused vessel networks with shrunken larger vessels, while blocked-duct models showed denser, wider, faster vessels. Molecular profiles tied the pictures to vessel growth, tissue remodelling, and energy rewiring. A small first human cohort showed the same contrast, hinting biopsy may one day be avoidable.
pmc-13426086:
Kankan Qu and colleagues set up a new drug abuse monitoring approach inside a medical institution in a 2026 study from Wuxi Mental Health Centre. Existing monitoring relies on fixed reporting from addiction centers, detention sites, and compulsory detox facilities, which delays detection and misses misuse in ordinary care. Prescription drugs, over-the-counter products, and new psychoactive substances increasingly appear in medical settings.

Their retrospective observation of patients diagnosed with drug or substance abuse tested structured monitoring and reporting within the hospital. Earlier, fuller reporting from medical institutions could help regulators spot emerging misuse patterns sooner. Staff in wards, clinics, and labs all feed facts to the new scheme, which cuts blind spots that the old fixed sites left wide open.
pmc-13427586:
Huimin Huo and co-authors report, in 2026, a greener way to pull healthful compounds from a medicinal fungus named Inonotus hispidus. The fungus is rich in polyphenols, plant-like chemicals that fight cell damage from oxidation. Their method uses ultrasound in a warm ethanol bath, which shakes loose more of the desired compounds while using less solvent. Early trials already beat two older methods, heat reflux and plain stirring.

A structured search then fixed the best recipe at 95 minutes, 60 percent ethanol, set power, and a temperature of 65 degrees. Yield rose by roughly a third over the starting method. A formal greenness score backed the claim of lower environmental cost. Extracts made the new way also scored higher on antioxidant tests, giving makers a cleaner route to a stronger product.
pmc-13427886:
Pisani and colleagues published a 2026 review on weight-loss drugs used around pregnancy. Drugs in the GLP-1 class treat diabetes and obesity in many adults. Whether use near conception ties to pregnancy blood-pressure disorders was unclear. The team pooled three studies covering 10,880 pregnancies in the United States.

Nearly 5,000 pregnancies had drug exposure before conception or in early weeks. Two studies hinted at lower risk, while one pointed the other way. Pooled, exposure showed no clear link to the disorders overall. The odds ratio sat near one, with wide bounds around it. The authors call for large forward-looking studies to settle the question. Only three studies qualified, so the evidence base remains very thin.
pmc-13427986:
Alansari and colleagues reviewed in 2026 a non-surgical treatment for intussusception in babies under 12 months old. In this condition, one part of the bowel slides into the next, blocking it, and it is the most common cause of bowel blockage in infancy. The treatment uses ultrasound guidance and water pressure from an enema to push the bowel back into place, avoiding surgery.

Alansari combined 22 studies covering 2,656 infants in a pooled analysis. The treatment worked in about eight of ten cases, the condition returned in about 8 percent, and bowel perforation, a tear in the bowel wall, occurred in about 2 percent of cases. Sedation and study design did not change outcomes, but perforation risk differed by country income level. The authors back the method for stable infants while calling for shared protocols.
pmc-13428786:
Sánchez Pérez and colleagues give the first molecular proof of two tick borne infections in dogs in Chihuahua, Mexico. The bacteria are Ehrlichia canis, which attacks white blood cells and can kill dogs, and Rickettsia rickettsii, the cause of Rocky Mountain spotted fever in people. Their 2026 study draws blood from 123 tick infested dogs held at the city's control center. It runs nested PCR, a DNA test, for one gene from each bacterium.

Ehrlichia DNA turned up in twenty dogs, about one in six, and Rickettsia DNA in four dogs. Sequencing six Ehrlichia samples and all four Rickettsia samples let the team build strain family trees. Both clustered with strains reported from the United States, fitting the brown dog tick's border crossing habits. Infected dogs at a city shelter signal risk for staff, adopters, and nearby homes. The authors argue for tick control as a public health step.
pmc-13431786:
Trang and colleagues ran a pilot study in Hai Phong, Vietnam in 2026 on how well the HPV vaccine works in female sex workers. This group faces four to ten times the usual infection risk yet is rarely studied for vaccine response. Sixty-three women aged 18 to 26 received three doses of the quadrivalent Gardasil vaccine, with swabs at entry and blood draws across seven months.

At entry, nearly three in ten women carried a high-risk HPV type and about one in ten carried the two types the vaccine targets most. After one dose, nine in ten women already had antibodies to HPV16, and by month seven every participant had antibodies to both HPV16 and HPV18. Women who started virus-free mounted higher antibody levels than those already infected. The authors say the vaccine is immunogenic in this group and call for effectiveness studies.
pmc-13433486:
Lee and colleagues share practical lessons from launching an MRI-only workflow for brain radiotherapy in this 2026 implementation study. MRI shows soft tissue far better than CT, but dose calculations traditionally need CT's density data, so software now builds a synthetic CT from MRI. Most earlier work compared doses on paper; this team instead catalogued what went wrong in real clinical use across twenty-eight patients.

Synthetic scans were successfully generated for 25 of the 28 patients scanned under their dedicated protocol. Nine synthetic datasets needed re-registration because patients moved between the four MRI sequences used. The problems fell into two families. Workflow issues included motion, poor coil placement, and marker interference. Algorithm errors were the second family. They mislabeled tissue, bone, and air, or degraded images around surgical meshes. The authors supply screening and quality checklists.
pmc-13434286: Tsuji and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their article on how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, first respond to tumor cells that have spread there. The notice fixes the author list: Katsuaki Sato was left off the original version by mistake. The online HTML and PDF versions now carry his name, and the author contributions and disclosure statements have been updated to match. The authors state their regret for the error. No results, figures, or conclusions of the article change.
pmc-13434486:
Untalan, Pagote, and Tejero argue that the Philippines shows a widening gap. Food and nutrition policies exist on paper, but what they deliver lags behind. The gap grows when economic shocks hit. The country maintains laws and a national nutrition plan. Yet stunting, micronutrient deficiencies, and rising obesity persist.

They name the pattern a shock-amplified implementation gap. Split government, weak aiming of aid, little working together between sectors, and low ability to adapt all worsen when food prices and energy inflation surge. Rising prices restrict access to nutrient-dense foods most sharply for the poorest homes. Program gains get undone during crises like price-surge periods. The authors call for stronger government systems and better follow-through. They want joined, adaptive food-system plans rather than more new laws. Their goal is lasting and fair nutrition outcomes that survive the next shock instead of falling apart under it.
pmc-13434786:
Baowen Zhang and coauthors build a two part mRNA vaccine to cure lasting hepatitis B in 2026. Lasting infection trains the immune system to tolerate the virus coat, so shots alone rarely clear it. Pairing the coat with a second virus part, preS1, won a screening contest.

In mice with lasting infection the vaccine cleared nearly all virus DNA. Coat levels fell sharply and cure type antibodies appeared. The second part drove killer T cell attack, while the coat acted as its own booster. Adding interferon raised gains and memory. Safety signs stayed sound in the tests shown.
pmc-13435986:
Skinner and colleagues set out a 2026 feasibility protocol for adapting an Easy 8 Form Tai Chi program for breast cancer survivors in regional Australia. Survivors often face a linked cluster of fatigue, poor sleep, and depression. Tai Chi helped this cluster in Chinese hospital studies, but the program must fit local community care. Survivors and local providers will codesign the adaptation together.

Stage one uses focus groups, interviews, and a workshop with women who have lived through breast cancer and with community clinicians, to reshape the protocol. Stage two pilots the adapted classes with a small survivor group. The main questions are whether the program is feasible and acceptable in this setting. Secondary measures track fatigue, sleep, depression, and quality of life before and after. Ethics approval came from Charles Darwin University, and results will guide a larger trial.
pmc-13436086:
Linxin Jiang and colleagues studied what shapes oral health literacy, meaning how well older adults grasp dental health, among people aged 65 to 74 in China. They used a well-known model that sorts influences into personal traits, daily habits, and health needs.

The study covered 423 adults who had dental exams and answered survey questions about beliefs and disease awareness. Root tooth decay and filled teeth linked directly to higher scores on both literacy measures used. Wearing a dental prosthesis, meaning a false tooth device, tied to stronger health beliefs, while dental visits tied to greater disease awareness. Gender and schooling shaped literacy only through other factors, so Jiang advises tailoring dental teaching to each group's needs.
pmc-13436686:
Marie Lajos and coauthors report a hidden device recording that caught a 22 second heart pause in a 63 year old man in 2026. His under skin defibrillator uses a filter to dodge false shocks. When signal waves run tiny, the filter switches off and the device records a tracing.

That quirk recorded the pause that matched his faint, months after implant. His heart muscle disease had shown no pacing need before the event. Stable artery disease and a preserved squeeze fraction gave no warning. The team swapped in a vein based dual chamber device with pacing. Serendipitous recordings deserve careful reading, the case argues.
pmc-13436786:
Yuan He and Shi-Lei Xue model necking in stretched epithelial sheets in 2026. Skin like tissues thin unevenly under pull, much like a plastic film necks. Their model joins single cell shape change and neighbor swaps to whole sheet stretch.

A neck starts when cell neighbor swaps pass a set condition, the math predicts. Computer vertex tests confirm both the start rule and the steady spread of the neck. Defects in messy tissues start necks early yet slow their spread. Necks can pinch into a thin thread, as seen in real embryos. The rules may help read birth defects of tube closure.
pmc-13437286:
Xiaojing Kan and colleagues built a computer model to tell harmless lung spots from cancerous ones using a special kind of CT scan. Dual-energy scanning measures how tissue handles two X-ray strengths, yielding values such as iodine content and atomic makeup. Their 2026 study gathered scans from 209 hospital patients with a single lung nodule each; 166 nodules proved malignant and forty-three benign.

The team first modeled the scan's measured values, then mined hundreds of image texture traits from several scan phases. Six learning methods were tried, and the best texture model was merged with the measurement model. In the held-out test set, the combined model reached an accuracy score well above either part alone. It caught eighty percent of cancers and correctly cleared over ninety percent of benign spots. The authors note the single-hospital, backward-looking design, so wider testing comes next.
pmc-13438386:
Ting Zhou and a large team review gastric cancer as the product of a three-way conversation among gut microbes, inherited genes, and epigenetic marks, chemical tags tuning genes without changing their code. Stomach cancer ranks among the world's deadliest cancers. The bacterium Helicobacter pylori, carried by half of humanity, is a proven driver, yet genes and habits decide who falls ill.

The circuit runs both ways. A person's genes and epigenetic settings shape which microbes settle in the stomach. Those microbes and their products then rewrite epigenetic marks, switching cancer genes on and tumor guards off. Epstein-Barr virus, salty diets, smoking, and alcohol feed into the same web. Walking through each strand and their crossings, the review assembles targets for prevention and treatment that single-lens research misses. The authors frame the triad as the field's organizing puzzle: decode the conversation, and precise intervention gets closer.
pmc-13439686:
Teng and colleagues presented EMmvGWAS in 2026, a faster engine for genome-wide association studies that test many traits at once. Single-trait scans waste the correlations between traits, yet joint analysis can boost power to find gene effects, including variants that sway several traits. The catch is cost: estimating complex covariance structures across the whole genome is slow.

The new method estimates the genetic and environmental covariance once, from a background model, using an expectation-maximization routine. It then holds their ratio fixed while scanning markers, which yields closed-form answers at each site and slashes run time without losing power. Tests on simulated data and real sets from rice, mice, and humans showed the speed held up in practice. The free R package also handles the single-trait case, and the authors pitch it for breeding and human genetics alike.
pmc-13439886:
Ze-Xuan Wu and colleagues test two weakened Toxoplasma strains as sheep vaccines against the widespread parasite, reporting in 2026. Toxoplasma gondii infects nearly all warm-blooded animals and causes abortion in ewes. The one sold vaccine has a short shelf life and may regain strength. Each test strain lacks a single gene that the parasite needs for full virulence. Sheep received neck-muscle injections, then faced parasite challenges at one month and again at ten weeks.

Both vaccines caused only brief fever after dosing. Antibody levels rose fast after challenge and stayed high. Vaccinated sheep showed mild organ changes, far less brain inflammation on tissue checks, and far fewer brain cysts than unvaccinated challenged sheep. Parasite loads also fell across measures. The authors present both strains as safe, protective candidates worth further development for flock use.
pmc-13439986:
Sghyar and a large team synthesize and analyze new tetrazole compounds in this 2026 chemistry study. Tetrazoles are five-membered rings rich in nitrogen that appear in medicines and corrosion inhibitors. The authors made two substitution families of these rings under phase-transfer conditions. They confirmed the structures with nuclear magnetic resonance and X-ray crystallography. Then they probed likely behavior with several kinds of computer simulation.

Synthesis yields ranged widely, from about a fifth to nearly quantitative, across the series produced. Quantum calculations showed one compound had the smallest energy gap between its key electron levels, at about 3.39 electronvolts in the reported model, hinting at high reactivity. Docking against Abl kinase, a cancer target, gave favorable binding scores for the best derivatives, and simulations showed the resulting complexes stayed stable over a hundred-nanosecond run.
pmc-13441286:
Petelinsek and colleagues published a 2026 teaching piece on coping after a patient dies. Emergency doctors face patient death again and again across their shifts. Few get formal training in how to carry that weight. The team shares a short breathing method built for busy clinical floors.

The Three Breath Method uses three slow, guided breaths to settle the mind. A four-minute teaching video walks viewers through the full routine step by step. The team surveyed doctors on the method and on a moment-of-silence practice. Both tools aim to cut stress and help staff process loss between patients. The piece reports how doctors judged their own ability to cope afterward. The routine takes under a minute, so it fits even hectic shifts.
pmc-13441786:
Xichun Wang and colleagues predict which ankle fracture patients will develop joint arthritis by feeding joint-fit mechanics from printed bone models into machine learning, reporting in 2026. Arthritis follows twenty to forty percent of ankle fractures even when surgery restores the anatomy on X-ray.
