Records covered 263 patients whose operations were planned on three-dimensional printed models between 2020 and 2024, each followed at least two years. Computer stress analysis of the prints yielded contact pressure and pressure unevenness measures.

Arthritis developed in about thirty-nine percent of patients. Those patients had shown far higher peak contact pressure and more uneven pressure maps on their pre-surgery models. The best algorithm, a gradient-boosted model, separated future arthritis well in validation, and clearly beat a version denied the mechanics data. Even among patients with textbook anatomic repairs, a high-pressure subgroup developed arthritis at triple the low-pressure rate.
pmc-13441886:
Matthias Meyer-Bender and colleagues release a Python toolbox that carries multiplexed tissue imaging from raw pictures to cell statistics in one framework, reporting in 2026. Multiplexed immunofluorescence stains many proteins in intact tissue at single-cell resolution, cheaply and at scale. Analysis, though, splinters across tools for cutting out cells, cleaning images, typing cells, and aligning coordinates. Their package, spatialproteomics, chains those steps together with shared coordinates across data types.

Demonstrations used lymph node and B cell lymphoma images from 132 patients. The full pipeline ran from raw slides to statistical portraits of how cell mixes and layouts differ between slow and aggressive lymphomas. The package also handled gigapixel whole-slide images, the largest routine pathology files. The authors aim the open toolbox at any laboratory wrestling highly multiplexed fluorescence data through a reproducible path.
pmc-13443186:
Hongyoon Kim and colleagues build a camera-based sensor that spots biomolecules without a spectrometer in a 2026 paper. Light gear that reads spectra is bulky and dear, which bars field tests. Their chip grades its surface pattern in a smooth slope, so each spot rings at its own light hue.

One camera shot thus reads a full spectrum, with steps as fine as 0.1 nm across a 30 nm band. The chip spans just 300 micrometers, a hair-scale footprint. Label-free tests caught proteins and DNA down to a limit of 388 picomolar strength. Sharpness marks beat many bulkier light sensors in their checks. The authors pitch the chip for cheap point-of-care tests that run outside stocked labs.
pmc-13443886:
Lindsey Hall and colleagues track drug-proof gut germs in a surgery intensive care unit in India in a 2026 study. The germs, CP-CRE, make enzymes that break carbapenem drugs, a last-line class. Patients gave rectal swabs at unit entry, unit exit, and hospital exit from July to November 2023, while ward surfaces faced checks as well.

Over a quarter of patients carried the germs on entry, at a 27 percent share of the cohort. Past hospital stays and two-plus drug rounds raised that risk. Among 148 who entered clean, 42 picked up the germs, a 36.5 percent share of those rechecked. Gene reads found blaNDM in 84 percent of isolates, with blaOXA next. Matched strains in E. coli and Klebsiella hint at ward spread.
pmc-13444186:
Hye-Mi Lee and colleagues update Korea's child sedation guidelines in a 2026 paper. Safe sedation for child procedures turns on drug picks, staff skill, right-size monitors, and each child's state. The Korean Society of Pediatric Anesthesiologists led the rewrite, the first full update since the 2017 edition.

Expert consensus weighed fresh drug and tech gains, tuned for bedside use. Rules span who may sedate, pre-checks and fasting, age-tied risk grades, and heart-lung watch. Depth grades, crisis steps for breathing trouble, and firm discharge marks fill the back half. The guide speaks to both clinicians and guardians who face procedure choices. The authors aim for even, safe care across Korea's varied sites, from big centers to small clinics.
pmc-13444286:
Marie-Lee Pelletier and colleagues probe how splicing of one intron leans on its neighbors in a 2026 study. Mammal genes cut out many introns in a set order, and late cuts can need early ones, for reasons that stayed murky. Their test rig copies the human gene EIF4G2 with its full intron set in miniature.

A late intron's tie to its neighbor ran partly through the next cut site downstream, which fits the exon definition model. Intron length played no part in the tie in their runs. The tie also needed a prior act of splicing downstream, not set marks in the neighbor introns. The authors say splicing acts form a linked chain, not solo cuts. That chain view may explain odd gene faults that skip whole exons.
pmc-13444486:
Aryan Mehta and Saraschandra Vallabhajosyula examine how body mass and old age shape results after catheter valve replacement in a 2026 paper. Aortic stenosis, a tight heart valve, hits about 5 percent of adults past 65 years in Western lands. Catheter replacement, TAVR, now treats severe cases across risk bands.

Fat states touch more than 40 percent of United States adults and color access paths, lung load, and scan reads in such care. Past work in many ills shows a so-called obesity paradox, where heavier patients fare better than lean peers. That odd pattern makes BMI a tricky risk mark for TAVR teams. The authors sort what registry and study data say on weight and age together, to guide pre-care risk checks.
pmc-13445486:
Reza Hemmati Baghbanani and colleagues test tweaks to timed breeding programs for Holstein dairy cows during summer, in a 2026 herd study. Such programs use hormone shots to line up ovulation for planned insemination, since heat signs in high-yield cows are faint. The team varied the gap between a first program and the breeding program, and added a hormone shot before breeding.

Stretching the gap between the two programs left follicle size at the first breeding shot unchanged, yet it lowered fertility. The added shot, prostaglandin F2α, lowered progesterone levels at that same point but did not change fertility. Summer herds gain a clear steer: keep the standard gap, and expect no fertility lift from the extra shot.
pmc-13446186:
Alok K. Mishra and colleagues comment on fresh evidence that gut stem cells keep a lasting chemical memory of inflammation, one that primes later cancer, in a 2026 piece. Long-term gut inflammation is a known cancer risk, yet how a brief flare can echo for years was unclear. The study under discussion, by Nagaraja and co-workers, tracked that echo in mouse colon.

After colitis healed, the stem cells' gene switches stayed altered for more than a hundred days, far past the gut lining's normal renewal span. Gene activity settled back to baseline while the switch layout stayed changed, a hidden readiness the authors call epigenetic memory. The piece frames that memory as a new axis of cancer risk, with promise for early markers and preventive drugs.
pmc-13446286:
Omar W. Azmeh and colleagues discuss a blinded trial of ear surgery for Ménière's disease, a disorder of spells of spinning, hearing loss, and ringing, in a 2026 commentary. The surgery under test blocks the inner ear's lymph duct, a gentle option long backed by loose reports rather than firm trials. The trial, by Schenck and co-workers, set blockage against a milder decompression operation.

No clear short-term edge for blockage appeared in spinning control, quality of life, ear function, or need for more care. Patients who entered with strong faith that surgery would help were more likely to gain, which fits the known pull of expectation in this disease. The commentary praises the blinded, multi-center design and urges doubt toward older unblinded claims.
pmc-13447086:
Igor Obreht and colleagues split the summer and winter arms of the South Asian monsoon in a sea sediment core off Pakistan, in a 2026 study. The core spans the last thaw, roughly sixteen thousand to twelve thousand years ago, read at finer than decade steps. Sea warmth there answers to winter winds, while ocean growth answers to summer winds, a rare natural split.

Summer winds tracked high northern climate swings on hundred to thousand year scales. Winter winds faded over the span in step with world warming, with faster wiggles laid on top. Weak winter winds went with more winter rain outside the monsoon pattern. The split reading sharpens how old rain records are read and may tune climate models for the low latitudes.
pmc-13447486:
Laurelle Jackson and a large team map early immune responses to a flu vaccine in place and time using spatial gene mapping in 2026 mouse work. Vaccines act first at the injection site, then in draining lymph nodes, yet detailed maps joining both places over time were missing. A recombinant flu protein with an oil-in-water booster, called an adjuvant, was the test vaccine.

Muscle and lymph nodes were collected one and seven days after injection for two spatial profiling methods. Lymph nodes showed early innate activation outside follicles on day one, then adaptive programmes inside follicles by day seven, with a growing cluster of germinal centre type B cells. Muscle showed chemical calls for immune cells on day one, concentrated in fibre-rich support layers. Blood signals rose briefly, and flu-specific antibodies increased alongside the tissue programmes.
pmc-13448086:
Chengkang Zhou and colleagues use a quantum information measure as a heat probe in frustrated magnets in 2026 computational work. Quantum spin ice is an exotic magnetic state where spins refuse to order and excitations split into fractions. Entanglement is central to such states yet hard to measure in real materials, since most lab tools see only local effects.

Quantum Fisher information, accessible through neutron scattering experiments, bounds how entangled a system is across many particles. New simulation methods computed that measure across temperatures and momenta for a three-dimensional lattice. Its pattern cleanly separated ordered, critical and two spin ice phases, and traced two crossover scales on cooling. Results connect to experiments on cerium-based materials, suggesting the measure works as a sensitive heat and motion probe for frustrated magnets.
pmc-13448686:
Guojuan Wang and colleagues report in 2026 a sintering method that takes only seconds yet improves ceramic phosphors for laser-driven lights. The rapid pulsed heating produced dense ceramics with fine grains at the same time, a pairing that is usually hard to achieve. Their test material was a cerium-doped lutetium aluminum garnet ceramic.

The fast-sintered ceramic converted light 31 percent more efficiently and resisted fracture about 1.5 times better than conventionally made material. A composite version glowed white under blue laser light with a color rendering index of 93. The team also built a model that predicts emission color within 5 nanometers across a wide range, pointing toward lights for displays and visible-light communication.
pmc-13448786:
Jiani Liu and colleagues recount in 2026 a breast cancer case where early weak response to standard pre-surgery treatment prompted a timely switch. The tumor was hormone-sensitive and tested in the middle HER2 range, confirmed positive by a second genetic test. After two cycles of dual HER2 antibody therapy with chemotherapy, scans showed only limited shrinkage.

The team changed the regimen to trastuzumab plus pyrotinib, a HER2-blocking pill, along with nab-paclitaxel. Surgery afterward found no remaining invasive cancer, the outcome known as total pathological complete response, which predicts better long-term survival. The only notable side effect was mild, manageable diarrhea. The authors present this response-guided switch as a strategy worth testing in larger groups, since roughly four in ten patients miss complete response on the standard approach.
pmc-13448986:
Arshad Hussain and colleagues report in 2026 a real-world study from Pakistan of a lower-cost biosynthetic form of semaglutide for type 2 diabetes. The thirty-week, multi-center study followed 217 adults starting the drug in routine outpatient care, without the tight controls of a trial. It tracked blood sugar, weight, waist size, patient satisfaction, quality of life, and side effects.

Average HbA1c fell from 9.27 percent to 7.41 percent, a drop of 1.86 points. By the end, 76.6 percent of patients were below 8.0 percent, and mean body weight had fallen by 7.84 kilograms, with three quarters losing at least 5 percent. Treatment satisfaction and physical quality of life both improved significantly. Side effects were mostly mild stomach complaints, and no severe low-blood-sugar episodes occurred, which the authors say matches the known profile of the original drug.
pmc-13449786:
Jos Timanta Tarigan describes in 2026 a preprocessing tool that strips invisible triangles from game characters before a top-down mobile game ever renders them. Such games lock their cameras inside a tight envelope of angles and distances, yet character meshes are usually built as if visible from anywhere, wasting rendering work every frame. The method, ACSCull, formalizes that envelope as an admissible camera set defined by pitch, yaw, distance, field of view, and aspect ratio.

Sampled cameras and poses render into a target that tags each triangle, and anything never seen is deleted, with the mesh re-exported in standard glTF Binary format for existing engines. The pass removes 27 to 55 percent of triangles from skinned characters. Image similarity against the uncut models stayed at or above 0.9999 within the envelope and 0.9997 under modest camera perturbations, and the tool composes with ordinary mesh simplifiers.
pmc-13451886:
Yantong Wu and a large team trace in 2026 how one gene change drives gum overgrowth in a child with a rare gum disease. The gene, KCNK4, builds a potassium channel, and the change swapped one building block in its chain. The team grew the child's gum cells, built matching mutant cell lines, and checked a mouse model.

Mutant gum cells divided faster, died less, and laid down more scar-like tissue. Gene reads pointed to a growth path, MAPK with its ERK branch, switched on too high. Drugs that block or boost that path shifted the imbalance, which backs the path as a driver. The work gives the rare disease a mechanism and a drug lead.
pmc-13452386:
Yubing Zhang, Madeline K Coates, Marta I Garrido, and Sarah M Tashjian study how the teenage brain judges safety. Their 2026 paper asks how brain circuits that weigh threat and protection change with age. Threat means cues that signal danger, while protection means resources that make a person safer.

Thirty three teens took part in scans with a strong 7 tesla MRI machine while they judged threat and protection. Younger teens, aged 12 to 14, drew more on the hippocampus, a region tied to memory. Older teens used a wider circuit that linked the hippocampus with the front lower part of the brain. A wider group of 63 people aged 12 to 40 showed the least exact safety judgments in mid to late teen years.
pmc-13453486:
Xia and colleagues reviewed in 2026 antibacterial sonodynamic therapy, a method that uses low-intensity ultrasound to switch on nanoscale materials that then flood bacteria with reactive oxygen species. Antibiotics are losing ground to resistance, and light-based versions of this idea reach only a centimeter into tissue. Ultrasound reaches several centimeters deep, which suits infections buried in bone or muscle.

The review traces the full chain. Sound triggers the particles, particles spawn the reactive oxygen, and that oxygen rips bacterial membranes and breaks DNA, ending in a ferroptosis-like death. It then sorts the design tricks that make particles stronger, from shaping their form to building in defects and tuned interfaces. Applications span bone infection, periodontitis, muscle infection, and chronic stomach infection.
pmc-13454586:
Pascal Schneider and seven colleagues analyze, in a 2026 study, why tree deaths are climbing across French forests. The team mined the national forest inventory for over 500,000 trees tracked from 2015 to 2023. Mortality rose across major species during those years. Ensemble models paired with explainable machine learning sorted the likely drivers.

Tree size, crowding, and seasonal weather oddities topped the list. Warm winters and springs appeared most often, perhaps by scrambling seasonal timing and letting pests survive the cold months. Three drought patterns emerged, matching slow starvation, sudden water failure, and blocked recovery after dry spells. Oddly wet springs also predicted deaths, above all in tall temperate species, perhaps because lush spring growth overshoots what later drought allows. The authors argue that seasons interact rather than single extremes acting alone.
pmc-13456386:
Dehua Liu and six colleagues map, in a 2026 bibliometric study, the research landscape around gas molecules and knee cartilage repair. Injured cartilage heals poorly because it lacks blood vessels and nerves. Medical gases such as nitric oxide, oxygen, hydrogen, and hydrogen sulfide have emerged as candidate helpers, alongside growth factors that rebuild cartilage and inflammatory signals that destroy it.

Using visualization tools on the Web of Science database, the team charted who publishes, what clusters together, and where attention is moving. Reactive oxygen species hold a double role in the literature, damaging cartilage yet also signaling repair. Most gathered work concerns slow degeneration rather than sudden injury, a gap the authors flag. Their maps aim to show newcomers the field's core authors, hot topics, and the thin spots where gas-based repair strategies still lack proof.
pmc-13456886:
Mariya B. Doctor and Sayan Basu describe, in a 2026 report, two eye patients whose chemical burns damaged a deeper corneal layer than doctors first treated. Burns usually scar the cornea's surface and starve it of stem cells. A transplant of limbal tissue, called SLET, can rebuild that surface. Both patients received it.

Despite stable grafts, their corneas stayed swollen and the surface kept breaking down. The pattern pointed deeper, to the endothelial pump layer that keeps the cornea clear. Detailed scans showed a thickened cornea, a wrinkled back membrane, and bumpy growths on the pump cells. Both patients then had that back layer replaced with donor tissue. Vision improved clearly, with a stable surface and a compact cornea at last review. The authors warn that hidden pump failure can masquerade as graft failure, and that scans can unmask it when cell counting is impossible.
pmc-13457286: TACE plus microwave destroying followed by immune therapy and anti-VEGF/TKI for liver cancer — success and safety. Yang Fang, Jiangyu Tan, and others test the combination. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is HCC combination therapy. It tests the multi-modal regimen's success and safety.
pmc-13459286:
Lele Wang and co-authors tested whether melatonin, a hormone best known for sleep, can also shield bougainvillea plants from drought both above and below ground. Drought shrinks the ornamental shrub's range and raises maintenance costs. Their 2026 pot experiment imposed natural drought on a bougainvillea variety, with and without melatonin treatment. It measured leaf physiology alongside the microbial community living around the roots, using DNA sequencing and network analysis to track how the root zone ecosystem responded.

Drought alone stressed the plants: protective enzymes and proline rose, but leaf water and chlorophyll fell and damage markers accumulated, while root microbe networks grew fragile. Melatonin pushed protection further, raising antioxidant enzyme activity and proline while cutting the damage marker and restoring leaf status. Below ground it enriched beneficial Proteobacteria, steadied fungal balance, and strengthened microbial networks and their carbon and nitrogen processing.
pmc-13459386:
Odong Christopher and co-authors asked whether poor diet in older Ugandans is linked with dementia, a link shown in wealthy countries but barely studied in low income settings. Their 2026 study reviewed 210 older patients from three Kampala hospitals, one public and two private. It sorted diet status from records and tested dementia links with models run separately for underfed and well fed patients, to reveal differing risk profiles in each group.

Poor diet affected 25 percent of the participants, who averaged about seventy six years old. After adjustment, underfed patients carried higher odds of dementia; the adjusted odds ratio was 2.57 in the primary model. Within the underfed group, a history of cardiovascular disease stood out, raising dementia odds to 5.80. Among well fed patients, only advancing age predicted dementia on its own, at seven percent higher odds per year. The authors urge diet screening in care of older adults.
pmc-13460186:
Yan Ren and colleagues examined in 2026 why kidneys fail after Sun's procedure, a major operation for acute type A aortic dissection, and who fares worst afterward. Their Zunyi cohort held 128 consecutive patients treated between January 2022 and October 2024. Kidney injury struck 91 patients, a strikingly high 71 percent, and sixteen needed continuous dialysis-style treatment.

Factors tied to injury included clamp time on the aorta, first-day kidney function values, ventilation duration, intensive care stay, and albumin-related measures around surgery. Albumin indicators survived the multivariable model as significant associations. Among injured patients followed for thirty days after discharge, comparisons between survivors and those who died hunted for warning signs. The authors argue that flagging high-risk patients early could focus protective care where it counts.
pmc-13460386:
Nazar, Ajaykumar, and Ayyappan test myristicin, a compound from nutmeg, against triple-negative breast cancer in this 2026 study. This cancer type lacks the hormone receptors that many drugs target, so chemotherapy remains central and new options are needed. The team treated MDA-MB-231 cancer cells in dishes, then gave the compound to mice carrying 4T1 breast tumors.

In cells, myristicin triggered mitochondria-mediated apoptosis. That is the self-destruction program run through the cell's energy centers. About 46 percent of treated cells showed death markers in flow tests. It lowered the protective protein Bcl2 while raising execution proteins such as caspase-3 and caspase-9 and the damage sensor p53. In mice, treatment shrank tumor weight and volume compared with untreated cancer controls, and tissue analyses confirmed stronger death signaling in the treated tumors.
pmc-13461386:
Kazuo Iwasa and colleagues compared in 2026 steroid-based treatment with steroid-sparing treatment in a small group of patients aged seventy or older with myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease that weakens muscles. Only twelve patients with the acetylcholine receptor antibody type, treated at one center, were included: seven took prednisolone with or without calcineurin inhibitors, and five took calcineurin inhibitors alone. Daily living and strength scores plus antibody levels were tracked for a year.

Daily living scores improved in both groups, more strongly with steroids, while strength scores improved only in the steroid group without a significant between-group gap. Antibody levels and time to minimal symptoms did not differ, and everyone reached minimal manifestations or better within a year. The authors stress how differently older patients respond, favoring tailored choices.
pmc-13461486:
Matko Spicijarić and colleagues present in 2026 a 47-year-old woman whose coronary artery tore spontaneously twice, the second time in the left main artery, the most dangerous address in the heart's plumbing. Her first dissection struck two months after childbirth four years earlier, causing a major heart attack. Stenting failed when doctors could not find the vessel's true channel and the attempt tore the artery further, so she underwent emergency bypass surgery instead.

Four years later a second heart attack revealed fresh dissection spanning the left main and two branches. This time camera-guided stenting inside the artery succeeded, and she went home stable with long-term follow-up and testing for underlying vessel disease planned. The authors stress personalized, multidisciplinary care for recurrent dissection.
pmc-13461586:
Cui and colleagues identified a 2026 set of mutations helping H5N1 bird flu adapt to mammals, centred on the viral PB2 protein. H5N1 circulates in wild birds and poultry and has spilled into United States dairy cattle and farm workers. Three PB2 changes kept appearing in viruses taken from cattle and other mammals between 2021 and 2024.

Tested singly and together, the changes E362G, D441N, and M631L cooperated to raise viral replication in mammalian cells, Cui found. The M631L change was the main driver, strengthening how PB2 grips a host protein called ANP32A that the virus needs. Mice infected with the triple mutant virus carried higher lung viral loads and worse lung damage. The authors flag M631L as a key marker to watch in surveillance.
pmc-13462186:
Sohaib Irfan and co-authors priced an ongoing antibody combo against a one time cell therapy for relapsed multiple myeloma, asking American payers which buys health more cheaply. The teclistamab plus daratumumab combo recently beat standard care decisively on progression free survival, while cilta-cel, a CAR T cell therapy, treats the same patients in a single infusion with heavy logistics. In their 2026 analysis, a partitioned survival model compared the two using their trial data from a United States payer perspective.

The antibody combo added 2.094 quality adjusted life years over the cell therapy in the model, a real health gain, but at an additional cost of about 565,686 dollars. At the standard willingness to pay threshold of 150,000 dollars per quality adjusted year, the combo did not count as cost effective against cilta-cel. Scenario checks, including lower real world adherence, left the conclusion intact.
pmc-13462286:
Xingxin Fu and colleagues hunt, in a 2026 data study, for gene markers tied to a cell death form, ferroptosis, in retinoblastoma, a childhood eye cancer. Ferroptosis depends on iron and fat damage, and may open treatment routes. The disease's drivers are incompletely mapped, and treatments remain limited. The team mined a public gene data set comparing tumors with healthy controls.

Screening narrowed to three ferroptosis-linked genes: NFE2L2, HSPB1, and JUN. All three were confirmed lower in a retinoblastoma cell line than in normal retinal cells. The genes' levels tracked with immune cells, including killer T cells and macrophages, hinting they shape the tumor's immune setting. Drug sensitivity predictions named three compounds whose effect varied with these genes. The authors present the trio as diagnostic markers for this eye cancer and as therapy leads, noting all drug ideas come from predictions, not patient trials.
pmc-13462386:
L Jai Vinita and V Vetriselvi propose, in a 2026 computing study, a layered learning system for connected vehicles that keeps data private while training models. Cars in the internet of vehicles generate uneven data, move constantly, and differ in computing power. Standard joint training, where cars send updates instead of raw data, slows under such conditions. Their design sorts vehicles through roadside units to a network controller, in three tiers.

Several tools work together: a normalized averaging method handling uneven local training, a reward scheme paying vehicles perks such as toll breaks, and a matching method borrowed from college admissions. In traffic simulations the system classified misbehavior with accuracy near 95 percent. It converged a third faster than the standard method and cut delay by nearly a third. The authors say the gains matter for crash response, where delays above a threshold endanger safety.
pmc-13462986:
Chenting Yan and colleagues report, in a 2026 chemistry study, the isolation of a rare germanium radical anion. The molecule carries both a negative charge and an unpaired electron on a germanium atom in a very low state. Such radicals are prized yet unstable, usually pairing up or falling apart at once. Bulky alkyl groups around the germanium shield it by sheer size, with little electronic help, letting the team bottle the species and study it.

The radical anion proved stable as a solid and in solution at room temperature. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy and computer modeling agreed the unpaired electron sits mostly on the germanium center. Reactivity tests showed behavior distinct from common carbon radicals, opening chemistry only a heavy-element center can offer. The authors offer the work as a step toward spin-based materials and new synthetic routes.
pmc-13463786:
Vargas-Garrido and co-authors analyzed Chilean insurance records in 2026 on recovery after commuting accidents. A commuting accident is an injury on the way to or from work. Their balanced sample held 10,940 accidents. Half involved absences of 90 days or more, and half were shorter. A statistical model estimated how each factor shifted the chance of prolonged recovery.

Clinical severity dominated the results. Cases classed as severe raised the chance of a long absence by well over half. Multiple diagnoses added about a fifth. Being male added roughly a tenth, and being 45 or older added slightly more. Accidents in the evening hours or from Friday to Sunday also tilted toward longer recovery. One surprise ran the other way. Injuries classed as traumatic came with much shorter absences than the rest. Return-to-work policy, the authors argue, should weigh timing and worker profile too.
pmc-13463886:
Liao Zhang and seven co-authors identify the touch sensor that lets worm-eating fungi spring their traps. These fungi build sticky nets or snare rings that inflate the moment a nematode worm brushes past. The sensor is a pressure-gated channel, a pore that opens under stretch, found across fungi with cell walls.

The channel gene woke up during hunts, early in the net builder and late in the ring builder. Fungi stripped of the channel grew poorly, made fewer spores, and formed weak traps. Ring traps in one species could not inflate at all. After worm contact the channel moved inside the cell and fired calcium signals that reset growth programs, marking touch as the trigger for the kill.
pmc-13465186:
Glasgow and colleagues turned the lens on implementation science itself in 2026. They tested whether a popular planning framework's parts relate the way its theory claims. Data came from 348 users of a free web tool. The tool walks projects through 21 questions based on the PRISM framework, which weighs local context. The RE-AIM framework supplies the outcome scores: reach, effectiveness, adoption, delivery, and upkeep of programs.

Seven of eleven pre-stated hypotheses held up fully or partly. Upkeep scores indeed ran lowest among the outcome dimensions, as predicted. Reach and effectiveness were not the least related pair, contrary to expectation. On every dimension, equity items scored consistently below the general ratings. Those items ask who benefits and who is missed, a pattern the authors find telling. Hypotheses about context items fared worse, perhaps because each context domain gets only one question. The exercise produced early norms and questions worth rewriting.
pmc-13465586:
Ya-Shun Lo and colleagues describe a microfluidic chip, published in 2026, that grows fibroblast helper cells alongside early mouse embryos. The device uses a layered polydimethylsiloxane design with flowing medium, aiming to copy body conditions better than a still culture dish can. Helper cell survival inside the flowing chip reached about eighty-five percent in the first stage of testing.

The second stage compared four ways of growing mouse embryos, from plain well plates to the chip with and without helper cells. Blastocyst formation varied widely across those setups, with the standard plate highest in this small run. The authors report the figures descriptively, without statistical testing, and treat the results as an early guide for refining the platform.
pmc-13466286:
Małgorzata Fortuna, Antonina Kaczorowska, Jacek Szczurowski, and Zofia Ignasiak compare physical ability in care home men with and without treated heart disease and high blood pressure, in a 2026 study. Seventy-four residents aged sixty-five to eighty took part. Forty-four had no cardiovascular diagnosis, while thirty lived with both coronary disease and hypertension under treatment.

A short performance battery scored balance, walking speed, and chair stands, and a six-minute walk measured exercise tolerance. The design tests a practical worry: treated heart conditions may still leave residents weaker than peers even when medicines control the disease itself. Results speak to how much structured activity care homes should build into daily routines for this group.
pmc-13467786:
Yilin Guo and colleagues test in 2026 whether adding a microbial inoculant, a polyacrylamide soil conditioner, or both can keep cotton roots healthy when irrigation alternates between brackish and fresh water. Alternating water sources stretches scarce supplies in dry regions, but salt degrades soil structure, stresses plants, and quiets root-zone microbes. The greenhouse pot trial compared five watering and amendment regimes.

Measurements covered soil water and salt levels, soil physical traits, nutrient availability, microbial activity, root growth, and nutrient uptake by the plants. A path-modeling analysis then traced how soil conditions flow through roots to plant performance. Cotton growers in arid regions need exactly this kind of evidence: whether cheap biological and chemical soil aids can make marginal water usable without wrecking the root zone over a season.
pmc-13468486:
Wei Pan and co-authors run a two-year field trial in 2026 on using less water and more organic fertilizer for maize in the dry oasis farmland of northwestern China. The 2024-2025 experiment crossed three irrigation levels, from full watering down to a 30 percent cut, with three nitrogen strategies replacing zero, 15, or 30 percent of chemical nitrogen with organic fertilizer. Yields, soil carbon and nitrogen pools, and water-nitrogen productivity were all measured.

Ear length differed significantly across treatments, peaking at 17.39 to 17.68 centimeters under moderate watering with 15 percent organic substitution, and bottoming at 14.52 centimeters under the driest, fully chemical regime. Kernel counts and weights varied more subtly. A formal multi-criteria scoring model ranked the combinations overall. The practical aim is a recipe that trims scarce irrigation water and synthetic fertilizer while building soil carbon, a triple win dryland maize regions need.
pmc-13468586:
Jose Luis Chavez-Torres and colleagues measured how vetiver grass roots strengthen seven different Andean soils against sliding and shear. Roots can anchor soil and transfer stress, but the team suspected the benefit depends on the soil itself, not just the roots.

Bare and rooted samples were sheared under three loads at three depths, with statistics comparing cohesion and friction gains. Roots raised strength in every soil, but the pattern split: one soil, OL, doubled its cohesion, a full 100 percent gain. Another soil, CH, gained most in friction angle, up 20.1 percent, while a third balanced both gains. Soil type, more than depth, controlled the response, Chavez-Torres reports, so engineers should test each soil rather than assume one root effect.
pmc-13469286:
Khurram Nasir writes an editorial in 2026 arguing that coronary computed tomography is transforming cardiovascular risk prediction. Standards, he says, must climb with image quality. Reporting the mood of the 2026 Society of Cardiovascular Computed Tomography meeting, he describes a field shifting from probability scores, like the pooled cohort equations, toward directly measuring plaque buildup itself. Seeing plaque types, aided by artificial intelligence and combined anatomy and physiology, moves decisions closer to biology, he contends.

Nasir reminds readers that a foundational tool already exists: non-contrast coronary artery calcium testing for people without symptoms, a proven measure of disease burden. His title states the thesis plainly: better pictures demand a higher bar. Prettier pictures tempt overconfidence, and his editorial presses the specialty to demand outcome-grade evidence before new plaque metrics rewrite prevention guidelines.
pmc-13469586:
Qiuming Nan and co-authors report in 2026 on a fiber optic method that watches cracks grow inside a large concrete beam in real time. Point sensors miss much of the story because cracks spread across space and time. The team fitted a sixteen meter beam with an array of ultra weak fiber Bragg gratings, which sense strain along the fiber, and loaded the beam at mid span until it failed.

The array caught the first crack near a load of about 849 kilonewtons and followed cracks as their shape changed. By failure the beam held ninety cracks, the widest just over a millimeter. Peak strain tracked crack width closely enough to support a simple formula for judging severity. Ordinary strain gauges dropped out after cracking, while the fiber array kept recording throughout.
pmc-13469886:
Fengshan Li and eleven colleagues published this 2026 review on hydrogen sulfide, a gas bacteria make, as a central player in antibiotic tolerance. Tolerance lets bacteria survive drugs without classic resistance genes. Such cells and dormant persisters underlie relapsing infections, so breaking tolerance could restore old antibiotics. The authors organise recent work into the gas's defence pathways. They also survey new drugs that block its production inside bacteria, plus probes that track it under drug stress.

They describe three core defences. The gas binds iron to shield cells. It makes reactive sulfur species that blunt antibiotics and switch on drug-export pumps. And it throttles respiration to push cells into protective dormancy. Because the enzymes making the gas are conserved across pathogens yet differ from human versions, inhibitors could strip tolerance with low risk of new resistance. The review maps which species' key enzymes remain unidentified, a priority for drug discovery.
pmc-13470686:
Axell Lins and colleagues compare in 2026 how two forms of the anesthetic ketamine change brain rhythms in the rat visual cortex. Ketamine comes as a mixture of mirror image molecules and as the single S form, and the two may not act alike on the brain. Adult rats received the S form, the mixed form, or salt water, and electrodes on the cortex recorded fifteen minutes of activity in three phases.

The mixed form pressed activity down across all rhythm bands and held that suppression steady. The S form behaved differently over time: slow rhythms surged late in the recording, suggesting the anesthesia was wearing thin. It also kept more of the faster rhythms overall, while the mixed form kept one high band elevated, a known signature of this drug class. The authors tie the profiles to anesthetic choice.
pmc-13471186:
O'Connor and colleagues explored in 2026 how orthopaedic surgeons in South Africa understand lifelong learning, a required competency curricula rarely define in practice. Sixteen people took part: eight senior surgeons coordinating training and eight registrars, spanning all eight universities with orthopaedic programs. Interviews and focus groups ran over fourteen months, and themes were built from the transcripts.

Three views emerged: some saw it as a natural trait, a curiosity some doctors simply have. Others saw a habit of mind that can be deliberately built, and a third group framed it as a professional value, part of being a good doctor. Suggested cultivation strategies matched the views: mentorship, protecting curiosity, journal clubs, and research participation. The authors argue programs should stop treating learning as a box to tick. Training should both invite engagement and teach the craft of learning itself, through critical appraisal and scholarly work.
pmc-13471286:
Halavi Anjar and colleagues tested in 2026 whether gentle electric stimulation of the scalp can protect thinking during whole-brain radiotherapy for cancer that has spread to the brain. Radiation to the whole brain often dulls memory and attention. The method, called tDCS, passes a weak current through electrodes and can nudge brain activity.

Forty adults were assigned at random to real or sham stimulation over 20 sessions during their radiation course. The real group improved far more on working memory and sustained attention tasks, with correct answers rising sharply. Brain-wave recordings shifted toward calmer patterns, with two fast and slow wave bands dropping in power. Blood tests showed the treatment blunted the rise of stress and inflammation proteins that radiation usually triggers. The authors present tDCS as a promising add-on, pending larger trials.
pmc-13471486:
Kharroubi and colleagues graded the methods used in Tunisian medical theses that adapt psychiatric questionnaires across languages and cultures. Their 2026 evaluation covered 43 doctoral theses validating 50 scales, scored against global guidance for translation steps and psychometric testing.

Every scale received a direct translation, and 43 of the 50 got the recommended back-translation check. An expert committee reviewed only 28 scales and a pretest was run for just 17 of them. Validation samples ranged widely, from 58 to 2,577 participants, and 37 scales relied on easy access rather than probability sampling. Nearly all the theses, 98% of them, were written in French, and the authors call for uniform validation training.
pmc-13471586:
Sunil and Acharya checked whether the standard 4 mg dose of the anti-nausea drug ondansetron is enough for high-risk surgical patients under a mixed anaesthetic regimen. Their 2026 prospective study enrolled 150 adults aged 18 to 60, all given ondansetron before propofol induction and sevoflurane maintenance, and watched them for the first two hours after surgery.

Early nausea and vomiting stayed low: just 14 of 150 patients, or 9.3% of the cohort, had an episode, and most episodes were mild. The group averaged 39.9 years of age and was 63.3% women, the sex usually at highest risk. No demographic or surgical factor, from age to smoking history, significantly predicted who got sick, which the authors read as the standard dose doing its job.
pmc-13472086:
Bian and co-authors review what role stress theory says about the shock of becoming a nurse. Their 2026 narrative review applies the organisational theory to newly qualified nurses. The theory examines strain from unclear, conflicting, or overloaded role expectations. These nurses carry high stress into their first posts. That has consequences for retention and care quality.

The synthesis organises current findings on how role stress shows up in this group and what managers can do about it. Recommendations rest on three principles: intervene early, support continuously, and integrate multiple levels at once, pairing individual psychological support with organisational changes matched to each career stage. The authors are frank about evidence quality, urging better-designed intervention studies, more randomised trials, and long-term outcome tracking. Intelligent management technologies are flagged as an emerging aid for supportive work environments.
pmc-13472786:
Ando and colleagues ran a 2026 trial of alpha-linolenic acid, a plant omega-3 fat, in 120 healthy Japanese adults who feel cold easily. Participants took oils with a lower or higher daily dose of the fat, or a placebo oil, for twelve weeks in a double-blind design where neither side knew the assignments.

After cold exposure, skin blood flow and skin temperature recovered better in the fat groups during the early measurement period. A standard artery function test showed no overall group difference, but participants who started with poor artery function improved significantly on the fat. Allergy symptoms in the eyes and nose did not differ between groups. Blood levels of the fat rose in both dose groups, confirming the oils were absorbed as intended.
pmc-13473286:
Liang and colleagues present a 2026 methods paper on finding lung disease in chest X-rays without labeled abnormal examples.  The authors name three flaws in current rebuilding methods: pixel matching misses global structure, single-layer comparison is shallow, and error scores trade sensitivity against fidelity.

Their fix works in two domains at once, image space and frequency space, with adversarial learning and constraints that hold features consistent across layers and images. A scan that the model rebuilds poorly in either domain stands out as anomalous, and the rebuilt comparison also highlights where the problem sits. Better unsupervised screening matters most where radiologists are scarce: a system trained on normal scans alone can still raise the first alarm.
pmc-13474586:
Wangjin Liang and co-authors judge a strict policy in 2026 aimed at cutting risky sex work practices in one Chinese city. The 2015 rules in Baise city were treated as a natural test, with data from eleven counties over eleven years. Nearly twenty thousand records tracked knowledge rates, condom use at last paid encounter, and active syphilis rates. Trend breaks around the policy year were checked with care.

Knowledge and condom use rose across the whole span, both before and after the rules. Syphilis rates fell after 2015, yet formal checks found that fall fit chance patterns rather than a policy effect. Robustness tests backed the same verdict. Mandates alone showed no clear link to safer behavior here.
pmc-13474686:
Zhaojun Song and co-authors compare two cement-based fixes in 2026 for crushed spine bones in older adults with weak bones. One fix injects cement alone, while the other first inflates a small balloon to restore height. Records covered more than six hundred patients on the first fix and more than seven hundred on the second. All were followed for at least three years.

Pain and disability scores improved in both groups by discharge and at one year, then worsened somewhat by year three. Gaps between the two fixes stayed small at each check. Cement dose ran higher with the balloon method. Factor checks named bone density, leak, and new fractures among drivers of later disability.
pmc-13474786:
Jing Zhang and colleagues build a pre-surgery chart in 2026 to predict heavy drain output after robotic bile duct repair in children. The surgery fixes a cyst on the bile duct, and drains are placed by routine. No tool existed to flag which children would drain heavily. Records of 129 children were split by weight-adjusted daily drain volume.

Younger age clearly predicted heavy output, while larger cyst size showed a weaker trend in the same direction. The final chart blends cyst size, age, body mass, and two blood measures. It sorted high from low drainers fairly well and matched observed rates closely. Such a chart could support earlier drain removal for low-risk children.
pmc-13474886:
Zhang and colleagues pooled studies in 2026 on malnutrition among older people living in nursing homes, where poor eating quietly worsens many other conditions. They searched seven databases for observational studies through September 2024 and combined results on how common malnutrition is and what raises its risk. The final set held 25 studies covering 51,915 nursing home residents in total.

Across the pooled studies, 22 percent of residents were malnourished, a share the authors call a widespread problem for care homes. Poor appetite carried the strongest single link, with odds of malnutrition about 7.6 times higher in residents whose appetite was low. Needing help with daily activities, weak swallowing, and care dependence also raised risk sharply. Having three or more illnesses did too, while higher body mass index was protective. The team therefore proposes risk prediction models for care homes.
pmc-13476686:
Zili Zhen and co-authors pair two epigenetic drugs in 2026 against a deadly child brain tumor called diffuse midline glioma. The tumor carries a histone fault that scrambles gene control genome-wide. Stem-like tumor cells from brainstem and spinal tumors of patients fed drug tests. Two blockers, one for each of two gene-silencing systems, were tried alone and together.

The pair worked far better together than alone across the cell panel. Growth, self-renewal, and division programs fell while death and maturation signals rose. Stem-cell share dropped by more than ninety percent under the pair. In mouse implants, the pair shrank tumors, cut spinal spread, and lengthened survival.
pmc-13476886: Correction: Chen and colleagues correct their 2018 Stem Cell Reports paper on engineering human embryonic stem cells. The paper inserted a switchable tracer at the AAVS1 site, used to follow cell fates during development. The polymerase chain reaction image in one figure panel, used for genotyping, did not match the original data. The notice supplies the revised figure. The authors apologize for the inadvertent error and state that no text or figure legend needed changing and that the error does not alter the study's results or conclusions.
pmc-13477386:
Yihao Li and coauthors published a 2026 genetic study of the LPA gene region that controls lipoprotein(a), a fatty particle linked to artery disease. The data came from exome sequencing in the Washington Heights Inwood Columbia Aging Project. Participants included Caribbean Hispanic, Black, and non-Hispanic White older adults, groups often missing from genetic research.

The team catalogued more than 1,400 variants in the repeated Kringle IV type 2 section of the gene. Many variants tracked with copy number, particle size, and lipoprotein(a) levels. Three newly described variants were linked to high blood pressure across ancestry groups, and one variant was tied to lower nonfasting glucose. The authors say the biology connecting these variants to blood pressure and glucose still needs explanation.
pmc-13478486:
Savaş, Aras, and Özdemir review cases of violence against older adults in this 2026 forensic medicine study from Turkey. As populations age, physical and mental decline can leave people aged 65 and over more exposed to harm. The authors examined 275 case files and forensic reports from Dokuz Eylul University. The evaluations ran from January 2016 to January 2025. They recorded who was hurt, by whom, and with what injuries.

Men made up nearly two-thirds of victims, and the average age was about 71 and a half years. Strangers were the largest group of attackers, followed by friends and neighbors, and just over half of incidents happened at or near the home. Physical violence alone accounted for 86.5 percent of cases, bone fractures appeared in more than a quarter, and about one case in thirteen involved life-threatening injuries.
pmc-13478586:
Amariucai-Mantu and co-authors report a greener way in 2026 to build hybrid molecules joining triazole and pyridine rings to polyphenol units, structures with known germ-killing potential. Their one-pot method mixes three components in a single vessel under ultrasound, which speeds reactions through tiny collapsing bubbles. The team checked the method against green chemistry metrics and then tested the products against bacteria and fungi.

Reactions gave yields of 65 to 90 percent, used less solvent, and ran faster than conventional heating in the comparisons reported. Swapping in bromine-bearing starting material lifted yields fourfold, a notable halogen effect the authors flag for future designs. Some products killed Gram-positive bacteria at nanogram-per-milliliter levels, extremely dilute, and handled Gram-negative bacteria and fungi at microgram levels, supporting the scaffold as an antimicrobial starting point.
pmc-13479986:
Zhang and colleagues surveyed nursing students at Anhui University of Chinese Medicine in 2026 to predict which students will actually use artificial intelligence tools in study and clinical placements. The survey covered 178 full-time undergraduate and graduate students, measuring their education level, attitudes toward AI, and AI literacy, meaning how well they understand and judge these tools. A prediction chart called a nomogram turned the answers into an intention score.

Three factors carried the prediction: educational background, attitudes toward AI, and AI literacy, each significantly shaping intention to use the tools. The combined model separated likely users from unlikely ones with an accuracy score of 0.79 on the standard curve measure, which the authors call strong. They advise schools to teach AI skills directly and build positive attitudes early, rather than assuming access alone will drive adoption among nursing students.
pmc-13480086:
D Meghana and A Manimaran present a 2026 effort to sharpen computer detection of tooth decay on dental X-rays. Decay spots can be faint, and detectors trained on one set of images often falter on another. The team added attention blocks to a standard detector and used a search method to tune its training schedule. Tests ran on 1,887 X-rays gathered at a dental institute in Guntur, split into training, check, and test sets.

The tuned detector scored near the top on precision and recall, with an F1 score in the mid-nineties. Gains over the next best rival were large on the stricter overlap measures. The authors argue that attention deep in the network, paired with careful schedule choice, lifts both finding rate and box tightness. Dentists could use such a tool as a second reader, though tests on outside image sets still lie ahead.
pmc-13480286:
Firas Jaly and co-authors report a 2026 trick for clipping a badly leaking tricuspid valve when the leaflets gape too wide to grip. Two patients had torrential leaks with gaps of fifteen and eighteen millimetres, well past the range where clips usually succeed. The right-sided valve leaks when the heart ring stretches, so easing the blood load should shrink the ring for a short window.

The team briefly blocked the upper great vein with a balloon, cutting return flow to the right heart during the grip. The ring shrank, the gap nearly vanished, and clips landed with success in both cases, cutting the leak sharply. The authors offer the manoeuvre as a backup for anatomy that defeats standard clipping, while noting that only two cases support it so far.
pmc-13480486:
Desai and co-authors review in 2026 how newborn kidney injury is recognized and handled across Australia and New Zealand, arguing the condition is still missed too often. Babies' kidneys are unfinished at birth, with filtering units still forming and blood flow control immature, which leaves them exposed during intensive care. A shared definition, the modified neonatal KDIGO criteria, has finally let units compare rates and study the problem together.

Even so, the review finds wide variation between units in how babies are monitored, diagnosed, and followed after an injury episode ends. The authors press for kidney injury measures inside quality registries, fairer access to kidney care for infants, and routine checks for survivors, who face later chronic kidney disease. Prevention gets equal weight: watching drug doses that strain kidneys, using caffeine-like methylxanthine medicines where they help, and writing shared care protocols across both countries.
pmc-13481386:
Ilaria Bufalari and co-authors report a 2026 study of body sense in people lost to harmful daydreaming. Maladaptive daydreaming means vivid, compulsive fantasy that eats into daily life. The team surveyed 137 Italian speakers, 83 with the condition and 54 matched peers, scoring daydreaming strength, drifting-away experiences, and felt body awareness.

Daydreamers scored far higher on drifting experiences, chiefly deep absorption and feelings of unreality. They scored lower on body awareness parts covering focus control, body listening, and body trust. Web-style analysis placed daydreaming at the hub linking drifting and body sense. The authors suggest fantasy may serve as an escape from unpleasant body states. Care that rebuilds body trust, such as mindfulness training, might loosen the habit's grip.
pmc-13482186:
Lin and co-authors probe in 2026 how squeezing speed changes a family of high-entropy alloys, metals blended from five main elements rather than built around one. They cast three versions of an aluminum, chromium, iron, nickel, and titanium alloy, shifting the aluminum and titanium shares across the set. Slow compression tests and high-speed impact tests then measured strength, stretch, and how the metal finally tore apart.

All three alloys formed the same two crystal structures side by side, a face-centered and a body-centered phase sharing the material in each sample tested. The version with the least aluminum and most titanium gave the highest yield strength under both slow and fast loading in the experiments. Its two siblings stretched further before failing, and speed changed the fracture look, from fish-scale dimples under slow loads to torn dimples and flat cleavage faces under impact, signaling lost ductility.
pmc-13483486:
Chang Chen and co-authors present a 2026 study of an MRI-based model that predicts hidden cancer spread in bladder tumours before surgery. Spread into tiny vessels, called lymphovascular invasion, darkens the outlook and shapes treatment, yet doctors usually learn of it only after removal. The team gathered 543 patients across eight centres and trained a hybrid model mixing deep learning with hand-crafted image measures from tumour and rim.

Tested on fresh patients, the hybrid beat ten rival models, scoring near 0.77 at home centres and 0.75 at outside ones. Patients the model flagged as invaded died sooner in the training and home test groups, though the outside group showed only a trend. A scan-based forecast could help surgeons grade risk and plan care before the first cut.
pmc-13483686:
Jinguang Chen, Bin Lin, and Zhenbin Zhan evaluate a small regulatory RNA as a blood signal for artery clogging disease. Their 2026 study enrolls 131 patients with atherosclerosis and 112 controls, measuring the RNA miR-425-5p and a partner gene product in blood. Cell experiments with vessel wall muscle cells exposed to oxidized cholesterol probe how the RNA drives harm.

Blood levels of the RNA ran high in patients while the partner factor KLF7 ran low, a pattern mirrored in the cell model. Higher RNA levels tracked with thicker neck artery walls and worse blood fat profiles, and testing separated patients from controls with good sensitivity and specificity. Blocking the RNA eased cell damage, including death, movement, and inflammation, while silencing the partner factor added further relief. A blood test plus a mechanism are both offered.
pmc-13483986:
Lee and fellow doctors in Taiwan tracked in 2026 the long fates of more than fifteen thousand people who had a bleed inside the brain. Such bleeds, called intracerebral haemorrhage, split into types by cause and spot: deep bleeds from high blood pressure, and other bleeds that often sit near the surface. The team sorted first and repeat bleeds into four groups and linked ward records to death records over fifteen years.

One group showed a survival paradox. First bleeds not caused by blood pressure killed the most people in the first month, near one in four. Yet those who lived past that month went on to survive best of all groups. Deep bleeds from blood pressure came back most often, in about half of cases. People with repeat bleeds fared worst overall, with pneumonia and diabetes driving many later deaths.
pmc-13484486:
Pradeep and team tallied the energy use, carbon emissions, and lifetime cost of nine road pavement designs, five flexible and four rigid. Indian road standards set the designs, which were sized for traffic from 30 to 150 million standard axles over their service lives. Their 2026 analysis counted both construction and scheduled maintenance, then tested greener swaps such as furnace slag replacing up to half the cement and recycled aggregates up to 30 percent.

Rigid and flexible designs traded advantages as traffic load grew, with thickness and material volumes driving the totals in the comparisons reported. The alternative-material scenarios trimmed embodied energy and carbon compared with the conventional mixes they mirrored. Maintenance cycles added a substantial share of lifetime impact, not just the initial build. Pradeep argues designers should weigh lifetime energy and carbon beside upfront price when choosing pavement types.
pmc-13485086:
Narayanan argued in a 2026 commentary that no single visual field test can fairly decide whether a person with sight defects is safe to drive, responding to a study of license applicants. The study had found that about one in twenty-two applicants had both-eye field defects that would fail British standards for heavy vehicles, with glaucoma the leading cause. Its authors proposed one standard field test and an accredited examiner panel.

Narayanan counters that real driving uses head and eye movement together, so a fixed-gaze test poorly matches the road. People also adapt: the seeing eye fills gaps, and experience aids coping. Telling whether a crash came from a field defect or a lapse of attention is nearly impossible. The commentary urges flexible standards and simulator testing rather than one rigid cutoff.
pmc-13487186:
Armengol-Badia and team explored why a common IV fluid calms inflammation in acute pancreas inflammation, focusing on tiny parcels that cells release into the blood. Those parcels, small outside-cell vesicles, can activate immune cells and spread inflammation beyond the pancreas. Their 2026 study treated vesicles from pancreatic cells with lactate, the active ingredient in Lactated Ringer's fluid, and also sampled vesicles from patients receiving that fluid or plain saline.

Lactate-treated vesicles provoked far less immune gene activity in macrophages, without being taken up any less by the cells. A chemical tag called lactylation rose modestly on vesicle proteins after lactate exposure. Vesicles from fluid-treated patients showed the same calming pattern, while saline patients' vesicles did not. Armengol-Badia proposes lactylation as the fluid's hidden mechanism, pending direct proof.
pmc-13487386:
Jerine AJ van der Eijk and four colleagues published this 2026 animal welfare study asking whether giving broiler chickens a choice of light brightness helps them. Vision drives much chicken behaviour, and slower-growing breeds are used more in production. The team compared uniform dim lighting at 20 lux with a gradient running from 20 to 200 lux, in pens of fast-growing Ross 308 and slower-growing Hubbard JA757 birds.

Birds were housed in groups of 346 per pen until reaching about 2.6 kilograms. Gradient lighting slightly reduced body weight and feed intake in both breeds. Slower-growing birds were cleaner under the gradient and grew more active in bright zones, while fast-growing birds gathered more in bright light and slower-growing birds in dim light. The gradient also reduced drinking and raised both fear of humans and play behaviour. The authors found no clear welfare gain or loss from offering the light choice.
pmc-13488286:
Poning Hu and co-authors pool evidence on tertiary lymphoid structures in bladder cancer in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. These structures are organized immune cell clusters that form inside tumors, a bit like temporary lymph nodes, and they may help the body fight cancer. Eight studies with 1,706 patients supplied survival data, while six more described response to immunotherapy, where drugs release immune brakes.

Cancers rich in these structures came with notably better overall, progression-free, and disease-free survival in pooled results. Starting levels alone predicted immunotherapy response poorly, yet growth in number, density, and maturity during treatment tracked with good response across the descriptive studies. The authors call for larger prospective work to confirm a monitoring role.
pmc-13488586:
Sibyl Siluvai and colleagues survey dental students on what makes classroom lectures work in a 2026 cross-sectional study at a dental college in Tamil Nadu, India. Two hundred eighty students answered a pretested anonymous questionnaire over three months, rating forty-five statements about lecture delivery on a three-point agree scale, alongside background and study history questions. Every invited student responded, and women made up the large majority of the sample.

Most students held a middle, average attitude toward lecture quality overall, with a positive lean in the authors' summary. Attitudes did not differ significantly across study years. The authors recommend regular checks of both teaching and student performance, plus more interactive methods to lift a format they describe as inherently passive, even when students rate lecturers kindly.
pmc-13493686:
Jonathan I Silverberg leads a seventeen-author team building in 2026 a durability index for three eczema biologics, asking which drug keeps working when real patients inevitably miss doses. Trial data for lebrikizumab, dupilumab, and tralokinumab included both stay-on-drug and stop-drug arms, so the index blends those results across every adherence level from zero to full.

Lebrikizumab beat dupilumab on clear-skin outcomes across most adherence levels up to roughly three quarters compliance, after which the two converged. Against tralokinumab it won at every adherence level on both scoring systems tested. Dupilumab in turn beat tralokinumab once adherence passed about seventy percent, and on the broader improvement measure at all levels. Because the index itself is brand new, the authors insist on independent validation before clinicians lean on it.
pmc-13493886:
Eltamaly and Almutairi predict how lithium-ion batteries wear out without the laboratory calibration each new battery chemistry normally demands. Their 2026 hybrid model mixes a learning network with hard physical rules. Ageing speeds up with heat in a known pattern, repeated stress tires materials like metal fatigue, and health can only decline, never recover. Training used ordinary operating data rather than lab-derived parameters, on one chemistry, checked on a second, and benchmarked on a third.

Despite the three chemistries ageing through different voltage patterns, the model's health estimates stayed within a fraction of a percent of measured values on the reported error measure. Its predicted health curves also kept sensible shapes on chemistries it had never been trained on, including the iron-phosphate type common in grid storage. The authors present the system as ready for battery managers in vehicles and storage plants that switch chemistries often.
pmc-13495286:
Miao-Miao Zhao and colleagues link, in a 2026 study from Beijing, Helicobacter pylori infection with insulin resistance and heart risk. The stomach germ infects over half the world and has been tied to ills beyond the gut, though its heart links stay disputed. The team studied 1,398 adults at health checks, testing for the germ with a breath test and scoring ten-year heart risk by a standard formula.

Infected adults showed higher scores on a sugar-and-fat index of insulin resistance, and those index values tracked strongly with heart risk scores. Estimated ten-year risk ran higher in the infected group, and the link held after other factors were counted. The tie stood out most in women, in those under fifty, and in people without classic risk factors such as smoking or diabetes. The authors float the germ as a non-traditional heart risk worth probing further.
pmc-13495386:
Jade Newton and colleagues build, in a 2026 article, rule-based language software that stages cancers for the Western Australian registry. Staging, which grades a tumor's size and spread, drives treatment and planning, yet collecting it by hand at population scale eats staff time. Their systems read pathology reports and hospital data to pull out staging parts and grade melanoma, breast, and bowel cancers by the standard manual.

Checked against hand-built collections, the systems staged about nine in ten cases right. The melanoma system scored highest, with breast and bowel systems close behind. The approach leans on expert-written rules rather than trained models, which suits places with little training data. The authors present the tools as a way to partly automate registry staging and free officers for the hard cases, with more data sources likely to lift accuracy further.
pmc-13495586:
Ana M Barragán-Montero leads a large team building, in a 2026 study, a deep learning model that draws the organs at risk for brain tumor radiotherapy. Treatment planning needs 25 such organs outlined on scans, following the European Particle Therapy Network atlas, yet many centers skip some because hand contouring is slow. The team trained the model on 74 patients and tested it with cross-validation so each patient was scored on unseen data.

A model fed both contrast MRI and CT scans won, matching expert outlines closely on standard overlap measures. Adding a third scan type, T2 FLAIR, brought no further gain. The authors present the tool as a way to spread uniform, atlas-grade contouring to centers that now omit organs for lack of time. That spread would also make side-effect data across trials easier to pool.
pmc-13499386:
Jung wrote an obituary in 2026 for Dr Wan-Kyu Cho, a founder of modern biological science in Korea, who died that July at the age of 98. Cho built his career at Seoul National University over some thirty-six years, working first under postwar scarcity so severe that basic lab supplies were missing. Turning to human genetics when bench work was impossible marked his path.

Cho pioneered developmental biology in Korea, above all the control of egg maturation. He showed that the signal molecule cyclic AMP could reversibly hold mouse egg meiosis in check, a finding that fed the wider understanding of cell-cycle control. His micro-tube culture method gave labs a cheap way to grow and move eggs and embryos. Jung credits Cho with shaping Korean science far beyond his bench, through educating generations, defending university autonomy, promoting biotechnology, and opening Korean science to the world.
pmc-13499686:
Pandya and colleagues compared caregiver burden between mothers living with HIV whose babies were exposed but uninfected and mothers without HIV. Their 2026 prospective cohort study ran in Worcester, South Africa. Raising an exposed infant adds clinic visits and vigilance to a mother's own treatment in a low-income, high-prevalence setting. Burden was measured at the child's first birthday with a twelve-item scale, in 187 mothers.

Pandya found burden scores low on average. Yet mothers with HIV reported moderate-to-high burden at about double the rate of other mothers, roughly one in four versus one in nine. After adjusting for age, income, household composition, and maternal depression, the odds remained about twofold but no longer reached statistical significance, leaving the result suggestive rather than proven. The authors frame the pattern as evidence that mothers living with HIV carry caregiving strain during motherhood and may need support within primary care.
pmc-13499986:
Vaia Sarli and co-authors review in 2026 why endometriosis so often defeats embryo implantation, even when fertility treatment supplies good embryos. In this disease, tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb, and beyond distorted anatomy and ovary problems it appears to make the lining itself unwelcoming. Chronic inflammation, resistance to the hormone progesterone, misdirected immune cells, and faulty signalling molecules combine into a hostile setting that breaks the dialogue between embryo and lining.

Attention falls on uterine natural killer cells and macrophages, two immune populations that normally help implantation. Candidate markers of poor receptivity also draw focus, including a protein called BCL6, adhesion molecules, receptivity test panels, and epigenetic marks, each weighed for promise and limits. Treatments reviewed range from hormone pretreatment and immune-calming approaches to regenerative options such as platelet-rich plasma and a growth factor therapy, framed as steps toward personalised care.
pmc-13500386:
Xu Guo and co-authors characterise in 2026 a newly found skin toxin from Staphylococcus felis, a bacterium that lives on cats and sometimes infects their skin. Exfoliative toxins split the skin surface by cutting desmoglein 1, a rivet protein holding outer skin cells together. The team made the toxin, named ExfA, in the lab, tested its enzyme activity and skin damage, and checked how often the gene appears in cat isolates from Japan.

Lab-made ExfA erased staining for the feline rivet protein while sparing a related protein, digested the isolated target directly, and caused superficial skin splitting when injected into newborn mice. Computer modelling suggested a closed reaction pocket and protease-like binding, consistent with its cutting behaviour. Just under half of clinical isolates carried the gene in the reported share, and most gene-positive culture fluids digested the target, hinting at a role in colonising and invading cat skin.
pmc-13501386:
Halah F Alenizi leads a thirteen-author team reporting a 2026 cross-sectional study of active ageing awareness among older adults in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The study enrolled 351 adults aged 60 or older attending family medicine clinics at a large referral hospital. Participants completed the WHOQOL-BREF quality of life questionnaire and an Active Ageing Awareness Questionnaire, and the team linked the two with regression models that adjusted for social and health factors. The average participant age was 68.2 years, give or take seven years.

Most participants, 79.8 percent, had never heard the term active ageing before. Even so, higher awareness scores were significantly tied to better quality of life in all four measured domains, covering physical, psychological, social, and environmental aspects. Each extra awareness point raised the odds of better quality of life slightly, with adjusted odds ratios around 1.02. Education and financial status also mattered independently.
pmc-13501586:
Yin-Hsi Chang leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 cohort study of tear duct surgery under local versus general anaesthesia in older patients. Endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy opens a new drainage path between the tear sac and the nose when the tear duct is blocked. The retrospective study covered 210 eyes from 162 patients treated at a tertiary centre between January 2019 and December 2024. General anaesthesia accounted for 159 eyes, while 51 eyes were done under local anaesthesia; the local group was older, near 72 years against about 62.

Surgical success was comparable between the two approaches, and the local anaesthesia operations finished faster. No major adverse events occurred in either group. A small tear sac emerged as an independent factor linked to surgical failure. The authors judge local anaesthesia workable, especially for elderly patients, while noting discomfort and a less controlled field as drawbacks careful selection can manage.
pmc-13501686:
Deniz Görgülü leads a four-author team with a 2026 mixed-methods study of how living through the 2023 quakes in Türkiye shaped trainee teachers' skills and self-perceptions. At İnönü University, 304 trainees who lived through the quakes filled in scales on how competent they felt and on critical thinking standards. Talks with 37 chosen trainees then probed the numbers in depth.

Critical thinking and felt competence correlated positively and strongly, with a coefficient of 0.657 in the reported analysis. Interviewees described sharper perspective-taking, empathy, and awareness after the disaster, consistent with post-traumatic growth. Yet distance learning flaws, communication breakdowns, and psychological strain dragged down their sense of competence. The authors conclude the quakes cut both ways, and they urge post-disaster teacher training to protect critical thinking, resilience, and confidence together.
pmc-13502186:
Sagar Kale and a large team report an asthma study, published in 2026. It uses interpretable machine learning. The aim is to separate severe asthma from mild to moderate disease. The separation is at the molecular level. The team compared gene activity in airway lining cells. They looked for signatures of severe disease. These go beyond its mixed immune pattern.

Severe airways overproduced two normally protective mucins. They were MUC1 and MUC4. A keratinisation programme was also switched on. This is the skin-like hardening process marked by the stress protein KRT16. These features tracked with worse lung function in two cohorts. Biopsies confirmed higher protein levels. The authors read this as maladaptive repair in severe asthma.
pmc-13503786:
Fatemeh Jafarieh, Leila Mahmoudieh, and Behnood Abbasi study whether a diet rich in antioxidants links to less kidney damage in type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 paper from Iran. Kidney damage is a common and grave side effect of diabetes. Oxidative stress, harm from reactive oxygen forms, is thought to drive much of it.

The team compared 103 patients with kidney damage to 103 without, all seen at one clinic in Tehran. A long food survey fed a score for diet antioxidant quality, based on five key nutrients. Higher scores went with lower odds of kidney damage, with odds cut by about a third at the top end. The link held after the team weighed age, weight, blood pressure, and other factors.
pmc-13503886:
Huseyin Hilmi Aslanbay and Fatih Altun study how round holes change the strength of concrete beams fixed at both ends, in a 2026 paper. Beams often need holes for pipes and ducts, yet holes focus stress and can trigger early failure. Most past tests used beams that rest freely, which misstates real behavior.

The team cast full-size beams with a mid-span hole at a fifth, two fifths, or three fifths of the beam depth. Four-point bending tests and matched computer models tracked how each beam bent and broke. Holes past two fifths of depth cut bending give sharply and caused sudden load drops. Past one fifth, the concrete ring around the hole became key to carrying load. The models matched the lab results closely.
pmc-13504786:
Katarzyna Kowal and Jan Domaradzki explore how adults in Poland absorb a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1, in a 2026 interview study. The genetic condition brings visible marks, uncertain health paths, and social strain. A diagnosis often lands as a turning point in how people see themselves.

The team held deep interviews with 93 adults and grouped their responses into four patterns. Some felt little shock, relief, or calm acceptance. Others threw themselves into learning about the condition. A third group denied or downplayed it, while a fourth fell into crisis with body anxiety and deep disorientation. Over time many reshaped their values and daily priorities. The authors urge timely emotional support and clear, kind communication at diagnosis.
pmc-13505386:
Jing Tang and Yusuke Yamauchi comment on a new route to making covalent organic frameworks with large, open pores.
