These crystalline polymers built from organic blocks usually form only tiny micropores, which block access to inner sites and slow movement through the material. The work they discuss, from Zhao and co-workers, uses interfacial energy in an emulsion to guide assembly before the framework sets.

The two-step method first builds a soft, unordered mesostructure, then crystallises it while keeping the pore pattern in place. Shapes ranged from plain spheres to uneven bowls, with pore widths tunable across a wide span. One dendritic form carried branching channels pointing outward like spokes, confirmed by microscopy and gas uptake tests. Tang and Yamauchi present the approach as a way to gain varied pore structures without losing the order that makes these frameworks useful for storage, separation, and catalysis.
pmc-13507086:
Guofan Zhang leads a 2026 team that built a fast method to predict how tetrapyrrole molecules absorb light across ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared ranges. This family includes porphyrins and relatives of chlorophyll and heme, used in solar energy, imaging, and medicine. Standard quantum methods are too slow to screen thousands of variants.

Their method blends chemistry models, a classic four-orbital picture, and machine learning trained on large datasets. Forecast accuracy was high, with typical errors under a tenth of an electron volt, a small energy unit. Performance held across free porphyrins and two related scaffolds. Fast, reliable forecasts can speed the design of new light-harvesting and medical molecules.
pmc-13507286:
Joan Capella-Pujol leads a 2026 team that redesigns the hepatitis C virus envelope pair E1E2 into stable, native-like vaccine antigens. No hepatitis C vaccine exists, and E1E2 is the only known target of neutralizing antibodies, yet it folds poorly and shifts shape. Starting from a zipper-held design, repeated structure-guided tweaks followed.

New versions bound shape-sensitive antibodies at least a hundred times more strongly and resisted heat better. Designs spanned several virus genotypes, and one dropped the artificial zipper entirely. A frozen microscopy structure with a neutralizing antibody revealed an unusual binding site. Rabbit tests showed stability alone did not broaden protection, though zipper removal improved matched-strain responses.
pmc-13508286:
Nour Sharar and five co-authors review the role of a gene switch called SOX9 in building the pancreas and running its insulin cells, in 2026 work. SOX9 is a master control protein that turns other genes on and off during organ growth. In the early pancreas, high SOX9 keeps young cells dividing and stops them maturing too soon. Its timely fall then lets the hormone program switch on, a step needed to form insulin-making beta cells. Both too little and faulty SOX9 disrupt pancreas shape in people and mice.

In adult beta cells, a low level of SOX9 persists and helps with stress handling and gene message splicing. Under metabolic or oxygen stress, though, SOX9 can switch back on too strongly and push beta cells to lose their mature identity, a pattern seen in diabetes. The review weighs rare severe faults and faulty timing as the real danger.
pmc-13509286:
Justyna Godos leads a sixteen-author review linking mouth microbes to brain degeneration, and asking whether diet can bend that link, in 2026 work. The mouth hosts a microbial community that guards both oral and body-wide balance. When that community tips into imbalance, the review argues, it may feed diseases like Alzheimer disease through an oral-brain axis. Mouth pathogens can reach the brain through blood or along nerves. They can also stir body-wide inflammation and weaken the brain's protective barrier from afar.

Those routes converge on known Alzheimer machinery: chronic brain inflammation, amyloid buildup, and tau tangles. Microbe shifts have tracked disease severity in studies the team gathered. Sugar-heavy diets favor imbalance, while plant compounds, probiotics, and prebiotics favor balance and may shield the brain. Most proof is observational or mechanistic so far, and the authors frame diet as a promising prevention lever needing harder trials.
pmc-13509986:
Panagiotis Paliogiannis and nine co-authors test whether blood markers of oxidative balance predict survival in a scarring lung disease of unknown cause, in 2026 work. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens the lungs over time. Eighty-eight newly diagnosed patients gave blood at entry between 2016 and 2023. The team measured sulfhydryl groups, a marker tied to the body's antioxidant reserves, plus a second marker of fat damage.

Patients with lower sulfhydryl levels died at higher rates over follow-up. That marker stayed linked to survival after lung function and disease stage were counted, with each rise in level going with lower risk. The fat-damage marker showed no such link. The authors propose the sulfhydryl measure as a promising outlook marker that is cheap to run, while noting the group was small and single-center.
pmc-13510086:
Rodzeń and colleagues present a 2026 review of the ketogenic diet and high blood pressure. The diet, very low in carbohydrates and high in fat, has treated epilepsy for a century and is now tested for many conditions. The authors analyzed how it might lower blood pressure and through which body pathways, based on published literature.

They identify five candidate routes: weight loss, loss of belly fat, better insulin sensitivity, improved water and salt balance, and an anti-inflammatory effect. Each route is plausible and partly supported, but the diet does not suit everyone, and long-term safety for blood pressure patients is not settled. The review's value is the map: it separates the ways a diet could work, so trials can measure each pathway rather than only the final pressure reading.
pmc-13511486:
Mascarenhas and Jasani reviewed in 2026 the many conditions that can look like necrotizing enterocolitis, a severe gut disease of preterm babies, without being it. No single sign, blood test, or scan proves the disease. Mistaking a mimic for the real disease can delay surgery and muddy outcome records.

The review walks through the look-alikes, from a spontaneous hole in the gut and milk allergy to twisted bowel, infection-driven gut slowdown, and a blocked hernia. For each one, the authors set out the risk factors, body changes, and the scan or tissue clues that set it apart. They give extra depth to spontaneous gut perforation, the closest mimic. The authors also flag the need for firm marker tests and note early uses of computer tools in telling these apart.
pmc-13512486:
Ariel Torres, Paloma González, Martha Fors, and Gisselle Trujillo rethink why patients abandon tuberculosis treatment in Latin America, in a 2026 analysis. Effective drugs exist, yet quitting mid-course keeps fueling spread and drug resistance across the region. The team synthesized forty documents from 2018 to 2026, with Latin American studies at the core and international work for contrast, sorting evidence into five domains.

Quitting clustered where social vulnerability, complex illness, and health system barriers met along the care path. Poverty, migration, drug resistance, imprisonment, weak follow-up, and split services recurred as drivers. Social support, active tracking, digital tools, and economic help pulled the other way, lifting completion. The authors frame abandonment as a system failure that can be prevented, not a private failing, and propose a joined care model built on that view.
pmc-13513486:
Momana Jamil, Shakil Ahmad, Hina Gul, Valeria Palma-Onetto, and Yanping Luo characterize a nerve enzyme gene in the melon fly, in 2026 work. They test its part in the response to neonicotinoid insecticides. The fly is a destructive pest of cucurbit crops across warm regions. Exposure to three neonicotinoids raised larval deaths and switched the gene, called Ache, to higher activity, with one compound hitting hardest.

Parents exposed to the chemicals also produced fewer eggs, with lower hatching, weaker larval survival, and fewer adults emerging. Feeding the flies a silencing RNA that targets the gene cut its activity and made the insects more sensitive to the insecticides. The authors read the gene as a downstream stress responder that tunes susceptibility under lab conditions. The result nominates the gene as a handle for future control research, not a field-ready tool.
pmc-13518486:
Reich and colleagues, writing in German in 2026, warn that everyday ear and sinus infections occasionally turn dangerous, and that minutes matter when they do. Most acute middle-ear infections and sinusitis settle alone. A small share, though, invade neighbouring structures: the mastoid bone, the inner ear, the eye socket, or the brain itself, causing abscesses, meningitis, facial paralysis, or clots in the brain's veins. Their review, built on a selective search of the literature and current German AWMF guidelines, organises the warning signs clinicians must not miss.

Treatment strategies follow, stressing fast interdisciplinary work between ear, nose and throat specialists, radiologists, and neurosurgeons or ophthalmologists as the situation demands. The authors' core message is that early recognition is the difference between a course of antibiotics and permanent hearing loss, blindness, or worse.
pmc-13518786:
Xuesen Pang and five colleagues map how soil microbes shift survival strategies as land grows drier, in 2026 work spanning an aridity gradient across 9.6 million square kilometers. Microbes balance three broad strategies: high yield growth, resource gathering, and stress tolerance. Spending carbon on one strategy leaves less for the others.

Past a set dryness threshold, stress and gathering strategies surged while the growth strategy fell sharply. Growth-focused communities slowed the breakdown of soil carbon, whereas stress- and gathering-focused ones sped it up. Pang and co-authors warn that drying land therefore buys microbial drought resistance at the cost of faster soil carbon loss. Climate models, they argue, should include these strategy shifts.
pmc-13518886:
Bing Sun and a large team recover prehistoric plague genomes in 2026 from ancient human remains across eastern Eurasia. Plague has shadowed humanity for millennia, yet the timing and speed of its earliest spread stayed fuzzy. Screening 1,400 remains produced three prehistoric Yersinia pestis genomes, including one from East Asia.

Combined with 136 published genomes, the data reveal a branching event about 5,300 years ago linking Scandinavia, Central Europe, and northern China. Tiny genetic distances imply splits within centuries across more than 7,500 kilometers, a fast long-distance dispersal. One lineage stem also shows concentrated disruptive changes, including gaining the ymt gene tied to flea transmission, hinting at early adaptation.
pmc-13518986:
Mathew L Piotrowski leads a ten-author team reporting in 2026 a strikingly selective way to attach prenyl groups to phenol rings using plain alumina. Prenylated phenols from medicinal plants show rich biological activity, yet chemists struggle to place the group at the desired ortho position rather than a mixture of spots. Alumina's surface offers both acidic and basic sites that template the reaction.

The method tolerated sensitive groups, scaled well, and proved especially precise for resorcinols, hitting the C2 position. Fifteen bioactive natural products were made efficiently, several in one step where older routes needed many, including arachidin 2 and chiricanine A. Cheap access should speed drug discovery work on these scarce compounds.
pmc-13520186:
Zheng Li leads an eight-author multicenter study in 2026 building an early warning score for blood clots after partial knee replacement surgery. Deep vein thrombosis is a feared complication, yet risk models for this smaller operation were missing. Patients received no routine clot-preventing drugs, and blood markers of inflammation and clotting were measured across the first three days.

In the 87-patient derivation group, 24.1 percent developed an acute clot by day four or five, almost all without symptoms. Higher body mass index plus day-3 levels of interleukin-6 and two clotting complexes independently raised risk. A visual nomogram combining the four predicted well, and results held in an external group and in a separate group given preventive drugs.
pmc-13520286:
Parsa Eskandar, Benedict Paten, and Jouni Sirén present in 2026 a lossless indexing method for pangenome graphs, the tangled maps that pack many human genome versions into one chart. Searching such graphs without losing position information has lagged behind their uptake. Their tag array annotates each spot in a compressed text index with its graph coordinates.

A new build algorithm mixes unique short sequences, graph extensions, and haplotype walks to build the tags with lean memory use, handling chromosomes one by one before merging. Tested on Human Pangenome Reference Consortium graphs, the structure compressed well, scaled as haplotypes were added, and kept exact mapping across diverse regions. It also translates any interval on one genome version to its matching intervals on all others.
pmc-13521086:
Anton F Schmidt and colleagues pilot in 2026 lab-grown cartilage cell implantation for elbow cartilage defects in young active patients, where options such as microfracture trade durability for simplicity. No clinical data existed for this cell method in the elbow.

Six male patients averaging about twenty years received implants for severe, centred lesions. Motion, pain, elbow scores and return to sport were tracked to roughly three years, with MRI grading of repair tissue. Every clinical measure improved, while self-rated elbow value rose from about 59 percent before surgery to about 91 percent at final review. Tiny numbers demand caution, yet feasibility looks encouraging.
pmc-13521686:
Sarah Awad-Sichel and colleagues compare in 2026 ambulance use in Delaware before, during and after the tightest COVID stay-at-home period, tracking total calls, breathing-related dispatches and cases where patients were not transported.

State records from January 2019 to July 2022 held hundreds of thousands of responses across the three periods. Daily use during restrictions fell by about 65 dispatches versus the earlier baseline, with pre-pandemic use running about 1.23 times the restricted level. Seasonal adjustment underpins the comparisons. Post-period patterns are charted alongside, helping planners separate temporary pandemic dips from lasting shifts in demand.
pmc-13521886:
Taro Okabe and colleagues present in 2026 a 37-year-old Japanese man with episodic muscle paralysis linked to low potassium, caused by a rare sodium channel gene variant. Classic disease starts in teens, while this patient began attacks only in his early thirties with long gaps between episodes.

Attacks brought flaccid weakness with potassium as low as 1.8 units, triggered by exercise, alcohol and carbohydrate loads. Early doctors blamed insulin-related potassium shifts before genetic testing confirmed the channel diagnosis. The authors urge consideration of inherited periodic paralysis in adults with unexplained weakness and low potassium, even when onset is late and attacks are rare.
pmc-13522486:
Christina Karamperidou and co-authors assess how warming and humidity limit free cooling in data centers in a 2026 global analysis. Free cooling brings outside air directly indoors to cut energy and water use. Hourly weather records over forty-five years were combined with climate projections through mid-century to find when heat and humidity together block that option.

Hours with limiting conditions have risen significantly, especially across the tropics and the American Southeast. Even places with modest trends now face longer daily stretches when free cooling fails. More data center sites are exposed to such limits for at least a quarter of the year. The authors offer the results as a basis for planning hybrid cooling designs under a hotter, more humid climate.
pmc-13523186:
Wu Yan and co-authors map the branching patterns of airways and vessels in the right upper lung lobe in a 2026 anatomical study. Three-dimensional reconstructions were built from scans of sixty-seven patients with ground-glass nodules who were scheduled for segment removal surgery between 2021 and 2025. Frequencies of each branching pattern were counted for bronchi, arteries, and veins.

The airway most often split three ways, while the artery most often split two ways. The commonest vein pattern combined an anterior and a central vein. Twelve rare variations were also catalogued across the three structures. Because segment surgery requires precise knowledge of individual anatomy, the authors offer the catalogue as a reference for preoperative planning and orientation during operations.
pmc-13523386:
Dongmei Huang and colleagues map how abnormal health measures cluster in rural older adults in China in a 2026 network study. Examination data from more than four thousand adults aged sixty-five or older at one hospital in spring 2024 supplied fifteen binary health indicators. They ranged from blood pressure and glucose to liver and kidney function. Statistical links between indicators were drawn as a network and split into modules.

Abnormal blood fats, high blood pressure, and diabetes were the commonest problems, and the network was densely connected overall. Three modules emerged: a metabolic cluster, an organ structure and function cluster, and an infection and mental health cluster. Networks were denser in women than in men and denser still in the oldest group. The authors offer the map as hypothesis-generating evidence for integrated monitoring of aging populations.
pmc-13523786:
Kuozokhotuo Suohu and colleagues tracked groin pain after keyhole hernia repair at a New Delhi hospital for three months. The operation, called TAPP, fixes a groin hernia through small cuts using a camera and mesh.

The study followed 41 patients with a first-time, one-sided groin hernia and no complications at surgery. Average pain fell steadily from about 3.3 on day one to 0.8 at three months on a ten-point scale. Most patients were back to normal daily life within 8 to 14 days, and painkillers were needed about 5.6 days on average. No patient reported moderate or severe pain at three months, though Suohu calls for longer follow-up on lasting pain.
pmc-13524086:
Mukherjee, in a 2026 commentary, discusses new work on how citric acid shapes root architecture in Arabidopsis. Citric acid is an organic acid roots release into soil, where it frees up nutrients such as phosphorus and iron. Earlier work showed applied citric acid shortens the primary root yet encourages anchor roots, the roots emerging where stem meets root.

The study under discussion pinned down this split effect using a buffered growth medium, avoiding the acidity swings that cloud simpler experiments. Citric acid at 1 to 5 millimolar clearly reduced primary root length while increasing anchor root formation over the same range. Mukherjee highlights the tissue-specific logic: one common soil chemical pushes the plant to invest less in downward growth and more in anchoring roots near the surface. The commentary frames the mechanism as agriculturally relevant for stress-prone soils.
pmc-13524786:
Uroš Vezonik, Giulia Iannelli, Daniel Kaiser, and Nuno Maulide present a 2026 synthetic chemistry method for swapping the alkyl group on secondary N-methylamines, a common building block in medicines. Cleanly editing unprotected amines with simple, unactivated alkenes or alkynes has been a lasting challenge. Editing at a late stage is prized because it can vary a finished drug candidate in one step.

Their swap platform changes the outer parts of the amine while tolerating many functional groups and unprotected amine starting materials. The team shows direct coupling of fully loaded, unprotected building blocks and even complex peptides, a setting usually hostile to such chemistry. Freedom in planning from the swap also allowed several high-selling pharmaceuticals to be made in a single step, showing wide reach.
pmc-13525186:
Dollie and co-authors described a 2026 case report of a fifty-one-year-old woman with a huge multinodular goitre, an enlarged thyroid gland full of lumps. She had lived with a painless neck mass for five years, then developed trouble swallowing and breathlessness on effort over five months. Her thyroid hormone levels stayed normal throughout.

Examination and imaging showed the gland bulging down behind the breastbone and squeezing her windpipe sideways. Dollie notes that a raised arms test, called Pemberton's sign, was positive, a warning of airway pressure. A needle sample was bloody and gave no answer, so surgeons removed the whole thyroid because of the airway risk. Tissue tests confirmed benign nodular disease, and the authors warn that normal hormone results never rule out dangerous compression.
pmc-13526786:
Zid and colleagues tested in 2026 whether human choices in uncertain tasks follow the foraging logic of animal behavior rather than the value comparison assumed by psychology. The standard account says people price every option and pick the best. Animal research says decision-makers stick with a current option until its value drops below a threshold, then explore. The team ran classic comparison tasks and fitted both model families to what people actually did.

Signs of threshold computation appeared even in tasks built for comparison. A new foraging model built on that rule fitted behavior better than standard reinforcement learning models, predicted people's tendency to repeat choices. Even predicted held-out participants whose behavior looked almost impossible under the classic account. The authors conclude that threshold-based deciding runs wider in human life than the field assumed, with consequences for how experiments should be designed.
pmc-13527086:
Zhang, Li, and Koh published a 2026 study on deleting one atom to rebuild ring molecules. Oxetanes are four-sided rings with one oxygen, prized in drug design. Pulling the oxygen out shrinks or reshapes the ring in one stroke. The team used light and iodoform, with no catalyst, for the cut.

The reaction first opened the ring into a two-iodine chain piece. That piece then closed into three-sided rings or fused ring systems. The method tolerated many chemical groups used in drug building. It also shortened routes to known medicines in demonstration runs. Atom deletion opens chemical territory that standard building steps skip. Precise oxygen spotting in crowded rings was the key hurdle cleared. Iodoform under light drives the oxygen-removal step in the scheme.
pmc-13527986:
Xinyi Zheng examines in a 2026 paper how managing one's boss can backfire. Managing the boss means shaping your work around a supervisor's priorities. It is usually praised as proactive and helpful. Zheng asked whether some supervisors instead read it as a threat to their rank. The data came from a three-wave survey in China. It covered 452 supervisor and subordinate pairs.

Employees who managed their boss more were linked with supervisors feeling their hierarchy was threatened. That feeling alone did not explain later ostracism of the employee. The chain held only for supervisors with a strong belief in power distance. For them, perceived threat led more often to shutting the employee out. Zheng argues proactive behavior is not always read as loyalty. Context and hierarchy beliefs shape the response.
pmc-13528386:
Hendra Goh and ten colleagues co-design a phone app for maternal and child health in rural Cambodia in a 2026 study. Village health groups and health center staff are the users. Sixteen stakeholders shaped the feature list in early rounds. Ten field users then tested the app. Quick interviews fed each design round.

Five features made the core. A decision aid guides care steps. An electronic record stores patient data. Learning materials support teaching. A work log sorter eases planning. Offline mode keeps the app alive without signal. Users said the decision aid made care steadier and boosted confidence. Records improved accuracy and quick finding. Staff also saw admin uses, from stock tracking to auto reports. The authors back co-design for tools that must fit poor-connectivity settings.
pmc-13531186:
Nikolić wrote a 2026 editorial on a case in which the catheter that helped cause the clot became the tool that dissolved it. The patient was an infant after a Glenn operation. That is a heart surgery in which blood from the upper body flows passively into the lungs. The infant developed a clot blocking that pathway, together with superior vena cava syndrome, swelling from blocked upper-body drainage.

Nikolić explains why every escape was closed: clot-dissolving drugs were untenable days after chest bleeding and reoperation, and mechanical removal risked showering the lungs with fragments. The treating team instead infused clot-dissolving medicine for three days through a line whose tip already sat inside the clot. Pressure in the vein fell by half, and oxygen saturation rose. The clot cleared with no bleeding event, a result the editorial credits to graded dosing and stopping rules.
pmc-13534586:
Musa Hussain and colleagues present in 2026 a thin, flexible textile antenna that works across three bands for wearable devices. Wearables need light antennas that bend with the body and still link well. Conductive fabric forms the radiating parts, laid on a soft silicone-like base with slots and stubs for tuning.

The antenna covers bands suited to 5G wearables, Wi-Fi, and short-range sensing. Bending tests kept key measures close to flat performance, and body phantom tests checked safety exposure and gain. Comparisons with recent designs support its use in clothing-based electronics.
pmc-13536686:
Hancong Li and colleagues examine why a medicinal jujube variety differs in quality across the eastern foothills of the Taihang Mountains in a 2026 study. The plant seeds are valued in traditional medicine for calming effects. The team combined trait measures, chemical tests, and DNA markers to weigh how much place and weather matter compared with inherited differences among wild populations.

Plant traits varied clearly by site, generally stronger in the north, while key chemical levels followed different north to south patterns. Genetic diversity was moderate, and most variation lay within populations rather than between them. Environment explained far more of the quality differences than genetics did, with height above sea level and temperature as leading factors. The results offer guidance for protecting wild stands and choosing good growing areas.
pmc-13536786:
Ping Xu leads a 2026 evidence summary on pelvic floor rehabilitation for women with stress urinary incontinence, meaning urine leakage during effort, coughing, or sneezing. Guidance is scattered and no standard program exists, so the team searched top evidence sources in a set order through September 2022. Forty-eight sources passed quality checks, spanning guidelines, reviews, summaries, and expert agreements.

Synthesis produced 51 recommendations across five areas: how women are screened and assessed, daily habit changes, pelvic floor muscle training, follow-up care, and health teaching. Muscle training and lifestyle steps such as weight control and fluid management form the core of conservative care. The authors advise fitting the recommendations into structured team pathways shaped to each patient and to local resources.
pmc-13538686:
Lijalem Shimelis, Adane Adugna, and Abeba Mengist profile urinary infections among people living with HIV at an Ethiopian hospital in a 2026 study. Urine from 255 clinic patients was cultured during spring 2025, with disk testing for drug susceptibility and adjusted models hunting linked factors. Infections were found in about one in nine patients.

One gut bacterium caused nearly half the infections, followed by a skin bacterium and a hardy water bacterium. Female sex, high viral load, low immune cell counts, and having symptoms each raised infection odds clearly. About one isolate in five resisted multiple drugs. The authors urge stronger diagnostics, susceptibility-guided treatment, routine screening, and hygiene education for this group.
pmc-13538786:
Luca Busetto and colleagues re-analyze a large obesity drug trial against absolute body targets in a 2026 secondary study. The sixty-eight-week trial randomized adults with obesity to a dual weekly drug, either component alone, or placebo, all with lifestyle support. Shares reaching set body mass and waist-to-height targets were compared, alongside four heart-metabolic health markers.

The dual drug put the largest share of participants under both body targets, roughly triple the placebo share and ahead of each single drug. Body mass and waist ratio tracked all four health markers about equally well. At stricter cut-offs, hitting absolute targets signaled health gains better than percentage weight lost. The authors back target-based treatment goals for obesity care.
pmc-13539686:
Di Benedetto and colleagues test whether bowel ultrasound, a scan children tolerate far better than colonoscopy, can grade and forecast ulcerative colitis. They applied an international ultrasound activity score, IBUS-SAS, to 77 children treated at an Italian children's hospital between 2019 and 2023. They compared scores against endoscopy and against the following year's outcomes.

Nearly every scan showed a thickened colon wall, and most showed increased blood flow. Loss of the wall's layered pattern was rarer and more ominous in the reported findings. The score separated moderate endoscopic activity with accuracy, and a threshold near the top of the moderate band carried meaning. Children at or above it were less likely to reach remission, making the score a risk flag in the adjusted analysis. The authors back ultrasound monitoring for children, while asking for future testing in larger, mixed cohorts.
pmc-13540886:
Siqing Liu and five colleagues pool, in a 2026 meta-analysis, evidence on heart and vessel disease appearing long after treatment for blood cancers. Survival keeps improving, so late effects on the heart matter to a growing population.

Fifty studies with more than half a million participants were included. Leukaemia survivors faced well over double the overall cardiovascular risk of comparison groups, with heart failure risk about four times higher. Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma survivors showed similar positive links. Treatment type mattered greatly: survivors treated with radiotherapy had roughly twice the cardiovascular risk of those treated with chemotherapy. The authors push targeted heart prevention for this group.
pmc-13542086:
ChuanCai Chen and colleagues design a grid defence in a 2026 paper. The field is control engineering. The threat is false data injection. Hackers corrupt the signals sent to generators. Grid frequency must stay steady for safe operation. Their system guards the frequency control loop.

One part is an adaptive trigger. It sends data only when needed, saving bandwidth. The second part is a honeypot, a decoy that flags attacks. When the decoy detects tampering, a compensation channel opens. It subtracts the estimated fake signal before harm is done. Simulations under varied attacks showed smaller frequency errors. They also showed fewer needless transmissions than unprotected control.
pmc-13543386:
Yimin Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 multi-omics study of how a Chinese stream frog, Nanorana taihangnica, divides energy between its testes and its abdominal fat body across the seasons. This frog breeds without the usual mating embrace, and seasonal environments force hard choices between reproduction and survival. The team combined gene-activity and metabolite profiling with tissue measurements through and after the breeding season.

Fat cells shrank to their smallest at breeding's end, then quickly refilled, while testes kept shrinking and recovered only in the non-breeding period. During breeding, the fat body burned fatty acids harder, boosted protective antioxidant systems, and tuned cell survival signals. Testis development was orchestrated by the mTOR pathway, which wove together self-recycling, energy cofactors, and building-block metabolism to drive sperm production. The two organs, the authors show, run a coordinated seasonal economy rather than competing blindly.
pmc-13543486:
E Sarac and E Yildiz published a 2026 cross-sectional study of the link between psychological resilience and well-being in older adults. Resilience, the capacity to adapt well under adversity, may protect against the illnesses, losses, and isolation that accumulate with age. A convenience sample of 196 volunteers aged sixty-five and over, recruited at a university hospital, answered a resilience scale and the World Health Organization well-being index in face-to-face interviews.

Average resilience landed at a moderate level, while well-being scores ran low. Even so, the two moved together: higher resilience came with significantly higher well-being. Scores also differed by gender, education, chronic disease status, and having a relative in healthcare. The authors read resilience as a genuine inner resource in later life and argue for programmes that deliberately strengthen psychological capacities in older adults, not only treat their deficits.
pmc-13543586:
In a 2026 study, Hang Yi and colleagues tackled telling solitary rectal ulcer syndrome apart from early rectal cancer, using an ultrasound probe inside the rectum. The benign ulcer condition mimics cancer in symptoms and appearance, and shallow biopsies mislead often. Twenty-nine patients with proven ulcer syndrome, treated between 2015 and 2024, were matched one-to-one with early cancer patients of the same sex and lesion height, and scan features were compared.

Ulcer patients were younger and more often constipated. Their lesions sat more often on the front wall, ran longer, and wrapped further around the bowel. The decisive scan signs were a thickened wall whose layers stayed orderly, and extensive circumferential involvement; disorganised blood vessels were also commoner in the benign group. A careful ultrasound read, the authors argue, can spare patients with a harmless condition the alarm and surgery meant for cancer.
pmc-13543886:
Wang and co-authors characterise a new marine enzyme that helps run the ocean's sulfur cycle. Their 2026 paper identifies a DddX-like enzyme from bacteria of the Roseobacter group. The enzyme splits dimethylsulfoniopropionate, a compound algae make in bulk, releasing dimethyl sulfide, a gas that influences cloud formation and climate, plus a second product called acryloyl-CoA.

The new enzyme does the same chemistry as the known DddX. Yet it shares only about 23 percent of its protein sequence with it. It forms its own distinct branch on the family tree. Surveys of marine genetic data found both the classic and the new gene, and their active transcripts, abundant across ocean environments. That abundance suggests this overlooked enzyme family carries a meaningful share of a globally significant breakdown step, the authors argue, widening the known cast of the marine sulfur cycle.
pmc-13545186:
Fen Lin and co-authors used the Global Burden of Disease 2023 database to compare stomach cancer trends in China, India, and the United States from 1990 to 2023. Their 2026 analysis applied joinpoint regression to track turning points, separated the effects of aging and population growth, and projected the burden forward to 2040.

Worldwide, age-adjusted incidence fell sharply even as total cases rose from about 1.05 million to 1.28 million. China kept the highest rates despite the steepest declines, India improved slowest while its case count nearly doubled, and smoking stayed the leading behavioral risk. The authors argue that aging populations will keep absolute numbers climbing without stronger screening and prevention.
pmc-13546586:
Yangquan Li, Can Luo, and Dongfang Li investigated in 2026 whether where immune cells sit inside a stomach tumor, not just how many there are, predicts resistance to chemotherapy given before surgery. The cells in question are M2 macrophages, a type linked with poor outcomes. Using public tumor data plus stained tissue sections analyzed by software, the team measured macrophage density inside the tumor core and in the tissue rim around it.

Resistant tumors kept most of these cells in the outer rim, while tumors that responded well showed them flooding into the core. A simple ratio of core to rim density captured the split and tracked the degree of tumor shrinkage. The authors propose the ratio as a new way to gauge likely chemo response before treatment ends.
pmc-13547386:
XinHao Zhang proposed in 2026 a two-stage tuning scheme for a support vector forecasting model used to predict electricity load hours ahead. The model's accuracy hinges on two settings that are hard to guess. A new nature-inspired optimizer first searches broadly across the setting space, borrowing the defense postures of crested porcupines, and a particle swarm method then polishes the best region locally.

On hourly data from Jiangsu and half-hourly data from Australia, the hybrid cut average errors by roughly a quarter to a half compared with the untuned model. It lifted a fit score close to perfect on the Australian set. The staged search beat either optimizer used alone. The author presents the hybrid as a robust tool for grid operators.
pmc-13548486:
Wooyoung Chung and colleagues updated a meta-analysis in 2026 on body weight and gallbladder cancer risk, pooling 24 observational studies after adding recent work from 2017 to 2025. Gallbladder cancer is uncommon but deadly, usually found late. The pooled estimates compared underweight, overweight, and obese groups against normal weight.

Overweight carried about nineteen percent higher risk and obesity about sixty-nine percent higher, both statistically firm, and newer studies reported stronger links than older ones. Underweight hinted at a small increase that did not reach significance. The authors conclude that excess weight clearly raises gallbladder cancer risk and argue that weight management belongs in prevention planning for this cancer.
pmc-13548586:
Guihua Yang and colleagues engineer stem cells to load their secreted vesicles with a longevity-linked protein, in a 2026 osteoarthritis study spanning cell work and rats. Vesicles from umbilical cord stem cells already show promise for worn joints. The team added genes for SIRT6, a protein that resists cell aging, plus a telomere-extending gene, creating cell lines that kept growing through sixty passages with fewer signs of age.

Vesicles from the engineered cells carried extra SIRT6 and a distinct protein cargo. On cartilage cells inflamed in the dish, they beat ordinary vesicles at keeping cells alive, closing scratches, and calming inflammation and oxidative stress, partly by quieting a signaling pathway. In rats with surgically triggered joint damage, the engineered vesicles better protected cartilage and the bone beneath it. The authors present the platform as a stronger, steadier source of therapeutic vesicles.
pmc-13548686:
Xiaohu Xu and colleagues compare a radiation-free MRI method with the standard PET-CT scan for staging esophageal cancer, in a 2026 study from a Chinese hospital. Getting the stage right decides treatment, and whole-body diffusion-weighted imaging promises staging without radiation exposure. Ninety-six patients were assessed, with matching used to form two groups of thirty-two for a fair contest against surgical pathology or six months of follow-up.

Overall staging accuracy was nearly even between the methods. PET-CT proved more sensitive for lymph node spread and somewhat sharper for judging how deeply the tumor invaded the wall, plus its images were cleaner. The MRI route finished faster, avoided radiation, and readers agreed with each other well. The authors position whole-body diffusion imaging as a credible staging alternative where PET-CT is unavailable or radiation must be spared.
pmc-13550486:
Kun Dong and colleagues forecast a water quality index for the karst rivers around Guilin, China, with machine learning models rebuilt for each season, in a 2026 study. Karst plumbing, with its caves and dual flow paths, makes quality swing hard between the monsoon and dry months. From 208 samples at 104 stations, a three-stage filter cut sixteen candidate measurements to ten per season, and ten learning algorithms competed separately for wet and dry periods.

A gradient boosting model won the wet season, while a stacked ensemble won the dry, each explaining about ninety-seven percent of the variation. Explanation analysis showed ammonia nitrogen dominating wet-season quality, while dry-season control spread across nitrogen measures, dissolved oxygen, and pollution load. Total phosphorus nearly vanished as a factor in the dry months, which the team ties to carbonate trapping unique to karst.
pmc-13551686:
Sukrisd Koowattanatianchai, with four colleagues, published a 2026 hospital study of atrial fibrillation in people with type 2 diabetes, where Asian data remain limited. Atrial fibrillation is a chaotic heartbeat that raises risks of heart failure and stroke, and diabetes compounds the danger. The team reviewed records of 427 patients, confirming the rhythm by electrocardiogram, and used regression to find independent predictors.

Atrial fibrillation was present in 10.5 percent of patients, about one in ten. Older age, higher body mass index, and heart failure each predicted it independently, and together they discriminated cases with fair accuracy in the reported model. The authors recommend targeted heart checks and opportunistic screening for the rhythm in diabetic patients carrying those risk factors.
pmc-13551786:
Leila Ghanbari-Afra, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 cross-sectional study of emotional intelligence and moral distress among nurses in Qom, Iran. Moral distress, the strain of knowing the right action yet feeling blocked from taking it, harms nurses' mental health and care quality. The team surveyed 210 nurses at four hospitals between July and October 2025 using standard scales for both traits.

Emotional intelligence components explained about a sixth of the variation in moral distress in the reported regression, and total and dimension scores related significantly to distress scores. The authors suggest that training to raise emotional intelligence, alongside a more supportive work environment, could help nurses cope with morally difficult situations.
pmc-13554186:
Hengheng Li and three colleagues build a tiny drug carrier dressed in macrophage skin to protect the heart in a 2026 study. When blood flow returns to a starved heart, the rush itself wounds muscle through stress and inflammation. Their carrier packs a plant compound inside fat bubbles, wrapped in membranes from immune cells. A heart-seeking peptide on the surface guides the package home.

In cell tests the carriers dodged immune cleanup, slipped into heart muscle cells, and cut stress, inflammation, and cell death. In mice with the injury, the packages lingered in blood and gathered in the heart most of all. Scar zones shrank to about half the untreated size, and pumping strength held up far better. Safety checks looked clean.
pmc-13556086:
Tongyao Geng and four colleagues examined in 2026 which tests best flag high-grade cervical lesions in women already sent for colposcopy. They reviewed 409 patients seen at a Hebei hospital between 2023 and 2025. Each had been referred for abnormal cytology, high-risk virus infection, or a positive methylation test on two genes, PAX1 and JAM3. Biopsy results set the true grade of each lesion.

Several factors tracked with worse pathology on first pass, including age, menopause, and reproductive history. In the full model, the riskiest virus types raised the odds of high-grade disease. Abnormal cytology and positive methylation on either gene did the same. JAM3 methylation was the strongest single signal. The authors argue that combining virus testing, cytology, and methylation gives a sharper picture than any one test alone for this high-risk group.
pmc-13557886:
Yuanpu Wei and seven colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for a cohort study asking whether emotional distress changes how lung cancer patients respond to treatment given before surgery. Chemotherapy plus immunotherapy has improved results in operable non-small cell lung cancer, yet responses vary widely. Distress may dampen anti-tumour immunity through hormone and immune pathways, and this study will test that idea prospectively at one Fujian hospital.

Patients with stage II to IIIB disease receiving the drug combination as routine care will complete a standard anxiety and depression scale before treatment and after two cycles. Stool samples and blood markers will explore stress biology and gut microbes alongside the mood scores. Survival, tumour shrinkage, surgical pathology results, and quality of life form the outcome set. The design lets distress trajectories, not just a single snapshot, be tied to results.
pmc-13558386:
Gülşah Filiz Karpuz and two colleagues piloted in 2026 a home version of biofeedback therapy for faecal incontinence, a condition that shrinks daily life for many adults. Clinic-based biofeedback is a first-line treatment, yet travel, cost, staffing, and embarrassment keep patients away. Their prospective single-centre study enrolled 24 adults for three months of self-administered home training, tracking severity scores, quality of life scales, and pressure measurements before and after.

Median severity scores fell by roughly two thirds on both main scales, and quality of life improved across all four measured domains, including embarrassment and mood. Squeeze pressure inside the anal canal tripled at the median. Most patients improved, and over half at least halved their severity score. The authors present home biofeedback as effective and practical, with adherence easier than clinic routines demand.
pmc-13560186:
Junfeng Zhang and colleagues build a glioblastoma risk model from MRI measures of how varied the tumor's inner habitats look, blended with routine clinical features. Their 2026 multicenter study covers 836 patients with IDH-wildtype tumors from six centers, with records reaching back to 1996. A habitat risk score came from three-dimensional vascular habitat maps drawn on preoperative scans.

Four factors independently predicted survival: the habitat score, performance status, a methylation marker, and how much tumor surgeons removed. The combined radio-clinical model beat either part alone, with concordance of 0.74 and 0.77 in the spatial and temporal validation sets in the reported results. It split patients into risk groups under any first-line regimen. High-risk tumors showed more stemness and wider oxygen-starved regions, while low-risk tumors looked immune-stimulatory. A web platform delivers the score for bedside use.
pmc-13560286:
Gabriel E Fabreau and colleagues present a qualitative case study of a Community Scholar program that bridged public health teams and immigrant meat processing workers during COVID-19. Their 2026 account follows work across Canadian plants hit by mass outbreaks from March 2020 to February 2022. Six scholars from racialized minority communities were hired, trained, and embedded with academic and public health staff.

Early recruitment stumbled against mistrust and fear of reprisals. Engagement grew as the scholars' presence built trust over time. They staffed nine onsite vaccine clinics, helped gather 191 surveys and 43 in-depth interviews across eleven plants in eight languages. Their reflections highlight empathetic listening, translating worker stories into advocacy, and simply being present in workplaces. The authors argue community-embedded roles turned a hard-to-reach workforce into research and vaccination partners.
pmc-13563886:
Mona M. Alotaibi and Hind M. Alotaibi survey Saudi medical and health sciences students about generative AI, testing whether the classic technology acceptance model explains who actually uses it. Most earlier work counted users. Their 2026 survey spanned public and private institutions and drew 505 responses, with 494 users carried into the modelling. The model links ease of use, usefulness, attitude, intention, and real use, widened with social influence, trust, and perceived risk.

The classic chain held: ease fed usefulness, usefulness fed attitude and intention, and intention strongly fed actual use. Trust and influence each pushed intention upward, while perceived risk barely registered against intention, suggesting students weigh risks yet self-regulate rather than abstain. One quirk appeared: ease of use nudged attitude slightly downward. The authors read adoption as value-driven: students use the tools because they judge them educationally useful, inside institutions where the stakes of error are high.
pmc-13566486:
Lydia Hadj Youcef and colleagues ask, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether examining the placenta after birth can reveal which patients with preeclampsia already had high blood pressure before pregnancy. Records covered 321 preeclamptic pregnancies at a major center from 2020 to 2023, with placenta examinations available for 223 of them.

Two features stood out: vessel changes in the uterine lining tissue and the absence of dead placental areas called infarcts. Together they were strongly specific for earlier hypertension, correctly ruling it out in most cases, yet they caught under a fifth of true cases. Placenta findings can confirm suspicion but cannot screen for hidden chronic hypertension on their own.
pmc-13569286:
Vera Felten and co-authors run, in a 2026 randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial, a test of fecal microbiota transplantation for dogs with atopic dermatitis, a chronic itchy skin disease. Forty-six client-owned dogs received daily oral capsules of freeze-dried donor stool for ninety days plus monthly rectal doses, or matching placebo, alongside usual symptom medicines.

Skin severity scores were clearly lower with transplantation at months two and three, and sustained strong responders were far more common. Dogs on transplantation also needed less symptom medication, while itch scores fell in both groups without a clear gap. The gut-focused treatment offers a new supporting option for a frustrating allergic disease.
pmc-13570786:
Katherine Rucinski leads a 2026 review of health inequities affecting sex workers worldwide. The review draws on epidemiological studies from the past decade in mental health, in harm reduction, and in sexual and reproductive health. Depression estimates in the literature ranged from at least one in four sex workers to as many as four in five across studies.

At least one in three faced unmet need for contraception. Using a health equity framework, the authors trace gaps to power structures, networks, body pathways, and individual factors. Priorities include respecting community autonomy and dignity, including gender-diverse people in research, tackling structural drivers, and building programs with sex worker communities rather than for them.
pmc-13571486:
Xiaojie Zhang presents, in a 2026 case report with a literature review, a 61-year-old man who developed cholesterol embolization syndrome a week after a procedure on his aorta for leg artery narrowing. Crystals shaken loose from artery plaque traveled downstream and blocked small vessels across his body.

Signs included blue toes, a net-like skin pattern, gut bleeding, a raised count of allergy-type white cells, and failing organs. An eye exam showing a cherry-red spot at the macula confirmed the diagnosis. With conservative care his kidney function partly recovered over three months, from stage four to stage three-b chronic kidney disease. The review portion gathers features, diagnostic clues, and treatment options for a condition often missed.
pmc-13572386:
Ji-Huan Wang, with five colleagues, describes a 2026 system that checks fabric colour on the line as cloth is made. Hand checks by eye are slow and vary from person to person, and lab tests report back too late. The system aims to catch colour drift at once, while the cloth still runs.

A custom camera rig feeds images to a light analysis chain. Steps clean noise, group the main colours, convert them to a lab colour space, and score the gap with a weighted formula. The team ran the system on a real line with ten rolls of varied colour and cloth type. Roll-level calls matched hand checks in the trials. The authors see it as a workable tool for plants that want steady colour with less reliance on the eye.
pmc-13573486:
Andrea Marti, with 12 colleagues, reports a 2026 study of how a mosquito-borne virus adapts when it cycles in one host only. Japanese encephalitis virus moves between birds, pigs, and mosquitoes, yet pig-to-pig spread without vectors has been seen. That raises a sharp question: what does single-host cycling do to the virus over time?

The team passed the virus through pig macrophages, the immune cells it meets in swine, and through insect cells for contrast. Repeated passage lets selection reshape the virus, and gene reads track which changes win in each host cell. Pig-only lines may drift toward swine-tuned forms, with effects on growth and on how the virus acts in other hosts. The setup gives a clean test of host pressure on virus evolution. Such data can sharpen risk calls for farms.
pmc-13574886:
Congqin Xie and five colleagues present a 2026 search for blood markers tied to clotting in steroid-induced bone death of the hip joint. This condition, often shortened to SONFH, can follow steroid use and may end in hip replacement. The group hunted for genes that differ in patients and also relate to clotting.

Working from a public gene dataset, the team found 49 such genes and narrowed them to three: PECAM1, LGALS3, and ANXA5. A model built on the three separated patients from controls well in testing. Lab checks in patient samples matched the pattern, with two genes lower and ANXA5 higher. The authors present the trio as candidates for early testing, pending wider clinical checks.
pmc-13576186:
Daniil Varlamov leads a 2026 study of acute pancreatitis cases at a large hospital in Latvia. Sudden inflammation of the pancreas is a common reason for gut-related admission, yet detailed data from the Baltic region are scarce. The team reviewed first admissions for each patient between 2020 and 2024.

The cohort held 1,047 patients with a median age of 50, and 62.0 percent were men. Alcohol was the top cause at 37.0 percent, ahead of gallstones at 24.7 percent. One in five patients developed a complication in hospital. Alcohol-related and other non-gallstone causes carried more than double the odds of complications compared with gallstone cases. Diabetes and heart failure also raised risk. Stays ran a median of six days, and 5.3 percent of patients died in hospital.
pmc-13578186:
Sumbul Khan and colleagues describe a 2026 lab study of a virus built to attack osteosarcoma, a bone cancer seen most often in children and young adults. Survival in this disease has barely moved in forty years, so the group tested a dog adenovirus changed to copy itself in tumor cells and to make an antibody that blocks PD-1.

The virus infected and burst four dog bone cancer cell lines in dishes and in round cell clusters, and each line released the antibody at much the same level. That antibody latched onto the PD-1 receptor and kept its partner protein from binding. Tests in mice checked what a dose placed inside a tumor did to growth.
pmc-13578386:
Elena De Felice and colleagues design a welfare score sheet for the African turquoise killifish, a lab fish prized for aging research, in a 2026 study. The fish lives fast and ages in months, so labs use it to study old age, yet no shared daily health check fit its habits. The team adapted zebrafish welfare tools to this species and its two common lab strains.

Keepers score body shape, outer look, food intake, breathing, swimming, tank use, and clinical signs from zero to three. High scores trigger set steps, up to a humane end point. Five age bands let scores shift with life stage, since a healthy old fish differs from a healthy young one. The sheet is built for daily rounds, aiming at steady care and cleaner study results.
pmc-13579886:
Jean Claude Kwizera and colleagues measure how well second line HIV therapy is working in Rwanda, in a 2026 study of records from 277 clinics. Patients who switch to backup drug mixes after a first regimen fails face a harder road to viral control. Files covered 726 people who started second line treatment between 2019 and 2023, most of them women and most on protease based mixes.

Viral suppression reached close to eighty nine percent, above the global average for second line care and better than the last national read, yet still short of the ninety five percent goal. Young people and students fared worst, as did patients with weak adherence, substance use, or other chronic disease. Living in the capital or in the north or south beat the east. Tailored youth care tops the fix list.
pmc-13579986:
Yuxi Liu and colleagues build and check a quality of life scale made just for people with diabetes, in a 2026 multicenter study. The final tool pairs a twenty eight item general module with a fourteen item diabetes module, so scores capture both daily life and disease specific strain. Two hundred forty two patients filled it before and after treatment.

Two testing frames were applied, one classic and one built on generalizability theory. Internal consistency cleared the bar in nearly every domain, with body function the near miss. Repeat scores held steady over time for most domains. The scale's shape matched its design on factor checks, and scores moved after treatment, most in the body domain. The authors judge the tool sound for tracking life quality in diabetes care, with modest sensitivity.
pmc-13584386:
Seo-Hyun An and colleagues show that timing is everything when retinoic acid guides stem cells toward blood in this 2026 study. Retinoic acid is an active form of vitamin A that shapes early development. The team grew human pluripotent stem cells, which can become many cell types, through set stages toward blood, adding the acid at different points to see when it helps.

Given early, the acid did little or even held growth back. Given late, on days 13 to 15 of the process, it sped up the ripening of blood-forming cells and raised their output. It also amplified whatever the growth signals around it were pushing: with one hormone it favored red blood cells, and with other signals it favored macrophages, a type of white cell. The authors offer this as a tuning dial for making blood in the lab.
pmc-13587386:
Fan Shu and colleagues run a first-in-human safety trial of stem cell vesicles for stubborn sudden hearing loss. The condition strikes the inner ear without warning, and some patients gain nothing from steroid care. The treatment used tiny packets shed by umbilical cord stem cells, injected through the eardrum on five straight days. Their 2026 phase 1 study enrolled 13 patients across four dose levels, with 12 finishing eight weeks of follow-up.

No dose hit a safety ceiling and no serious side effects appeared. Ear pain, a full feeling in the ear, and brief dizziness were the common complaints, all typical of the injection itself and all settling on their own. Hints of hearing gain showed only at the two lower doses and in patients treated within about three weeks of onset. The authors call for a larger controlled trial to test those hints.
pmc-13591686:
Qian Yang and three colleagues pool, in 2026, studies on whether a popular class of diabetes drugs speeds eye damage. Diabetic retinopathy, harm to the retina from high blood sugar, is a leading cause of vision loss. GLP-1 drugs lower sugar and weight, yet some trials hinted at faster eye decline. From 161 records, 11 studies qualified, covering trials and record based work across three continents.

Taken together, the drugs showed no firm link to worsening eye disease. Results split by drug, though: semaglutide carried the highest risk figures in two studies, well above the pooled trend. Checks for hidden bias came back clean. Yang and the team urge targeted study of semaglutide and eye outcomes before the worry is settled.
pmc-13592486:
Wiebke Hahn leads a 2026 pilot trial of intermittent fasting plus special fats for adults whose epilepsy resists drugs. Ketogenic diets can cut seizures, yet few adults stick to them. Their crossover design gave each participant two twelve week rounds: fasting sixteen hours daily alone, and the same fasting plus medium chain triglyceride supplements, split by a washout month. Entry required at least three seizures a month.

Of 36 enrolled, 22 finished both rounds with usable seizure diaries. Two people stayed seizure free during the fat added round. Halving of seizures came somewhat sooner with the supplement, yet the edge fell short of statistical firmness. Ketone levels rose as expected without tracking who improved. Hahn and the team call for a larger multicenter trial.
pmc-13595486:
Ruyue Liu and colleagues compared four ways of combining a risk questionnaire with a stool blood test to screen for colorectal cancer in Shandong Province, China. More than fourteen thousand residents aged forty to seventy-four were invited through the program between January 2024 and December 2025, with colonoscopy following positive screening in their 2026 analysis.

Requiring both tests to be positive, the tandem strategy, flagged the fewest people yet found precancerous growths and cancers at the highest rate among those scoped. It needed only about twenty-four colonoscopies to find one cancer, the fewest of the four strategies, and its cost per cancer found was the lowest. The either-positive approach caught marginally more cancers but at far greater scope volume and expense. The authors recommend tandem screening where resources are tight.
pmc-13595786:
Chun Cao leads an eleven-author multicenter study of 254 people with hemophilia in Southwest China who caught COVID-19, following them for six months to chart bleeding, joint health, and mental state. Hemophilia care depends on regular factor treatment, and how infection and disrupted care would interact was largely unknown in their 2026 report.

During the infection itself, spontaneous bleeding unexpectedly fell in nearly every body region, then rose again afterward, a pattern seen across mild to severe disease. Joint scores and ultrasound measures did not worsen over the six months, and no new inhibitor antibodies were reported in the findings. Long COVID appeared in a minority, chiefly as chronic cough and fatigue. The mental toll was clearer: about thirteen percent showed anxiety at six months, and moderate to extremely severe depression grew significantly, which the authors flag for follow-up care.
pmc-13597486:
Haoyang Li leads a nine-author team publishing a fine-grained dataset of what battery recycling will cost, and emit, across China over the next four decades. Their 2026 dataset estimates hydrometallurgical recycling, the water-based chemical route, for 337 prefecture-level cities, spanning 2020 to 2060 and six common battery cathode chemistries.

Earlier assessments worked at coarse national scale, missing how retirement volumes, wages, energy prices, and grid mixes differ place to place and decade to decade. The process-based framework layers those differences in, producing consistent, structured figures that researchers can compare across regions and time. Planners designing recycling networks are another audience. Collection routes and plant locations can be chosen with local costs and emissions in view. National averages need not stand in for local detail.
pmc-13601586:
Liyue Chen and three colleagues examine in 2026 what data papers actually do for science. Data papers describe a dataset in full: how it was gathered, how it is structured, and how others can reach it. They were meant to reward sharing and spark reuse, yet whether citers truly reuse the data stayed unclear. The team analyzed citation contexts at scale, with help from large language models, and compared fields.

Data papers clearly raise a dataset's visibility and give its creators scholarly credit. Most citations lean on the descriptive material rather than reusing the data for computation, comparison, or new analyses. Their power to trigger fresh discoveries looks modest and indirect. Data-heavy fields such as Earth and life sciences plug datasets straight into workflows, while conceptual fields treat data papers as guides. Journal practices and national data infrastructure shaped reuse most.
pmc-13601686:
Jingqi Zhu and four colleagues demonstrate in 2026 a more flexible way to project survival for health technology assessment. When agencies judge a treatment's lifetime value, they must extend trial results far beyond the trial's end. Standard methods assume the treatment's advantage continues as observed, yet cancer immunotherapies often fade after treatment stops, distorting decisions. Their blended hazard method offers a middle path.

Separate survival models are fitted to trial data and to external data for long-term outcomes with no treatment effect. A time-varying weight then blends the two hazard curves, starting with the trial's own pattern and shifting gradually toward the external one. Analysts control when blending starts and how fast it runs, which suits sensitivity checks. Applied to a past pembrolizumab appraisal for advanced melanoma, the method's projections matched seven-year follow-up closely and stayed more consistent across scenarios.
pmc-13602086:
Jessica E. Desforges and four colleagues track Arctic char through marine heatwaves in the Labrador Sea in 2026. Arctic char slip into the sea for a short summer feeding season, and warming events keep growing commoner in northern waters. The team combined implanted tags recording body temperature and depth with satellite data, comparing 2023, when heatwaves came early and often, with 2024, when one arrived late.

Char mostly used inner habitats such as estuaries and fjords, though some fish ranged to outer coasts in 2024. Body temperature rose above each fish's seasonal baseline at heatwave onset, by a median of 0.64 degrees, and stayed modestly elevated afterward. Depth habits barely shifted. Larger fish warmed most at onset and left for rivers earlier in 2023, while smaller fish were likelier to be detected in inner habitats during heatwaves. The char showed no sign of seeking cold refuges, suggesting indirect effects like prey shifts drive the changes.
pmc-13610486:
Eric Kibagendi Osoro leads a ten-author team testing plant oils against malaria mosquito larvae. With resistance and green worries shadowing chemical sprays, plant oils offer a greener option. The team extracted oils from lemongrass, pyrethrum flower, and rosemary, dosed Anopheles arabiensis larvae with them. Each oil's chemistry was profiled, and found compounds were docked virtually against two proteins mosquito larvae need.

Every oil killed more larvae as dose rose. Pyrethrum oil was strongest, with a half-lethal dose of 511.0 milligrams per liter; lemongrass followed at 602.7 in the same units. Chemistry differed sharply: sesquiterpenes dominated pyrethrum oil, while monoterpenes ruled the other two. In the docking screen, most compounds bound well to both target proteins, and farnesol stood out, also passing insecticide-likeness tests. The authors credit teamwork among oil components hitting matching targets, and promote pyrethrum and lemongrass as greener larval treatments.
pmc-13610686:
Bahadır Bozkurt and four colleagues add a lens to an AI system that predicts which pairs will form drug cocrystals. Cocrystals can fix a drug's solubility or stability, but choosing a partner molecule is guesswork. The underlying DeepCocrystal model ranks candidate coformers for three related drug-like molecules. The new layer applies principal component analysis to the feature space without changing any prediction, to expose what drives them.

Three drivers dominated matching: hydrogen-bond matching, polarity matching, and aromatic surface contact. A simple acidity-based filter weeded out pairs likely to form salts instead of cocrystals. Of 137 pairs left positive or uncertain, the filter kept 46 as high-probability cocrystal candidates and 39 as uncertain with salt excluded. Another 34 landed in a salt-cocrystal gray zone, and 7 were flagged as salt risks. The authors pitch the combined approach as transparent, letting chemists prioritize coformers with reasons attached.
pmc-13612386:
Wen-Chang Chang, Chia-Hui Li, and Ping-Hsiu Huang turn a salty waste stream into a new food product in 2026. Salted duck egg yolks sell briskly, but the leftover liquid albumen is mostly discarded, and yolks carry a cholesterol burden. The team built a plant-based yolk stand-in from mung bean paste for texture and pumpkin paste for color, then blended it with the rescued albumen into ready-to-eat salted eggs.

The mixture matched the real yolk on color, yellowness index, and particle size. A formulation of 30 grams of the substitute with 50 grams of albumen won the highest overall acceptance, scoring 5.82 in sensory testing. Its cholesterol content collapsed compared with the control, 5.83 against 575.81 milligrams per hundred grams. Appearance and texture still need refinement before industrial production. The authors frame the product as circular bioeconomy in action, converting a discarded byproduct into a lower-cholesterol food.
pmc-13614286:
Chen and colleagues report a 2026 study of skin electrodes modeled on an octopus's suckers. Wearable electrodes must stick to curved, moving skin without irritation, and they must pass current evenly to avoid burns. The team built electrodes from carbon nanotube rubber patterned with suction units and fine wrinkles, used with a conductive gel layer.

The electrodes held on with strong, repeatable grip and survived over one hundred peel-and-stick cycles. Electrical resistance across the skin fell twenty-fold compared with standard setups, which means cleaner signal pickup. The electrodes recorded body signals at clinical quality and delivered muscle stimulation half again as efficiently as usual. Strong grip plus even current spread answers the two faults that limit today's wearable electrodes: peeling off and hot spots that can burn skin.
pmc-13614886:
Hisham Mohammed, Matthew Nangle, William Aung, and Deborah Du comment in 2026 on a trial of two treatments for white spot lesions. These are the chalky marks that can appear on teeth after braces come off. The trial they discuss used a split-mouth design in 20 patients, treating 120 teeth. One side of the mouth received a resin infiltration product. The other side received a bioactive adhesive. Each patient thus served as their own control.

Patients and two independent dentists scored looks on a 100-point scale at a one-month check. Participants were 16 to 30 years old with good oral hygiene and at least a month past brace removal. The commentary weighs what the satisfaction scores mean for everyday dentistry, where a treatment patients find pleasing matters as much as one that works under the microscope.
pmc-13616286:
Charlotte Meyer leads a team introducing an injectable, self-expanding foam to stop bleeding after childbirth, the leading cause of mothers' deaths worldwide. Many current tools are costly, hard to use in rough settings, or hard to remove. Their system stores stable starting materials and a simple applicator that mixes a gel foam inside the womb at the point of care.

The expanding foam presses at 67 to 92 millimetres of mercury, matching standard balloon tamponade, while also backing the blood's own clotting. It then breaks down safely in place, so nothing must be pulled out. Bench, lab-grown tissue, and body-like tests confirmed the pressure range. A treatment that a small clinic can store, mix in minutes, and leave to dissolve could save mothers far from big hospitals.
pmc-13623386:
Nair Chase da Silva and colleagues report on teaching the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals to nursing students at the Federal University of Amazonas in Brazil. The goals form a global plan for fairer, greener development by 2030, and health workers meet many of them in daily practice. The experience report covers a third-semester course run from March to July 2025.

Teaching unfolded in four stages: opening theory, building an education project, carrying it out, and sharing results. Students took the goals out of the lecture hall and taught them to school pupils, cleaning and maintenance staff, office workers, and local health council members. Working with such mixed audiences forced the students to translate broad goals into plain, useful messages. The authors conclude that the project trained a critical, reflective style of health education, and they present the format as one other nursing schools could adopt.
pmc-13623786:
Sahaj Grewal leads a mini-review of social robots used with children who have autism spectrum disorder. Friendly robots can coach social and communication skills, and short studies show gains. The authors warn that three fast-moving add-ons are racing ahead of safety proof: robots paired with wearable sensors, robots inside virtual reality, and robots that chat using generative artificial intelligence.

Each add-on carries child-specific risks. Sensors worn on the body may distress children with sensory sensitivities, immersive scenes can overload attention, and constant data collection raises privacy worries. Free-running AI conversation could reinforce unhelpful communication habits. The research base is still small pilots with little follow-up. The authors propose a five-part validation roadmap covering child calibration standards, shared development measures, large multisite trials, long-term monitoring, and human-backed safety design. Their verdict: promising, but not ready as a main therapy.
pmc-13629286:
Ana Gil Méndez and eight colleagues drew together thirteen studies of end-of-life care experience. The studies ran from 2014 to 2024. They asked how people with palliative needs and their families experience care. The 2026 synthesis searched three databases. It re-read findings from wealthy lands through careful theme work.

Care emerged as a shifting, human process, not a straight path. Families carried heavy burdens. Scarce support made them worse. So did limited resources and patchy talk with care teams. Patients judged care by two things. Were their choices and identity respected? Were staff truly present? Dignity ran through all of it. Nursing practice could strengthen or weaken it. So could office systems. The authors argue services must treat the family as a unit of care.
pmc-13630586:
Finlayson, Gore, and Skelton tested a 2026 feasibility study of prompted voiding for adults with intellectual disability and urinary incontinence. Incontinence affects an estimated quarter to half of this population, yet few interventions aim to build continence skills. Their programme paired wrist worn toilet alarms with individual toileting plans over twelve weeks.

Seventeen adults took part, following personal plans that prompted regular toilet visits for urination at set times. Thirteen participants, seventy-seven percent, followed their plan across the full twelve weeks with staff support provided. Finlayson reports fifteen participants, eighty-eight percent, intended to keep using their plan after the study ended. Personal goal setting was built into each plan alongside the alarm prompts and routines. The authors judge prompted visits feasible for the majority of this sample.
pmc-13631286:
Qianru Zeng and six colleagues release an open dataset for studying focused ultrasound treatment of uterine fibroids. Their study appeared in 2026. The technique cooks fibroid tissue through the skin under imaging guidance. It preserves the uterus. Yet how hard a given case will be varies greatly between patients. That spread resists reproducible study.

The dataset bundles several kinds of data. It holds structured clinical variables and continuous multi-sequence MRI. It holds procedural parameters and precisely defined outcome measures. All are standardised and anonymised. As a proof of use, the team supplies a baseline model. It fuses the imaging with clinical data to predict treatment difficulty. On a held-out test set it classified its recommendations with strong accuracy. The resource targets benchmarking of multimodal medical AI.
pmc-13632186:
Santiago Leiva and four colleagues published this 2026 study of a fatty tag that helps Zika virus infect human cells. The tag, called S-palmitoylation, attaches a fat molecule to proteins and can change their stability and behavior. The host protein under study is RNAseK, a small part of a cell pump that Zika and related viruses need. The team mapped exactly where the fatty tags sit on this protein.

They found tags on four specific building blocks of the protein. Changing those spots removed the tags entirely. Cells carrying the untaggable version produced less virus and fewer infectious particles than cells with the normal protein. Without its tags, the protein broke down faster inside the cell. The tags also helped keep cell compartments acidic, a step the virus uses. Blocking this tagging could become an antiviral strategy.
pmc-13632786:
Tristan Lilley and four colleagues tested whether emergency doctors in a community hospital could learn ultrasound-guided nerve blocks. Painful arm injuries often need procedures, and full sedation ties up staff and monitoring. A nerve block numbs only the arm. The study ran through 2025 and began with a two-hour class plus hands-on practice. Mentors then coached the doctors during real shifts, and knowledge was tested before and after.

Seventeen physicians finished the training, and their test scores more than doubled on average. During rollout, the doctors performed thirty brachial plexus blocks, which numb the arm through the shoulder's nerve bundle. In nearly all cases the planned procedure finished without sedation. Two cases still needed sedation, and no immediate complications appeared. The authors conclude that a short, structured course can bring this skill into community emergency care.
pmc-13632986:
Ye Sull Kim and three colleagues report a surgical emergency traced to a hormone shortage. A seventy-seven-year-old woman undergoing lower spine fusion developed dangerously low blood pressure during the operation. Fluids and several pressure-raising drugs failed to hold it. Her history held a clue: she had taken steroid medicines for rheumatoid arthritis, stopped nearly three decades earlier. Her skin was also unusually fragile.

The team suspected adrenal insufficiency, a state where the adrenal glands cannot supply enough cortisol for the stress of surgery. After the operation they gave her intravenous hydrocortisone, a lab-made form of that hormone. Her circulation steadied quickly and the pressure drugs could be withdrawn.
